domains.name: Active Directory Security
domains.tagline: Map, audit, and score Active Directory attack paths — graph enumeration, LDAP/ADSI querying, Kerberos/NTLM protocol tooling, legacy CVE PoCs, GPO/ACL abuse, credential-exposure testing, and risk health checks — for authorized assessments and blue-team defense.

tools.name: SharpHound
tools.desc: C# collector for BloodHound CE that runs on a domain-joined Windows host and exports users, groups, sessions, local admins, ACLs, GPOs, trusts and more via LDAP and SMB — the dataset the whole graph is built from.
tools.when: Authorized collection from a domain-joined host with valid credentials; feed the produced zip into BloodHound CE for graph analysis.
tools.install: Download the SharpHound CE collector from the BloodHound CE UI (Settings → Download Collectors) or the SpecterOps release page

tools.name: BloodHound.py
tools.desc: Python/Impacket ingestor that collects users, groups, trusts, ACLs, sessions, and local admins from Linux using only credentials — no Windows host or SharpHound binary required.
tools.when: When you need BloodHound data for an authorized scope but only hold a Linux foothold or domain credentials.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/dirkjanm/BloodHound.py && pip install -r requirements.txt (or the bloodhound-ce fork's CLI)

tools.name: BloodHound CE
tools.desc: Current-generation attack-path engine: ingests SharpHound data into Neo4j and reveals how users, groups, computers, sessions, GPOs, ACLs, trusts, and ADCS enrollments chain into paths to Domain Admin, including ADCS, NTLM, and delegation abuse conditions.
tools.when: The core analysis step after collection: visualize and triage which abusable identity relationships are the shortest paths to Tier-0 in your own estate.
tools.install: curl -L https://ghst.ly/BHCE-QS | bash (official CE quickstart, or the Docker Compose deployment from the docs)

tools.name: PlumHound
tools.desc: Wraps BloodHound's Neo4j Cypher backend into repeatable HTML reports and task lists; surfaces the busiest paths to Domain Admin and which relationship to break to sever a given path.
tools.when: Turn collected BloodHound data into operations-ready findings for blue/purple-team remediation planning and scheduled reporting.

tools.name: Adalanche
tools.desc: Standalone attack-graph visualizer from lkarlslund that collects and graph-explores who is *really* Domain Admin, rebuilding the effective reachability without a Neo4j stack.
tools.when: A lighter-weight second opinion alongside BloodHound in labs or quick scoping when you want immediate graph answers without standing up the full CE stack.
tools.install: Download the release binary and run the built-in collector against your AD read credentials or an existing dump

tools.name: adPEAS
tools.desc: Active-Directory-flavored PEAS: a PowerShell sweep that checklists misconfigurations across users, groups, GPOs, ACLs, Kerberos, and delegation from a single domain-joined run.
tools.when: Fast, readable AD hygiene sweep during authorized testing or internal audits when you want a findings checklist before deeper graph work.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/ajm4n/adPEAS && run adPEAS.ps1 from an authenticated domain session

tools.name: Purple Knight
tools.desc: Free commercial scoring (Semperis) that rates hybrid AD, Entra ID, and Okta estates against 150+ indicators of exposure and compromise, with MITRE ATT&CK mapping and prioritized guidance.
tools.when: Complement PingCastle when you also manage Entra ID or Okta and want an easy scorecard plus IoC checks over the hybrid estate.
tools.install: Download the Windows agent from https://www.semperis.com/purple-knight/ (free registration required)

tools.name: ldapsearch
tools.desc: OpenLDAP's ubiquitous CLI for anonymous and authenticated LDAP queries — users, groups, computers, GPOs, ACLs, and schema, filterable on any attribute.
tools.when: The first read-only look at any authorized directory: quick non-invasive enumeration and attribute mining that touches nothing on disk.

tools.name: ADFind
tools.desc: Joeware's battle-tested Windows LDAP search tool with terser output and built-in switches for common ADC, trust, PSO, and password-policy queries.
tools.when: Scripted one-line AD queries from Windows during audits where switch-friendly output beats raw LDIF.

tools.name: windapsearch
tools.desc: Python LDAP enumerator tuned for penetration workflow: dumps domain users with their group memberships, computers, privileged groups, and more from a single credential.
tools.when: Fast user/group enumeration during authorized testing when you want structured output instead of hand-rolled ldapsearch filters.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/ropnop/windapsearch && pip install -r requirements.txt

tools.name: ldapdomaindump
tools.desc: Dumps the entire domain object surface — groups, users, computers, GPOs, DNS zones, trusts, and shares — to browesable grep-friendly files using just domain credentials.
tools.when: Baseline full-directory export during authorized engagements for later offline review and scripted analysis.

tools.name: Active Directory Explorer (AD Explorer)
tools.desc: Sysinternals viewer that snapshots and browsably compares the full AD database — including every security descriptor and ACL — with hex views of attribute values.
tools.when: Interactive ACL/attribute forensics and before-after comparison of changes during an authorized assessment or blue-team review.
tools.install: Download AD Explorer from the Microsoft Sysinternals page (https://learn.microsoft.com/sysinternals/downloads/adexplorer)

tools.name: ADSI Edit (MMC)
tools.desc: Microsoft's built-in snap-in for direct read/write access to every AD object and attribute, including configuration and schema partitions.
tools.when: Point-and-click verification of specific attribute values and ACLs during audits without writing scripts.
tools.install: Add via 'Turn Windows features on or off' → AD DS and AD LDS Tools (native on domain controllers)

tools.name: NetExec
tools.desc: The maintained successor to CrackMapExec: multi-protocol (SMB, LDAP, MSSQL, SSH, WinRM, RDP) credential validation that rapidly tests which identities work where, sprays passwords, and enumerates shares, users, sessions, domains, and password policy across a fleet.
tools.when: Fast credential-driven health-check across many hosts in one pass — including `nxc ldap` for user/policy enumeration — during authorized assessments.

tools.name: Rubeus
tools.desc: C# toolset for raw Kerberos interaction — ticket requests, passthe-ticket, overpass-the-hash, ticket forging, Kerberoasting, AS-REP roasting, and s4u delegation testing, compiled to run on Windows.
tools.when: Windows-side Kerberos validation: check which service accounts are Kerberoastable and how delegation and ticket caching expose lateral movement in your domain.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/GhostPack/Rubeus && dotnet build (or run a compiled release binary)

tools.name: Impacket GetUserSPNs
tools.desc: Impacket example script that requests TGS tickets for every registered SPN account and exports the encrypted segments in crackable hashcat/Hashcat format from Linux.
tools.when: Linux-side Kerberoasting with just domain credentials — pair the output with hashcat to prove weak service-account passwords in authorized tests.

tools.name: Impacket GetNPUsers
tools.desc: Impacket example script that requests pre-authentication-free AS-REPs for accounts with 'Do not require Kerberos pre-authentication' and exports crackable hash segments.
tools.when: Identify and prove weak passwords on accounts without Kerberos pre-auth during authorized audits from Linux.

tools.name: ASREPRoast
tools.desc: HarmJ0y's PowerShell toolkit that retrieves crackable hashes from KRB5 AS-REP responses for user enumeration and pre-auth-disabled account auditing.
tools.when: Windows-side AS-REP roasting when you are already in a network session and want the native PowerShell route.

tools.name: Impacket getTGT / getST
tools.desc: Impacket scripts that obtain TGTs (with password or NT hash via AES/RC4) and service tickets via S4U2Self/S4U2Proxy, enabling constrained-delegation and resource-based-delegation validation from Linux.
tools.when: Prove unconstrained/constrained/resource-based delegation abuse paths in authorized tests without any Windows-side pieces.

tools.name: kekeo
tools.desc: Gentilkiwi's Kerberos suite for ticket generation, renewal, and fabrication (including golden/silver tickets and s4u abuse) as a lighter companion to Mimikatz.
tools.when: Windows-native ticket forging and delegation testing where you want a purpose-built alternative to the C# tooling.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/gentilkiwi/kekeo && build with Visual Studio (binaries under x64/Release)

tools.name: Kerbrute
tools.desc: Go tool that validates AD usernames and tests passwords through Kerberos AS-REQ/AS-REP exchanges; its userenum mode never triggers account lockout, while passwordspray/bruteforce do and are meant for policy-aware testing.
tools.when: Discover which candidate usernames actually exist during recon, and safely prove a single reused weak password across a user list you monitor in your own logs.

tools.name: DomainPasswordSpray
tools.desc: Dafthack's PowerShell sprayer that gathers the user list from AD, checks the domain lockout policy, and tests one password per user (or a small set) with delay controls to stay under thresholds.
tools.when: Lockout-safe password-spray audit of your own domain when you need built-in policy-awareness and randomized delays.

tools.name: Responder
tools.desc: The reference LLMNR/NBT-NS/mDNS poisoner and SMB/HTTP/LDAP rogue-server that captures NetNTLMv2 challenges for cracking or relay in lab and authorized bipedal-spook-and-serve testing.
tools.when: Confirm whether name resolution poisoned traffic and NTLM challenge responses are being accepted on your own lab network.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/lgandx/Responder && sudo python3 Responder.py -I eth0

tools.name: mitm6
tools.desc: IPv6 DNS poisoning tool (by the PetitPotam author) that answers DHCPv6/RA traffic to route a victim's updates to an attacker-controlled DNS, enabling WPAD or LDAP relay chains.
tools.when: IPv6-first poisoning in lab environments to demonstrate why IPv6 without mitigations is a relay avenue.

tools.name: Inveigh
tools.desc: Kevin-Robertson's Windows PowerShell/C# LLMNR/NBT-NS/mDNS/SMBv1 responder and NTLMv1/v2 challenge-capturer with Console and Web GUI views.
tools.when: Windows-native poisoning lab where you want a pure-PowerShell or compiled alternative to the Linux Responder.

tools.name: Impacket ntlmrelayx
tools.desc: Impacket's NTLM relay server that forwards captured NetNTLM challenges to SMB, LDAP(S), HTTP(S), and MSSQL targets, with built-in modules for dumping SAM, creating users, and targeting printers (CVE-2019-1040 MIC-removal support).
tools.when: In a controlled lab, relay an intercepted challenge to an authorized target to prove what NTLM-signing-off and relay protections are really enforcing.

tools.name: printerbug.py
tools.desc: Decoder-it's DCERPC-only printerbug.py that triggers the MS-RPRN printer bug to coerce a host into authenticating to your listener — the cornerstone of unconstrained/relay abuse chains.
tools.when: Coerce an authorized target machine account to authenticate to your relay/responder in lab environments for relay and delegation abuse scenarios.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/decoder-it/printerbugnew && python3 printerbug.py domain/user:pass@target attacker_ip

tools.name: SpoolSample
tools.desc: The original MS-RPRN spoolsv.exe abuse PoC that forces a target to authenticate back to you, historically tuned for unconstrained delegation attacks.
tools.when: Lab-only coercion lab where you want the original Windows-side compiled spooler-sampler reference implementation.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/leechristensen/SpoolSample && build with Visual Studio

categories.name: Legacy Attack Labs (PoC repos — lab only)

tools.name: Zerologon PoC (CVE-2020-1472)
tools.desc: Dirkjanm's canonical PoC for the Zerologon Netlogon cryptographic bypass that resets a DC machine-account password to empty and allows Domain-Admin takeover.
tools.when: Practice reproducing a fully-patched-against critical flaw in an isolated lab domain controller only; restore passwords immediately as in dirkjanm's reinstall/restore flow.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/dirkjanm/CVE-2020-1472 && pip3 install -r requirements.txt (lab VMs only)

tools.name: PetitPotam
tools.desc: EFS-prone authentication coercion PoC (CVE-2021-36942) that forces a Windows host to authenticate to your listener via the Encrypting File System RPC — enabling relay to LDAP-based DC-auth abuse.
tools.when: Lab demonstrations of EFS-based coercion and NTLM relay to LDAP(S) signing; SMB signing and LDAP channel-binding mitigations should be validated as the control.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/topotam/PetitPotam && python3 PetitPotam.py attacker_ip target (lab only)

tools.name: smbclient (NTLMv1 dialect)
tools.desc: Samba's authenticated SMB client whose `-m NT1` mode forces the legacy NTLMv1/RC4 dialect, making it a quick probe for whether a host still accepts NTLMv1.
tools.when: Lab-only check that a test host rejects NTLMv1 (LanMan-compat) as configured, or proving a downgrade lane in an isolated test environment.

tools.name: ADACLScanner
tools.desc: the SysArc ADACL scanner that reports dangerous ACL entries — GenericAll/WriteDacl/WriteOwner/ForceChangePassword — across domain, OUs, groups, and users in readable HTML.
tools.when: Read-only ACL risk sweep of your own domain to find object-owner and self-abuse-style issues before an attacker graphs them.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/canix1/ADACLScanner && .\ADACLScan.ps1 from a domain-joined Windows host

tools.name: Impacket dacledit
tools.desc: Impacket example script that leverages a control-established object ace (WriteDACL/WriteOwner/GenericAll) to edit target ACLs — including adding a full-control ACE for the attacker.
tools.when: Step through shelf ACL-abuse chains in a lab — the standard 'I own the ACE, so I own this object' proof step.

tools.name: SharpGPOAbuse
tools.desc: C# tool that edits GPO DACLs you already control to add immediate scheduled tasks, services, or registry changes — the standard Writeable-GPO machine-takeover primitive (kept alive by the ReversecLabs mirror).
tools.when: Demonstrate the impact of writable GPOs in authorized tests once a user holds a GPO-modify privilege; roll back the GPO after testing.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/ReversecLabs/SharpGPOAbuse && dotnet build (or run a compiled release binary)

tools.name: pyGPOAbuse
tools.desc: Hackndo's Python port that adds an immediate scheduled task to a writable GPO from Linux, mirroring SharpGPOAbuse without a Windows binary.
tools.when: GPO-edit proof from a Linux foothold during authorized multi-step chain construction in labs.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/Hackndo/pyGPOAbuse && python3 gpoabuse.py -d domain -u user -p pass ...

tools.name: Mimikatz
tools.desc: The canonical Windows credential tool: `sekurlsa` extracts plaintext passwords, NTLM hashes, PINs, and Kerberos tickets from LSASS memory while `lsadump` covers SAM, LSA secrets, DCSync, and DCShadow.
tools.when: On an authorized host with local admin to prove whether LSASS-accessible credentials leak and whether protections like LSA Protection or Credential Guard actually hold.

tools.name: pypykatz
tools.desc: Pure-Python reimplementation of Mimikatz's sekurlsa that parses live LSASS memory or minidumps on any OS to recover NT hashes, plaintext credentials, Kerberos tickets, and DPAPI keys.
tools.when: Analyze an LSASS minidump from Linux during incident-response or assessment when you hold the dump rather than a live Windows host.

tools.name: lsassy
tools.desc: Python tool that remotely dumps LSASS (comsvcs, Procdump, nanodump, and more methods) over SMB/WMI from whole fleets and extracts credentials in place with pypykatz.
tools.when: When you hold admin on an authorized set of Windows hosts and want to audit logged-on credential exposure across the fleet without interactive sessions.

tools.name: Impacket secretsdump
tools.desc: Impacket's flagship script that remotely extracts SAM/LSA/DRSUAPI/NTDS passwords and hashes in mimikatz-compatible format over DCOM, registry, and hypothetical replication.
tools.when: The standard authorized way to audit password-hash hygiene on DCs and hosts from Linux — directory-replication rights permitting.

tools.name: PowerView
tools.desc: Pure-PowerShell AD enumerator (PowerSploit) turning LDAP into one-liner cmdlets for users, groups, computers, GPOs, ACLs, shares, and trust maps; also hunts which machines specific users log into.
tools.when: From a domain-joined PowerShell session when you need fast, scriptable situational awareness without dropping a binary on disk — and to see exactly what attackers enumerate first.

tools.name: PowerUp
tools.desc: PowerSploit module that audits a Windows host for common local privesc misconfigurations — unquoted service paths, writable service binaries, modifiable services, AlwaysInstallElevated — with abuse-ready detail.
tools.when: Local privilege-escalation audit of a single host during sanctioned testing or hardening a fleet that lacks LAPS and least-privilege discipline.

tools.name: LAPSToolkit
tools.desc: Leoloobeek's PowerShell suite that audits LAPS-deployed estates — enumerating computers with expired/missing passwords, readable LAPS attributes, and delegations that expose admin passwords.
tools.when: Verify LAPS coverage and that delegation groups can't read passwords, before attackers abuse unexpired or overly-broad LAPS delegation.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/leoloobeek/LAPSToolkit && .\LAPSToolkit.ps1 (Windows LAPS also ships as built-in AD/Entra policy tooling)

tools.name: PingCastle
tools.desc: Active Directory risk and maturity audit (by Netwrix) that scores a domain 0–100 across ~10 axes — accounts, ADCS, Kerberos, trusts, delegation, GPOs, infrastructure — with a CISO-ready HTML report via read-only healthcheck.
tools.when: The default first formal AD security assessment: minutes to run, zero writes, ideal as a recurring blue-team health check or engagement kickoff.
tools.install: Download standalone PingCastle.exe from https://github.com/netwrix/pingcastle/releases and run on a domain-joined Windows host (.NET 8)

tools.name: ADRecon
tools.desc: PowerShell tool that extracts a wide slice of AD state — users, groups, OUs, GPOs, trusts, ACLs, password policies, DNS zones, optionally LAPS/BitLocker keys and Kerberoastable SPNs — into a summary Excel workbook.
tools.when: Broad read-only documentation of an environment for audit reports; runs as an ordinary domain user and works from non-member hosts over LDAP.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/adrecon/ADRecon && .\ADRecon.ps1 on a Windows host

domains.name: Binary Exploitation & Reverse Engineering
domains.tagline: Debug, disassemble, decompile, and understand binaries — your own code, lab targets, and CTF challenges.

tools.name: Ghidra
tools.desc: Free software reverse-engineering suite with a GUI and a real decompiler that emits C-like pseudocode, plus a scriptable Python/Java API.
tools.when: Full static analysis of binaries you own or CTF challenges — the decompiler output reads far closer to source than raw disassembly.
tools.install: Download the release zip from the Ghidra releases page, unzip, and run ./ghidraRun

tools.name: IDA Free
tools.desc: Hex-Rays' freeware edition of IDA, a mature interactive disassembler with decompiler support for x86/x64/ARM and a plugin ecosystem.
tools.when: A free, officially supported disassembler when you prefer IDA's workflow for x86/x64 binaries over the Ghidra GUI.

tools.name: Binary Ninja
tools.desc: Commercial reverse-engineering platform with a modern Python API, cross-platform analysis, and both an interactive GUI and headless mode.
tools.when: Scriptable binary analysis with an expressive API, or when team licensing matches your lab workflow.

tools.name: radare2
tools.desc: Command-line reverse-engineering framework with built-in analyzer, disassembler, ESIL emulation, and scripting via r2pipe.
tools.when: Headless or scripted analysis, quick on-box triage, and when the whole analysis pipeline should live in one terminal tool.

tools.name: rizin
tools.desc: Actively maintained fork of radare2 aiming for a cleaner, better-tested codebase while staying command-compatible and offering rz-pipe bindings.
tools.when: Same CLI workflow as radare2 when you prefer the fork under active development for its language bindings and released packages.

tools.name: Cutter
tools.desc: Qt GUI built on the Rizin engine giving point-and-click disassembly, patching, control-flow graphs, and a decompiler view.
tools.when: Visual exploration and annotation of binaries without a terminal-heavy workflow.

tools.name: GhidraSnippets
tools.desc: Curated Python and Java snippets for the Ghidra scripting API covering common auto-analysis, function, and disassembly tasks.
tools.when: Steal working, tested Ghidra script patterns instead of re-deriving the API for each new analysis task.

tools.name: ghidra-scripts
tools.desc: Maintained collection of Ghidra Python scripts for pattern-based analysis, function identification, and decompiler querying.
tools.when: Drop-in automation scripts for reversing binaries or firmware in an iterative lab analysis session.

tools.name: r2ghidra
tools.desc: Plugin that embeds the Ghidra decompiler into radare2/rizin so terminal workflows gain C-like pseudocode output.
tools.when: Bring a decompiler view into your radare2/rizin session without switching to the Ghidra GUI.

tools.name: GDB
tools.desc: GNU debugger supporting breakpoints, watchpoints, register and memory inspection, and scripting for ELF, PE, and Mach-O binaries.
tools.when: The backbone of all dynamic work; run it plain for minimalism or host pwndbg/GEF on top of it.

tools.name: pwndbg
tools.desc: GDB plugin with exploit-focused conveniences: heap/stack views, ROP-gadget search, cyclic pattern generation, and prettier disassembly.
tools.when: CTF pwn challenges or reversing binaries you own when plain GDB layout gets too noisy.

tools.name: GEF
tools.desc: Dependency-light, single-script GDB plugin with heap visualizations, format-string helpers, and live memory introspection.
tools.when: A pwndbg-style workflow with almost zero setup beyond one curl command, on any GDB build.

tools.name: LLDB
tools.desc: LLVM's debugger, well integrated with clang-generated debug info and Mach-O, Swift, and Objective-C symbols.
tools.when: Analyzing Apple-platform binaries or anything built with the LLVM toolchain where GDB support lags.

tools.name: Frida
tools.desc: Dynamic instrumentation toolkit that injects JavaScript into a running process to hook functions and read live memory without recompiling.
tools.when: Trace calls, intercept functions, or inspect a live process — especially on targets where a traditional debugger struggles.

tools.name: strace / ltrace
tools.desc: Syscall and library-call tracers that log every system call (or libc call) a process makes, with arguments and timing.
tools.when: Map a binary's runtime behavior by watching the syscalls it issues during a controlled run on your host.

tools.name: QEMU
tools.desc: Full-system and user-mode emulator running and tracing binaries for foreign architectures, with a GDB remote stub.
tools.when: Execute and debug cross-architecture ELF (ARM, MIPS, PPC) from firmware or CTFs when no native hardware exists.

tools.name: Qiling
tools.desc: Advanced binary emulation framework that runs and instruments cross-architecture binaries inside a controlled Python sandbox.
tools.when: Automated, scripted emulation of cross-platform binaries with hooks, memory inspection, and reproducible lab runs.

tools.name: Unicorn
tools.desc: Lightweight CPU emulator framework exposing per-instruction hooks so you can emulate only the instruction flow you care about.
tools.when: Embed instruction-level emulation into your own analysis or fuzzing scripts for lab targets.

tools.name: pwntools
tools.desc: CTF pwn toolkit providing packing (p64/u64), ELF parsing, cyclic patterns, ROP-chain builders, and managed local/remote I/O.
tools.when: Prototype and test exploit behavior against binaries in a lab or CTF — the standard glue for the whole workflow.

tools.name: angr
tools.desc: Python binary analysis framework using symbolic/concolic execution to explore paths and solve constraints against a binary you control.
tools.when: Automated pathfinding — such as deriving inputs that satisfy checks — when manual reversing is too slow.

tools.name: ROPgadget
tools.desc: Scans binaries for return-oriented-programming gadgets and can dump the full gadget set or filter specific instructions.
tools.when: Collect usable ROP gadgets from a stripped binary you own before assembling a chain.

tools.name: Ropper
tools.desc: Python tool to inventory ROP gadgets and build chains from ELF, PE, and Mach-O binaries; powers gadget search inside pwndbg.
tools.when: Quick gadget inventory across multiple binary formats in a lab when auditing which sequences are constructible.

tools.name: one_gadget
tools.desc: Matches libc builds to single-address execve('/bin/sh') gadgets whose register constraints are simple to satisfy.
tools.when: You have a libc build in a lab or CTF and want short candidate gadget addresses before scripting the constraints.

tools.name: Z3
tools.desc: Microsoft's SMT solver used to solve constraints over bitvectors, powering automated deobfuscation and input recovery.
tools.when: Solve the arithmetic and bitvector equations that symbolic execution or manual analysis hands you.

tools.name: Speculator
tools.desc: IBM Research framework to analyze speculative-execution attacks (ret2spec/spectre class) and their mitigations across architectures.
tools.when: Academic-lab study of ret2spec-family microarchitectural attacks and how current mitigations cover them.

tools.name: Retbleed PoC
tools.desc: Research proof-of-concept from the ret2spec lineage demonstrating arbitrary speculative code execution via return instructions.
tools.when: Reproduce published speculative-execution research artifacts in a lab to measure the impact of mitigations.

tools.name: Capstone
tools.desc: Disassembly engine that decodes raw bytes into platform-pinned instructions for many architectures, usable from Python, C, and more.
tools.when: Programmatically decode instruction streams inside your own scripts, emulators, or plugin code.

tools.name: Keystone
tools.desc: Assembly engine that turns mnemonics into machine code at runtime, complementing Capstone for code generation.
tools.when: Assemble shellcode or encoding routines on the fly inside your own lab scripts and tooling.

tools.name: checksec
tools.desc: Bash/Python script that reads ELF headers and reports active mitigations: PIE, NX, canaries, RELRO, Fortify, and more.
tools.when: First move on any binary in a lab or CTF — establish the mitigation baseline before choosing deeper tooling.

tools.name: file
tools.desc: Identifies a file's type from magic bytes, including format and target architecture (e.g. ELF 64-bit x86-64).
tools.when: Instant triage of any unknown artifact to confirm what you are looking at before deeper analysis.

tools.name: strings
tools.desc: Prints printable character sequences from a binary, exposing embedded literals, format strings, and library references without executing it.
tools.when: Grab a quick inventory of interesting strings — prompts, /bin/sh, format specifiers — before disassembling.

tools.name: objdump / readelf
tools.desc: binutils disassembler and ELF reader providing symbol tables, sections, headers, dynamic imports, and per-arch disassembly.
tools.when: Zero-dependency static lookups — grep symbols, inspect section layout, or dump disassembly without a full RE suite.

tools.name: Diaphora
tools.desc: Binary diffing tool matching functions across two binaries and importing names and symbols, working with Ghidra, IDA, and Binary Ninja.
tools.when: Compare patched vs unpatched firmware or file versions to spot the instruction-level changes behind a fix.

domains.name: Command & Control Frameworks
domains.tagline: C2 / post-exploitation frameworks, communication profiles, payload & beacon kits, and infrastructure helpers — for authorized adversary simulation, C2-traffic detection testing, and lab post-exploitation.

tools.name: Sliver
tools.desc: Open-source cross-platform adversary-emulation framework (BishopFox); Go implants are dynamically compiled with per-binary encryption keys and support C2 over mTLS, WireGuard, HTTP(S), and DNS.
tools.when: Your default lab/red-team C2 when you want a framework blue teams can profile exhaustively without commercial licensing.

tools.name: Mythic
tools.desc: Collaborative, Docker-based post-exploitation platform whose core ships no agents; you install agent payload types (Apollo/.NET, Athena/Rust, and others) and C2 profiles as separate containers via mythic-cli and the Mythic scripting API.
tools.when: Long-running lab engagements needing a pluggable, community-vetted agent ecosystem, cross-team collaboration, and GraphQL/automation hooks for red-team reporting.

tools.name: Empire
tools.desc: BC-Security's maintained fork of PowerShell Empire: PowerShell, Python, and C# agents with HTTP, HTTPS, HTTP(S)-SMB, and WebSocket listeners plus a REST API that Starkiller builds on.
tools.when: Classic PowerShell-heavy post-exploitation tradecraft whose agent traffic pairs naturally with the Starkiller UI; still the reference for Empire-style stager patterns.

tools.name: Havoc
tools.desc: Modern malleable post-exploitation framework pairing a Qt client with a Go teamserver; the Demon agent speaks AES-encrypted HTTP(S)/SMB and uses indirect syscalls. Maintenance stopped — repo archived Feb 2026 — yet it stays a heavily studied, MITRE-tracked (S1229) traffic class.
tools.when: Lab and detection research against a well-documented post-exploitation stack (tunnel, AMSI/ETW patching, BOF/COFF loading) whose artifacts most EDRs now fingerprint.

tools.name: Merlin
tools.desc: Go-based post-exploitation server/agent pair communicating over HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, h2c, and HTTP/3 (QUIC) — a practical model for non-TLS and modern protocol beaconing.
tools.when: Lab tests of HTTP/2 and QUIC transport detection, since most defensive tuning focuses on plain HTTPS beacon patterns.

tools.name: Covenant
tools.desc: Collaborative .NET C2 with a browser UI whose Grunt implants are dynamically compiled C# — the canonical worked example of .NET post-exploitation patterns (in-memory loading, AMSI/ETW patching, SMB P2P). Effectively unmaintained since ~2021 (last push 2024); now a lab/museum reference and signature-rich detection target.
tools.when: Studying .NET post-exploitation design and beating on well-known signatures in the lab; treat it as a legacy framework, not for live operations.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/cobbr/Covenant && cd Covenant/Covenant && dotnet build -c Release

tools.name: Villain
tools.desc: High-level stage 0/1 C2 handler for many reverse-TCP and HoaxShell (HTTPS) shells, shipped with Windows/Linux payload templates, fileless scripting, and cross-instance session sharing.
tools.when: Quick-sided Kali lab work that needs concurrent shell handling and payload-template experimentation without standing up a full framework.

tools.name: PoshC2
tools.desc: Python-based C2 with PowerShell and C# tasking, impacket-driven implant generation, and in-memory staging — a lightweight, well-documented write-up of multi-listener C2 architecture.
tools.when: A small, quick-to-stand-up C2 for teaching listener/server concepts or comparing stager patterns against a mainstream framework.

tools.name: Metasploit Framework
tools.desc: Rapid7's framework in its C2 role: multi/handler listeners, staged Meterpreter/Python payloads, session and pivot management, plus the post-exploitation and exploit modules that hash-complete the ecosystem behind msfvenom.
tools.when: A lab C2/orchestrator when you want built-in listeners plus post-exploitation modules in one place; the baseline everyone's detection stack is tuned to.

tools.name: Cobalt Strike
tools.desc: Commercial threat-emulation platform (Fortra) and the de-facto reference C2; Malleable C2 profiles reshape HTTP(S)/DNS beacon traffic into the traffic shapes blue teams tune their detections around. Vetted licensing only: new licenses roughly $3.5k–$10k/user/yr, with cracked builds aggressively taken down.
tools.when: When you are an authorized red team that can buy it, or to study the beacon patterns that dominate C2 detection research.

tools.name: Starkiller
tools.desc: A community-built Electron UI over Empire's REST API: manage listeners, agents, modules, and credentials visually instead of via the cli client.
tools.when: Pair with Empire when a GUI makes listener/agent management and lab demos easier to follow.

tools.name: C2concealer
tools.desc: Red Siege's generator that crafts random, unique Malleable C2 profiles for Cobalt Strike and validates them by checking profile syntax against a reference server.
tools.when: Generate a fresh, randomized C2 profile per lab campaign so beacon traffic doesn't match known profile hashes.

tools.name: Malleable-C2-Randomizer
tools.desc: BluScreenofJeff's framework of profile-randomization scripts that shuffle URI paths, user-agents, and headers to defeat simple static signature matching.
tools.when: Lab experiments in yanking profile parts around and measuring how detection shifts between variants.

tools.name: pyMalleableC2
tools.desc: byt3bl33d3r's Python library that reads and rewrites Malleable C2 profile files programmatically, letting scripts tweak jitter, URIs, and headers in bulk.
tools.when: Deterministic profile transformation in scripts rather than hand-editing .profile files.

tools.name: rsmudge malleable-c2-profiles
tools.desc: Raphael Mudge's reference profile collection shipped alongside Cobalt Strike docs: the canonical .profile examples (amazon, gmail, outlook, etc.) that blue teams dissect to learn beacon shaping.
tools.when: Start from maintained, syntax-correct profiles when learning the Malleable C2 language and its transforms.

tools.name: threatexpress malleable-c2
tools.desc: TrustedSec's Malleable C2 profile and kit repo with sleep-jitter variants, AMSI/ETW patch examples, and profiles modeled on common user-agent traffic.
tools.when: Pick measurement-ready profiles with documented jitter/sleep tunables for detection lab comparisons.

tools.name: BC-SECURITY Malleable-C2-Profiles
tools.desc: Andy Hsu's curated profile set with editor/validator support and packaging guidance — a maintained alternative to the older collections.
tools.when: Structured, commented profiles for education and easy diffing against base beacon defaults.

tools.name: dnscat2
tools.desc: iagox86's DNS command-and-control tunnel: data rides inside DNS queries/responses (TXT/NS/CNAME/MX), by default plaintext unless you enable its built-in encryption.
tools.when: Proving DNS-based C2 in a lab where only DNS egress is allowed; watch the channel via passive-DNS correlation.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/iagox86/dnscat2.git && cd dnscat2/server && sudo gem install bundler && bundle install

tools.name: msfvenom
tools.desc: The payload generator inside Metasploit: raw, shellcode, and staged/stageless payloads for Windows, Linux, macOS, Android, and web platforms, with encoders and format outputs for every delivery stage.
tools.when: Authorized tests needing a payload in exactly the format your C2 staging (or a loader like Donut/ScareCrow) expects.
tools.install: apt install metasploit-framework  # then: msfvenom --list payloads

tools.name: Donut
tools.desc: Generates position-independent shellcode that stages .NET assemblies, PE files, and VBS/JScript entirely in memory, so a lab agent can be delivered without touching disk on the test host.
tools.when: Producing an in-memory delivery stage for a lab agent and observing how loaders that patch AMSI/ETW look from a defender's perspective.

tools.name: ScareCrow
tools.desc: Tylous's loader builder that wraps position-independent shellcode in benign-trusted formats (MSI, XLL, DLL sideload/renamed, HTA) using signed JScript/JS patterns for lab delivery testing.
tools.when: Lab research on how standard loaders hold up against modern EDR signatures — generate a loader and see what telemetry it leaves behind.

tools.name: CrossC2
tools.desc: Extension that generates cross-platform beacons for Cobalt Strike (Linux, macOS, Android/ARM, even ESXi) from a configured HTTPS listener, via genCrossC2 plus automatic Malleable C2 profile handling.
tools.when: Extending a Cobalt Strike lab to authorized non-Windows assets where stock Beacon cannot run, or studying cross-platform beacon metadata.
tools.install: Download genCrossC2 + CrossC2.cna from the GitHub release

tools.name: SILENTTRINITY
tools.desc: byt3bl33d3r's cross-platform post-exploitation C2 shell with a Python audit kit whose agents stage C# assemblies entirely in memory over HTTP — a reference for IronPython/C# and memory-only agent design.
tools.when: Studying memory-only C# stager architecture and the older 'Tasking the CLR' implant generation model in a lab.

tools.name: COFFLoader
tools.desc: TrustedSec's COFF (Common Object File Format)-in-memory loader that converts Cobalt Strike BOF object files into self-contained Windows executables and libraries, so BOFs run standalone.
tools.when: Run a library of lab BOFs (situational awareness, etc.) standalone, or turn BOFs into binaries that other tooling can invoke.

tools.name: CS-Situational-Awareness-BOF
tools.desc: TrustedSec's collection of Cobalt Strike BOFs for host situational awareness (enumeration, tokens, events) that doubles as a documented corpus of BOF/COFF development patterns.
tools.when: Lab practice: run battle-tested BOFs via COFFLoader or your C2 and study what beacon/BOF behavior defenders watch for.

tools.name: Ligolo-ng
tools.desc: Tunneling/pivoting tool that exposes a TUN interface and routes TCP/UDP through an agent over reverse TCP/TLS, reaching remote lab subnets without SOCKS/proxychains, with a web UI and autoroute since v0.8.
tools.when: Reaching the rest of an authorized test network from a C2 foothold — pivot activity blue teams should recognize and alert on.
tools.install: Download proxy & agent binaries from GitHub releases

tools.name: Chisel
tools.desc: Single-binary fast TCP/UDP tunnel carried over HTTP(S)/WebSocket (SSH-secured) with reverse port-forwarding and SOCKS — communication that reads as ordinary WebSocket/web traffic to defenders.
tools.when: Bridging egress-filtered lab segments to your C2, or tunnelling any service where the traffic should blend with normal HTTPS.

tools.name: cdncheck
tools.desc: ProjectDiscovery's CLI (with Go library and nuclei integration) that tags an IP/host as CDN, cloud, or WAF and can surface the true origin, mapping whether your C2 listeners sit behind hosted edge layers.
tools.when: Before fronting a C2 listener: know whether there's already a CDN/WAF in front of a host and whether the origin leaks elsewhere.

tools.name: cloudflared
tools.desc: Cloudflare Tunnel client: exposes a local listener through Cloudflare's edge (e.g. quick tunnels) so inbound C2/redirector traffic arrives via a CDN hop rather than your bare IP.
tools.when: Putting a lab C2 behind a legitimate edge service and validating that middlebox-only checks still detect your channel.

tools.name: gost
tools.desc: GO Simple Tunnel: multi-hop proxy chains (SOCKS5/HTTP/SSH/relay) with port forwarding, load balancing, and protocol obfuscation — a scriptable chaining engine for C2 redirector piping.
tools.when: Chain multiple redirectors/proxies on an authorized lab path and get per-hop logs while tuning traffic shapes.

tools.name: Stowaway
tools.desc: ph4ntonn's anti-detection multi-hop proxy for C2: agent mesh nodes support Socks5 and SSH forwarding with each hop adding a layer of encryption.
tools.when: Multi-hop proxy meshes in lab engagements where you want per-node encryption layers instead of plain port-forwarding.

tools.name: C2 Matrix
tools.desc: The community-maintained comparison of C2 frameworks: features, capabilities, listeners, transports, BOF support, and reporting across close to 100 frameworks, with a lab harness and Slingshot VM for testing them.
tools.when: Pick a C2 or compare implementation kits: one table to evaluate listeners, transports, and reporting before you install anything.

tools.name: MITRE ATT&CK
tools.desc: The authoritative knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques — read the C2-relevant techniques (T1071 Application Layer Protocol, T1573 Encrypted Channel) and the data sources defenders link back to them.
tools.when: Map which techniques your framework exercises and check the data sources you'll need to capture while testing.

tools.name: DetectionLab
tools.desc: Chris Long's Packer/Vagrant suite that builds a Windows domain pre-loaded with Sysmon, WEF, osquery, and Splunk plus hardened logging defaults (no longer actively maintained since 2023, but still widely used).
tools.when: Stand up an instrumented AD lab to show blue teams exactly what your C2 traffic emits across endpoints and network.

domains.name: Cryptography Toolkit & Cryptoanalysis
domains.tagline: Decode/encode data, identify encodings, and break weak ciphers and RSA on materials you own: CTF crypto, historical ciphers, and flawed implementations. Password recovery lives in 'passwords'.

tools.name: CyberChef
tools.desc: GCHQ's browser 'Cyber Swiss Army Knife': 480+ chainable operations for decoding/encoding (Base64, hex, URL, Rot13), hashing, XOR and compression, plus the Magic operation that auto-detects and unwraps multi-layer encodings. Entirely client-side, zero install.
tools.when: First stop for any blob, hex dump or encoded string: click the Magic icon to auto-decode, then drag operations to peel off the layers you identify.

tools.name: CyberChef (self-hosted)
tools.desc: The same GCHQ app run from the official pre-built Docker image (or a downloadable static build) so every operation executes inside your own network with no outbound traffic.
tools.when: Offline, air-gapped or VM work where the input must never leave your machine - identical recipes and Magic, no internet dependency after the image pull.

tools.name: hashID
tools.desc: Python 3 tool identifying 220+ hash types by regex and reporting the matching hashcat mode (-m) and John format (-j) for each candidate, replacing the outdated hash-identifier.
tools.when: Any recovered hash before cracking: feed it the value, note the top algorithm plus its hashcat/John mode, then jump to the passwords domain.

tools.name: file (libmagic)
tools.desc: The standard `file` command built on libmagic: identifies thousands of file types from magic bytes, from PEM/DER keys and PKCS#12 bundles to plaintext/uncompressed containers.
tools.when: Determine what a raw blob actually is before decoding — distinguish a DER key, a zlib stream, a base64 text, or a random-looking ciphertext file.
tools.install: sudo apt install file && file suspect.bin

tools.name: dCode
tools.desc: Web reference hosting hundreds of small solvers for classical schemes (Caesar, Vigenère, Enigma, ADFGVX, Playfair...) plus a Cipher Identifier that scores which of 300+ ciphers a message fits via n-gram and index-of-coincidence analysis.
tools.when: CTF or challenge text in a historical cipher: paste it into the Cipher Identifier for a ranked guess, then open the matching solver for the plaintext.

tools.name: CrypTool
tools.desc: Legacy university/open-source cryptology suite (CrypTool 2.1 + JCrypTool) for experimenting with classical ciphers (Caesar, Vigenère, Enigma, ADFGVX) and their built-in automated cryptanalysis on paste-in text.
tools.when: Interactive analysis of historical substitution/transposition ciphers or learning the attack against a classical scheme on your own text, where a GUI beats hand-rolled scripts.

tools.name: xortool
tools.desc: Python tool for multi-byte XOR cipher analysis: guesses key length via equality-based scoring, recovers key bytes from the most frequent plaintext character, with charset filtering and known-plaintext (-p) options to confirm candidates.
tools.when: Ciphertext is XOR-encoded with an unknown repeating key - feed the raw bytes, let it rank key lengths, then solve for the right length and character.

tools.name: cribdrag
tools.desc: Interactive crib-dragging script for stream-cipher keystream reuse: XOR two ciphertexts (or against a guessed crib) and step through candidate plaintext substrings interactively.
tools.when: Two ciphertexts share a one-time pad key, or a stream cipher reuses its keystream — drag a known plaintext word to recover the keystream and decrypt the rest by hand.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/SpiderLabs/cribdrag && python2 cribdrag.py encrypted.hex

tools.name: PadBuster
tools.desc: Perl script automating padding-oracle attacks: decrypts arbitrary CBC ciphertext, encrypts arbitrary plaintext, and probes an endpoint to fingerprint the oracle that leaks padding validity.
tools.when: A web app returns distinguishable error codes on bad PKCS#7 padding and the app is yours to test — recover and forge CBC messages without the key.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/GDSSecurity/PadBuster && cd PadBuster && perl padBuster.pl https://app.example/decrypt -encoding 0

tools.name: hash_extender
tools.desc: Ron Bowes' C tool for the hash length-extension attack on MD4/MD5/RIPEMD-160/SHA-0/SHA-1/SHA-256/SHA-512/Whirlpool: given a secret-prefix hash, forges a valid hash for appended data without knowing the secret, iterating guessed secret lengths.
tools.when: A service signs 'secret || message' with a Merkle-Damgård hash (CTF or your own app) and you can control appended data - produce the new payload+signature pair the server accepts.

tools.name: Hashcat
tools.desc: GPU/CPU password cracker with 300+ attack modes and thousands of hash types; the full profile and masking/rule tooling live in the passwords domain. Linked here so crypto-work can confirm hash formats and modes.
tools.when: A recovered hash or extracted TGS ticket needs cracking; pair the hashcat mode from hashID with a rule/mask attack after confirming the target algorithm.
tools.install: sudo apt install hashcat && hashcat -m 1000 ntlm.hash rockyou.txt

tools.name: John the Ripper
tools.desc: CPU-first cracker (jumbo build) covering hundreds of hash formats including magic formats like Kerberoast/AS-REP tickets and encrypted OpenSSL/archive containers; full profile lives in the passwords domain.
tools.when: Cracking on CPU with the jumbo format set, or when a target format (gpg, ssh, rakefile) is only handled by John rather than Hashcat.
tools.install: sudo apt install john && john --wordlist=rockyou.txt hashes.txt

tools.name: RsaCtfTool
tools.desc: Python RSA multi-attack harness (60+ attacks): weak-key factorization (Fermat, Pollard rho, ECM, SIQS), lattice attacks on small d (Wiener, Boneh-Durfee), Hastad broadcast, shared-factor pools, ROCA, past-CTF/gimmick primes and Factordb integration; recovers the private key and/or decrypts files.
tools.when: Given a weak RSA public key and ciphertext (CTF, lab, keys you own) without knowing the weakness - run the default attack set, then target the specific winning attack.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/RsaCtfTool/RsaCtfTool && cd RsaCtfTool && pip3 install -r requirements.txt

tools.name: SageMath
tools.desc: Open-source mathematics system with built-in number theory used for RSA cryptanalysis: lattice basis reduction (LLL), Pollard p-1/p-ρ, discrete log, small-roots (Coppersmith), and private-key reconstruction from recovered parameters.
tools.when: When no one-shot tool covers the attack — hand-build a lattice basis, solve a modular equation, or derive d from partial parameters with a few lines of Sage.

tools.name: FactorDB
tools.desc: Online database of integer factorizations with a plain API (https://factordb.com/api?query=N) that returns a number's status (FF/C/PRP) and known factors, including factorized prime records.
tools.when: A modulus (or any big integer) may already be factored in the public corpus - script the API from curl; RsaCtfTool queries it automatically via --attack factordb.

tools.name: yafu
tools.desc: Automated integer-factoring command-line utility chaining trial division, Pollard, ECM, SIQS, and GNFS on numbers up to ~200 digits, with prebuilt Windows binaries and clean `factor(n)` syntax.
tools.when: A 256–1024-bit modulus you own that defeats online lookup — run `yafu 'factor(n)'` and let it auto-select the fastest factoring stage.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/bbuhrow/yafu && cd yafu && make yafu

tools.name: msieve
tools.desc: Quadratic-sieve and number-field-sieve library/demo for factoring integers up to ~120 digits (QS) and larger via GNFS, the classic engine behind CTF modulus-factorization writeups.
tools.when: Factoring tasks where yafu stalls or where you want the standalone QS/NFS engine; typically invoked from a script that feeds candidates one at a time.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/radii/msieve && cd msieve && make

tools.name: rsatool
tools.desc: Small Python tool that reconstructs the full RSA key set (n, e, d, p, q, CRT params) and writes an OpenSSL-compatible PEM/DER private key from just (p, q) or (n, d), including n+dp-based factoring.
tools.when: After any attack yields p and q (or n+d): turn recovered parameters into a real private key file you can decrypt with, instead of rolling the CRT math by hand.
tools.install: wget -O rsatool.py https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ius/rsatool/master/rsatool.py && pip3 install gmpy2 pyasn1

tools.name: testssl.sh
tools.desc: Bash TLS cipher/protocol testing on any port: enumerates protocols and cipher suites, flags weaknesses (BEAST, heartbleed, ROBOT, TLS1.0/1.1, weak DHE), checks client simulation, and emits JSON/CSV/HTML.
tools.when: Full TLS configuration audit of an endpoint you own; the default single-line invocation yields findings graded vulnerable/weak/OK you can drop straight into a report.

tools.name: sslscan
tools.desc: Fast TLS cipher scanner built on a rewritten backend that detects SSLv2/SSLv3 and TLSv1.3 regardless of linked OpenSSL, flags CBC (POODLE), 3DES, RC4, NULL/weak ciphers, and weak DHE keys, with XML output.
tools.when: A quick closed-port cipher enumeration or legacy-protocol check where you want one line per cipher and color-coded strength annotations.
tools.install: sudo apt install sslscan && sslscan example.com:443

tools.name: SSLyze
tools.desc: Python TLS scanning library/CLI: cert, cipher suite, and elliptic-curve analysis plus known-attack checks (Heartbleed, ROBOT, CCS injection), with Mozilla-config comparison and JSON output for automation.
tools.when: Automated TLS gate in CI/CD or bulk scanning of many hosts; exit code flips on Mozilla 'intermediate' non-compliance, so it doubles as a regression check.
tools.install: pip3 install sslyze && python3 -m sslyze example.com

tools.name: OpenSSL
tools.desc: The de-facto CLI crypto Swiss-army knife: AES/ChaCha20/RSA/ECDSA encryption and decryption, key generation and parsing (PEM/DER), X.509 cert/genrsa/inspect, digests, and CMS/PKCS#7 envelopes in one command.
tools.when: Quick symmetric or asymmetric encrypt/decrypt of your files, dumping or inspecting keys and certificates, and validating algorithm behavior against a standards reference implementation.

tools.name: GnuPG
tools.desc: GNU Privacy Guard: full OpenPGP implementation for asymmetric and symmetric encryption, signing/verification, keyring management, and export/import interop with PGP e-mail workflows.
tools.when: Working with .gpg/PGP messages or OpenPGP keys where the PGP container format - not raw OpenSSL cipher - is expected.

tools.name: age
tools.desc: Simple, modern, audited file encryption (X25519, optional passphrase; hybrid post-quantum ML-KEM-768 since v1.3) with small explicit keys, no configuration and UNIX-style composability; interoperable Rust port is 'rage'.
tools.when: Modern default for encrypting archives/files you own end-to-end (backups, secrets transfer) when you want minimal friction and small keys over legacy OpenPGP keyrings.

tools.name: GnuTLS certtool
tools.desc: CLI from the GnuTLS project for X.509 certificate/key generation, PKCS#12 bundles, certificate and private-key inspection, and PKCS#11 token operations through a single binary.
tools.when: Generating or inspecting certificates and PKCS#12 files with readable options, or poking at PKCS#11 tokens, when OpenSSL's flag surface gets in the way.

domains.name: Exploitation & Payload Generation
domains.tagline: Build, source, and deliver exploits and payloads against systems you own or are authorized to test.

tools.name: Metasploit Framework
tools.desc: Modular exploitation framework packaging thousands of exploit, auxiliary, and post-exploitation modules behind one console, kept current by Rapid7.
tools.when: Your first stop when a known CVE has a module: select the target, pick the module, review its options, and run it against a lab host you control.

tools.name: Empire
tools.desc: Python-based post-exploitation and red-team framework (actively maintained fork of PowerShell Empire) with cross-platform agents and its own payload generation.
tools.when: Authorized engagements and labs when you want a Python-native agent framework rather than a Ruby-based console, especially across Windows targets.

tools.name: pwntools
tools.desc: Python exploit-development library that assembles shellcode, packs addresses, and interacts with local processes and sockets to make PoCs repeatable.
tools.when: Write a reliable exploit script (buffer overflow, format string) for a vulnerable binary you own, with assembly and encoding helpers built in.

tools.name: SearchSploit
tools.desc: Offline command-line search into a local copy of the Exploit-DB archive, filtering by platform and port without touching the network.
tools.when: Search for public PoCs before building anything CVE-specific, even on an air-gapped Kali box.

tools.name: Exploit-DB (web)
tools.desc: Web interface to the same OffSec archive, adding full-text search, verified-PoC badges, and paper writeups behind each entry.
tools.when: Browse recent additions and read the writeup behind a PoC when the offline search gives you just a filename.

tools.name: PoC-in-GitHub
tools.desc: Automatically collected index of GitHub PoC repositories mapped per CVE, keeping a browsable per-vulnerability view of public exploit code.
tools.when: Find whether real exploit code exists for a CVE and jump straight to the repository that hosts it.

tools.name: Trickest CVE
tools.desc: Community-maintained mapping of CVEs to their GitHub PoC repositories, describing each with ready-to-run command snippets.
tools.when: Cross-check CVE-to-PoC links when a tracker site gives you a CVE but not the exploit repo.

tools.name: CVE.org
tools.desc: Authoritative CVE record catalog maintained by the CVE Program, confirming IDs, affected products, and references before you hunt for exploit code.
tools.when: Validate which products and versions a CVE identifier really covers before searching for a matching PoC.

tools.name: NVD
tools.desc: NIST vulnerability database attaching CVSS scores, CPE identifiers, and affected-version ranges to every CVE.
tools.when: Pin down exploitability metrics and version ranges for a CVE during remediation planning or PoC triage.

tools.name: GitHub Advisory Database
tools.desc: GitHub Sourced advisories (GHSA) with affected ranges, patched versions, and a machine-readable API for ecosystem packages.
tools.when: Cross-reference advisory data against a package manager ecosystem when a CVE only has partial vendor info.

tools.name: awesome-exploit-development
tools.desc: Curated list of exploit-development resources — books, courses, tooling references, and intentionally vulnerable applications.
tools.when: Plan a learning path or find vetted training materials before diving into low-level binary exploitation practice.

tools.name: SecLists
tools.desc: The security tester's companion list collection, including payloads, web-shells, and fuzzing seeds used to drive exploit attempts in labs.
tools.when: Grab canonical payload and fuzzing seed lists for your own authorized test boxes rather than writing them by hand.

tools.name: msfvenom
tools.desc: Metasploit's payload generator producing shellcode or packaged payloads from a huge payload-by-format-by-architecture matrix.
tools.when: Produce a reverse or staged payload for a specific OS and architecture, then hand it to a listener you control in your lab.

tools.name: Veil
tools.desc: Payload-generation framework that compiles C, Python, PowerShell, and other language payloads in an interactive menu.
tools.when: Generate payloads in languages other than raw shellcode for repeatable lab testing of your own golden-image detection rules.

tools.name: Donut
tools.desc: Position-independent shellcode generator that converts .NET assemblies, EXEs, or DLLs into loadable shellcode blobs.
tools.when: Turn an existing test executable into in-memory shellcode for payload chaining experiments in an isolated lab.

tools.name: RevShells
tools.desc: Web generator that prints ready-made reverse-shell one-liners across bash, netcat, PowerShell, python, socat, and more.
tools.when: Copy a correctly-encoded one-liner for a specific listener IP and port instead of re-memorizing shell syntax.

tools.name: Shellerator
tools.desc: CLI/TUI tool generating reverse, bind, and web shells in many languages from a small command line or interactive menu.
tools.when: Generate a shell one-liner from a terminal, offline, without opening a website.

tools.name: PayloadsAllTheThings
tools.desc: Curated repository of web, injection, and reverse-shell payloads organized by vulnerability class with copy-paste examples.
tools.when: Grab the right payload shape for injection, deserialization, or file-upload cases instead of hand-writing it from memory.

tools.name: socat
tools.desc: Bidirectional data relay that handles TCP/UDP, TLS, and exotic address types, making raw shell handling robust.
tools.when: Stand up the relay that receives an outbound shell or forwards it to a second hop on test infrastructure you own.

tools.name: ncat
tools.desc: Nmap's modern netcat build with SSL, proxy chaining, and credentialed listener options for quick TCP/UDP shell handling.
tools.when: The quickest minimal listener, or when you need SSL or proxy support on a box that only has classic netcat.

tools.name: pwncat
tools.desc: Reverse-shell handler in Python that imparts a stable pty-like session, privesc helpers, and scripting hooks on top of raw sockets.
tools.when: Upgrade crude reverse shells to interactive, auto-reconnecting sessions inside a lab before manual further testing.

tools.name: sbd
tools.desc: Netcat-style tool with AES-128 encrypted connections and multi-connection waiting, bundled with Kali.
tools.when: Whip up an encrypted shell listener/client pair on test infrastructure so intra-lab traffic is not plaintext.

tools.name: BeEF
tools.desc: Browser Exploitation Framework that hooks a browser via a small JavaScript payload and then commands it through a web UI.
tools.when: Client-side testing where the goal is to exercise browser-based controls (cookies, XSS) in a browser you control.

tools.name: RouterSploit
tools.desc: Python framework for embedded-device exploits (routers, cameras, and other IoT gear) with a searchable module tree.
tools.when: Vulnerability-test your own router or camera firmware; pairs with the firmware-image tooling in this repo's IoT domain.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/threat9/routersploit && cd routersploit && pip install -r requirements.txt

tools.name: Nuclei
tools.desc: Fast, template-driven scanner that replays community vulnerability checks against a target to verify a CVE applies.
tools.when: Validate whether a published advisory applies to a service you operate by running its matching template with egress control.

tools.name: nuclei-templates
tools.desc: Community template library (thousands of HTTP, DNS, network checks) that Nuclei runs against your target hosts.
tools.when: Pull the latest verified checks as YAML templates before a scan, or write your own template in the same format.

tools.name: sqlmap
tools.desc: Automated SQL injection detection and exploitation tool that fingerprints backends and extracts data safely when configured correctly.
tools.when: Verify a blinds or error-based SQLi in a web-facing database service you own and demonstrate data impact on a test database.

domains.name: IoT, Embedded & Firmware Security
domains.tagline: Reverse, emulate, and attack embedded devices in your lab: firmware extraction and boot-level emulation, UART/JTAG probing and flash dumping, side-channel and glitching rigs, RF protocol analysis (BLE/Zigbee/Z-Wave/MQTT), companion-app taping, and device databases.

tools.name: binwalk
tools.desc: Scans firmware blobs by magic signature and carves out embedded kernels, U-Boot images, squashfs/cramfs/JFFS2/ubifs filesystems, and config partitions, with entropy plots to spot encrypted or compressed regions.
tools.when: Every firmware image starts here: carve the filesystem out of the blob before anything else can be analyzed.

tools.name: firmware-mod-kit (FMK)
tools.desc: Extract-and-repack toolkit for router firmware (squashfs/cramfs/JFFS2); lets you patch binaries or files and rebuild a bootable vendor image. Largely unmaintained, so expect to fix toolchain issues before it works.
tools.when: When you actually need to modify and re-flash a vendor image (e.g. inject a telnetd) rather than merely read it.

tools.name: U-Boot Tools
tools.desc: Bootloader utilities (mkimage, dumpimage, fw_printenv, fw_setenv, mkenvimage) that inspect, unpack, and modify U-Boot FIT images and boot-environment blobs.
tools.when: Unpacking U-Boot FIT images, decoding kernel/dtb parts, or reading a target's boot environment from a flash dump.

tools.name: Firmwalker
tools.desc: Bash script that greps an extracted or mounted filesystem for secrets: shadow/passwd, SSL keys and certs, config files, admin/password keywords, dropbear/ssh artifacts, and URLs.
tools.when: Ten seconds after extraction, to surface default creds, key material, and backdoors before you read anything by hand.

tools.name: fwanalyzer
tools.desc: Filesystem audit tool from Cruise Automation that analyzes an extracted root filesystem image for setuid binaries, world-writable paths, insecure file modes, passwd-in-NSS, and other configuration smells, producing a custom report format.
tools.when: A structured, repeatable triage pass over an extracted filesystem instead of ad-hoc grep hunting.

tools.name: fwupd
tools.desc: Linux firmware-update framework (fwupdmgr/fwupdtool) that enumerates devices and applies signed firmware; in a lab it exposes device firmware versions, EFI capsules, and update/rollback flows on Linux-based research targets.
tools.when: Exercising a Linux target's firmware update path and enumerating what firmware components it reports.

tools.name: FirmAE
tools.desc: Fully-automated emulation framework (Firmadyne-derived) that uses arbitration heuristics to boot router/IP-camera firmware at ~79% success, exposing the web UI and SSH so you can fuzz and exploit it dynamically.
tools.when: Batch full-system dynamic analysis of Linux-based IoT firmware, on images Firmadyne-style boot failures block.

tools.name: Firmware Analysis Toolkit (FAT)
tools.desc: Attify's one-command wrapper around Firmadyne that boots Linux router firmware in QEMU without the PostgreSQL dependency; prints the emulated IP so you can reach its web server from the host.
tools.when: Quick, scripted boot of a single firmware image to poke its web UI and userland by hand.

tools.name: QEMU
tools.desc: Full-system and user-mode emulator covering ARM, MIPS, RISC-V, and more; boots extracted root filesystems end-to-end, and qemu-user builds run single cross-arch binaries, which every emulation framework sits on top of.
tools.when: The foundation of the whole emulation stack: boot a rootfs, or dynamically trace one bare-metalstripped binary before standing up full-stack tooling.
tools.install: sudo apt install qemu-system-arm qemu-system-mips qemu-user-static

categories.name: Hardware Debug Ports, Flash & Fault Injection

tools.name: PulseView / sigrok
tools.desc: Open-source logic-analyzer software stack with protocol decoders for UART, SPI, I2C, and 1-Wire; works with cheap 8/24-channel analyzers (Saleae clones, fx2lafw) as well as the Bus Pirate.
tools.when: Identifying unknown serial pads, decoding an unknown baud rate, and sniffing chip-to-chip buses on a target board you own.

tools.name: Saleae Logic 2
tools.desc: Polished commercial logic-analyzer software (free for low channel counts) with one-click UART/SPI/I2C decoding and robust triggering; pairs with genuine Logic 4/8/16 hardware or the popular HzKit clones.
tools.when: Fast, friendly decoding and decode-while-capturing when you have the hardware on the bench.

tools.name: Bus Pirate
tools.desc: Open-source serial multi-tool (current Bus Pirate 5): drives SPI/I2C/UART/1-Wire, reads SPI flash and EEPROMs, sniffs buses, and doubles as a low-speed logic analyzer and host adapter from any serial terminal.
tools.when: Talking directly to a chip over SPI/I2C, reading EEPROMs, or probing a bus before you break out a dedicated analyzer.

tools.name: minicom
tools.desc: The classic serial terminal for UART consoles at arbitrary baud rates; the everyday tool for reaching a bootloader, root shell, or firmware-upgrade prompt over the debug UART.
tools.when: UART pads or test points are exposed, and you want bootloader or shell access immediately.

tools.name: picocom
tools.desc: Lightweight, scriptable serial terminal with freshline handling and a minimal config; drops into non-interactive scripts, so it's ideal for logging UART sessions or pasting bootloader commands.
tools.when: Headless or scripted UART sessions where minicom's interactive menus get in the way.

tools.name: flashrom
tools.desc: Universal flash programmer with hundreds of supported chips and bus protocols (SPI, I2C, parallel, and via ch341a/mstarddc/ft2232 programmers); reads and writes BIOS, firmware, and SPI NOR chips with verification.
tools.when: Reading an on-board SPI flash out of circuit (or via clip) to obtain a full firmware image, or restoring one.

tools.name: CH341A SPI Programmer
tools.desc: Five-dollar USB SPI/I2C/parallel programmer (and its clones) that flashrom drives directly; the budget way to dump 25-series SPI flash with a SOIC-8 clip without desoldering.
tools.when: Cheap, disposable SPI reads on consumer hardware where you don't want to risk a J-Link or full probe.
tools.install: sudo apt install flashrom && use with ch341a_spi programmer

tools.name: OpenOCD
tools.desc: On-chip debugger for JTAG/SWD with a large catalog of CPU and flash targets, dozens of adapter drivers, and TCL scripting; halts CPUs, sets breakpoints, and reads back flash via the debug port.
tools.when: You found a JTAG/SWD header (or expose a testpad): OpenOCD plus a cheap probe gives you a debugger, and its flash readback doubles as a dump path for lockdown-immune devices.

tools.name: J-Link (SEGGER)
tools.desc: Commercial debug-probe family with polished SWD/JTAG software, flash loaders across thousands of microcontrollers, and RTT for fast printf-style logging from target firmware.
tools.when: A board already exposes a J-Link/SWD header, or you want a trouble-free flash-and-debug flow instead of fighting adapter quirks.
tools.install: commercial hardware + download J-Link Software pack from segger.com

tools.name: Pinecil
tools.desc: USB-C smart soldering iron with fast heat-up, excellent temperature control, and a huge tip selection; the go-to for tacking flywires onto UART pads, test points, and SOIC-8 clips.
tools.when: Practical lab work: soldering header pins, hooking UART/SPI flywires, and reattaching damaged pads before probing.
tools.install: hardware: order from pine64.com and power over 20V USB-C

tools.name: Hakko FR-301
tools.desc: Self-contained desoldering gun that cleanly removes through-hole components and chip pulls without collateral pad damage, invaluable for harvesting flash chips or isolating a faulted module.
tools.when: Removing a flash chip, connector, or BGA-adjacent through-hole part from a curious board without killing the board.
tools.install: hardware: FR-301 unit plus replacement nozzles

tools.name: ChipWhisperer
tools.desc: Open-source, open-hardware lab for power/EM side-channel analysis and voltage/clock glitching: capture power traces, run correlation power analysis to recover keys, and glitch to skip checks (CW-Lite, CW-Husky).
tools.when: Assessing a secure MCU's resistance to key extraction or fault injection on hardware you own, where the chip is the oracle.

tools.name: TrueRandom Debounce Adapter
tools.desc: Solder-free tag-connect breakout kit from TrueRandom that reroutes narrow-pitch debug headers (and exposes them) so you can desolder nothing, attack multiple boards in series, or chain a glitcher into the target.
tools.when: On small IoT modules whose debug adapters break off, or to insert a glitch/analog probe cleanly between connector and target.
tools.install: hardware: order the Debounce adapter set and clip onto the tag-connect header

tools.name: Z-Wave JS UI
tools.desc: Standalone web front-end (formerly Home Assistant's add-on) over node-zwave-js that pairs, configures, and interrogates Z-Wave devices through a USB stick, exposing command classes, values, and raw frames.
tools.when: Lab controller to inspect what a Z-Wave device advertises and to script device interactions while researching its behavior.

tools.name: Z-Wave JS
tools.desc: The core Node.js Z-Wave protocol stack powering Home Assistant and Z-Wave JS UI; parses command classes at a protocol level and is directly scriptable to send raw, non-standard frames to a device.
tools.when: Driving Z-Wave from code for fuzzing or deep protocol interrogation, or extending Home Assistant-based research setups.

tools.name: Killerbee
tools.desc: Python framework for 802.15.4/ZigBee security testing: scanning channels, sniffing and decrypting (default-link-key) traffic, and injecting/replaying frames with a supported radio (ATUSB/RZUSBstick).
tools.when: Live ZigBee interception and frame injection against Personal Area Networks in your own test environment.

tools.name: ZigDiggity
tools.desc: Bishop Fox's Zigbee pentest toolkit with a hardware setup around the RaspBee/Atmel RZUSBstick; ships attack scripts for insecure rejoins, ACK attacks, and lock identifier/enumeration against Zigbee home networks.
tools.when: Structured attack playbooks (beacon, scan, unlock, insecure-rejoin) beyond ad-hoc Killerbee usage.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/bishopfox/zigdiggity && pip3 install -r requirements.txt

tools.name: zigbee2mqtt
tools.desc: Bridges off-the-shelf Zigbee adapters instead of vendor hubs so devices are attached and controlled over plain MQTT; exposes the individual clusters/eps of devices, ideal for observing how 'dumb' devices really communicate.
tools.when: Local lab network to enroll consumer Zigbee devices and drive them from MQTT while you capture and study their traffic.

tools.name: BetterCap (BLE modules)
tools.desc: Swiss-army network tool whose ble.recon/ble.sniff/ble.spam/ble.uart modules enumerate BLE devices, read/write GATT characteristics, sniff packets, and even drive a serial-over-BLE UART on a target.
tools.when: Rapid BLE recon, characteristic enumeration, and interactive testing of a wearable or smart device's GATT service.

tools.name: nRF Connect
tools.desc: Nordic's desktop/mobile app that scans BLE devices and browses GATT services, characteristics, and descriptors with clear D-Bus-ish tree views; the fastest way to map what a peripheral exposes.
tools.when: First look at a BLE device's services and charactistics before you script anything with a full toolchain.
tools.install: download nRF Connect for Desktop from nordicsemi.com (deb/AppImage)

tools.name: nRF Sniffer for Bluetooth LE
tools.desc: Wireshark plug-in plus nRF52840 dongle firmware that decodes BLE advertising and data channels, with RSSI trackers; the de facto way to observe full BLE link-layer traffic, including encrypted sessions for offline analysis.
tools.when: Capture-level BLE analysis (advertising, pairing, connection events) without modifying the target in any way.
tools.install: download nRF Sniffer for Bluetooth LE from nordicsemi.com and load .pcap into Wireshark

tools.name: mqtt-pwn
tools.desc: Akamai's Python toolchain (mqttez, mqtts-tv, mqttgama) that scans MQTT brokers, recovers credentials from device images, and lets you interact with topics (subscribe/inject) against smart devices running MQTT.
tools.when: Assessing an MQTT-enabled IoT fleet on a lab broker: credential hunting and topic-level injection.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/akamai/mqtt-pwn && pip install -r requirements.txt

tools.name: MQTT Explorer
tools.desc: Desktop broker browser that visualizes topics as a live tree structure with retain/retained values and history, making it trivial to spot insecure 'state' topics or mis-labeled sensor data.
tools.when: Grabbing a visual, real-time map of topics and retained payloads when investigating a live broker in the lab.

tools.name: MQTTX
tools.desc: Cross-platform MQTT client with scripting and a clean multi-connection UI; handy for pushing crafted payloads to topics and replaying captured values at scale.
tools.when: Scripted by-hand publishing/subscribing to MQTT topics during protocol testing of smart devices.

tools.name: tuya-convert
tools.desc: Jailbreaks firmware-locked Tuya IoT devices (wall switches, bulbs) by MITM-ing their provisioning phase and flashing an open firmware over the air, removing vendor-cloud dependency for lab control and re-flashing.
tools.when: Liberating a Tuya-based device from vendor cloud services so you can flash, control, and analyze it locally.

tools.name: Tasmota
tools.desc: Open-source firmware for ESP8266/ESP32 smart-home hardware that replaces vendor builds; its console exposes serial/MQTT/web interfaces and detailed logs that make a repurposed device an instrumented research target.
tools.when: Running a stable, instrumented firmware on a device you control, with full console and MQTT logging for traffic observation.
tools.install: flash release .bin with esptool or tuya-convert

tools.name: Frida
tools.desc: Dynamic instrumentation framework for Android/iOS that injects JS/TS hooks into a running companion app to trace crypto, dump secrets, bypass SSL pinning, and call internal APIs live.
tools.when: Tapping the device's companion app to observe cloud interactions, API calls, and key handling in real time.

tools.name: objection
tools.desc: Runtime mobile exploration toolkit built on Frida that patches APKs/IPAs, bypasses root, disables SSL pinning, and dumps the app's runtime state (keychains, class instances) without writing hooks by hand.
tools.when: Fast-win companion-app poking: unpin, dump keystore, and inspect the app's live memory before writing custom Frida scripts.

tools.name: jadx
tools.desc: Dex-to-Java decompiler with a GUI and CLI that turns a companion APK into readable source for static review of hardcoded creds, endpoints, and embedded SDK calls.
tools.when: Static pass over a companion app: find API keys, vendor-cloud endpoints, and logging before you attack the running app.

tools.name: Shodan
tools.desc: The internet-wide device search engine par excellence; query banners, ports, and products to catalog exposed routers, cameras, PLCs, and MQTT brokers, with Shodan CLI/scripts for pipelining results.
tools.when: Mapping exposure of a device model or product family (support/account required) before any lab testing against your own instances.

tools.name: Censys
tools.desc: Internet-wide scan and certificate transparency search (sweeping TLS/SSH/HTTP banners) that indexes devices by product string, useful for wide data pulls on banners and certificates for IoT gear.
tools.when: Banner/certificate-level device fingerprinting at scale, especially where Shodan's vantage set differs.

tools.name: cve-search (CIRCL)
tools.desc: Offline CVE database with Mongo/Elastic backends that correlates CVEs to vendors, products, and CPE strings, letting you answer 'what is known-bad for this router chipset' without touching the internet.
tools.when: Correlating a firmware version or chipset CPE against published CVEs during lab triage.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/cve-search/cve-search && cd cve-search && make

tools.name: NVD API
tools.desc: NIST's public REST API for the National Vulnerability Database; keyword-searchable CVE records with descriptions, CVSS, and affected configurations for quick lookups indexed by product.
tools.when: Direct, no-infra CVE lookups scoped to a product/CPE during a device assessment.

tools.name: Exploitee.rs
tools.desc: Wiki aggregating router/IoT hardware exploits, firmware analysis write-ups, and device-specific notes maintained by the community; excellent starting reference before you re-derive anything yourself.
tools.when: Looking up an existing method or exploit note for a specific router/device model during lab research.

tools.name: Proxmark3
tools.desc: The Swiss-army RFID/NFC research device (125 kHz + 13.56 MHz) covering low- and high-frequency tags, Mifare, iClass, HID, ISO14443/ISO15693, and EMV; use the actively maintained Iceman (RfidResearchGroup) firmware fork for sniff, clone, and direct attacks.
tools.when: Reading, sniffing, or cloning badges, keyfobs, and access-control cards you legitimately test, plus auditing a site's RFID exposure.

tools.name: libnfc
tools.desc: Low-level NFC library with CLI tools (nfc-list, nfc-mfclassic) that read, write, and clone ISO14443A tags through cheap USB readers like the ACR122U.
tools.when: Quick reads (UID, Mifare classic blocks) with a plain USB NFC reader before reaching for a full Proxmark3.

domains.name: Mobile Application Security (Android & iOS)
domains.tagline: Testing your own or authorized Android & iOS apps: static analysis, decompilation, runtime instrumentation, traffic interception, emulators, and CTF practice grounds.

tools.name: jadx
tools.desc: One-step DEX-to-Java decompiler (CLI and GUI) that rebuilds readable Java source, resources, and AndroidManifest.xml into a searchable project view.
tools.when: Default first pass on a fresh APK you are authorized to test: navigate the reconstructed project and follow flows across classes.
tools.install: Download the latest zip from GitHub releases (or brew install jadx)

tools.name: jadx-gui
tools.desc: The graphical frontend bundled with jadx for interactive cross-referencing, renaming obfuscated identifiers, and exporting decompiled selections.
