tools.when: Interactive exploration and annotation when reading a flat decompile is not enough and you want quick class-to-class navigation.
tools.install: Launch the gui main class from the jadx release zip (or brew install jadx)

tools.name: apktool
tools.desc: Decodes resources and AndroidManifest.xml into editable form and exposes smali/baksmali bytecode, then rebuilds the APK for repackaging tests.
tools.when: Edit res/ or smali and repackage the APK for behavior/repackage checks on apps you are authorized to modify.
tools.install: Download the jar wrapper from GitHub releases (or sudo apt install apktool)

tools.name: Bytecode Viewer
tools.desc: Swing viewer that combines dex2jar, CFR, and Procyon so one window shows decompiled Java plus raw bytecode for side-by-side review.
tools.when: Triage a stubborn APK when a single decompiler misses, and compare decompiler output in one place.
tools.install: Download the release jar from GitHub releases

tools.name: frida-dexdump
tools.desc: Dumps in-memory DEX files from a running app through Frida, defeating packers and protectors that only materialize code at runtime.
tools.when: Analyze a hardened or packed app: launch it on your test device, dump the loaded dex, then feed the recovered classes back into jadx.

tools.name: androguard
tools.desc: Python library plus CLI to parse DEX/APK graphs, list permissions and exported components, and script custom static checks.
tools.when: Scriptable static analysis and bespoke rules on apps you test when click-through GUI tools are not enough.

tools.name: Quark-Engine
tools.desc: Obfuscation-aware APK scoring engine that matches the app's call graph against suspicious-behavior rules (crypto misuse, dynamic dex loading, C2 calls) with confidence scores.
tools.when: Quick second opinion on an APK for risky behavior patterns after MobSF, or building your own detection rules from reversed code.

tools.name: APKiD
tools.desc: YARA-based detector of packers, protectors, and obfuscators (DexProtector, Bangcle, qihoo) inside an APK or DEX before any reversing effort.
tools.when: Scope a hardened app early: knowing it is packed tells you static-only analysis is not enough and runtime dexdump is needed.

tools.name: Frida (Android)
tools.desc: Injects frida-server onto a device to hook functions at runtime: bypass SSL pinning and root detection, trace crypto calls, and inspect memory.
tools.when: The runtime layer of most Android tests — bypass pinning, trace sensitive APIs, and probe internals static analysis cannot reach.
tools.install: pip install frida-tools && push a matching-version frida-server to the device

tools.name: objection
tools.desc: Frida-powered runtime exploration toolkit: one-liners to disable SSL pinning and root checks and browse storage (SharedPrefs, cache) without writing JS.
tools.when: Quick interactive runtime pass on your own app when hand-rolled Frida scripts are overkill.

tools.name: drozer
tools.desc: On-device agent that assumes another app's identity to enumerate and test exported activities, content providers, services, and broadcast receivers from a console.
tools.when: After static analysis, map the app's IPC/component attack surface and probe each exported component for authorization and data-exposure flaws.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/ReversecLabs/drozer.git && cd drozer && pip install . (plus the drozer agent APK on the device)

tools.name: DIVA (Damn Insecure Vulnerable App)
tools.desc: Deliberately vulnerable Android app with a dozen fixed challenge categories (insecure logging, input validation, hardcoded keys) built for hands-on practice.
tools.when: Warming up static/dynamic skills or validating your toolchain before touching a real engagement target.
tools.install: Download the APK from GitHub releases and install it with adb install

tools.name: InsecureBankv2
tools.desc: Purposefully vulnerable banking app exposing auth bypass, SQL injection, and exposed adb port issues for controlled practice.
tools.when: Practicing mobile banking app tests (auth, crypto, IPC, storage) in an environment you fully control.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/dineshshetty/Android-InsecureBankv2 && run the bundled server, then install the APK via adb

tools.name: mitmproxy
tools.desc: Interactive HTTPS intercepting proxy built for mobile workflows: install its CA on the device, rewrite or replay HTTP/2 and gRPC, and script with Python addons.
tools.when: Any network-level test of your own apps — log, tamper, or replay API traffic from a rooted device or emulator, paired with a Frida pinning bypass.

tools.name: Charles Proxy
tools.desc: Commercial GUI HTTPS proxy with click-through SSL proxying, breakpoints, and a request timeline — the macOS-centric alternative to a terminal proxy.
tools.when: Point-and-click interception and rewriting during manual iOS testing on a workstation when you prefer a GUI over mitmproxy.
tools.install: Download from charlesproxy.com (trial, then paid license)

tools.name: MobSF (Mobile Security Framework)
tools.desc: All-in-one analyzer for APK and IPA: permissions, exported components, insecure crypto and network config, hardcoded secrets, all surfaced in a web UI with a REST API; its dynamic module also captures app HTTP traffic.
tools.when: Always the first automated pass on a binary you are authorized to test — read the findings report, then drill into specific hits manually.

tools.name: Genymotion
tools.desc: Fast x86 Android emulator with snapshots, sensor simulation, and drag-and-drop APK install — a convenient third-party run target for testing.
tools.when: When Android Studio's AVD is too heavy and you want quick snapshots and containerized test images for your own apps.
tools.install: Download the Genymotion bundle from genymotion.com (free personal-use desktop license)

tools.name: Waydroid
tools.desc: Container-based Android that boots a full Android userspace directly on Linux without a VM, scriptable from the CLI.
tools.when: Android testing on your Linux workstation with a container-native device instead of a heavyweight emulator.

tools.name: adb (Android Debug Bridge)
tools.desc: Google's core device bridge from Android platform-tools: install apps, push/pull files, shell in, install CA certificates, capture logcat, and port-forward.
tools.when: Every device setup step — reach the emulator or handset, push frida-server and test certificates, and snapshot app data before and after a run.

tools.name: Magisk
tools.desc: Systemless root with module support for dedicated test devices; gives Frida, adb, and injected agents the root context most dynamic tests need.
tools.when: Prepare a personal test device with an unlocked bootloader when an app refuses to run on stock or detects the emulator.
tools.install: Install the Magisk APK or fastboot boot a patched boot image on an unlocked-bootloader device

tools.name: LineageOS
tools.desc: The most widely used custom ROM: build or flash a controlled test image on your own device, enable adb root, and strip vendor bloat for cleaner testing.
tools.when: Standing up a long-lived controlled Android test device with root and current security patches before dynamic testing.
tools.install: Follow the device build instructions on wiki.lineageos.org and flash via adb/fastboot

tools.name: smali/baksmali
tools.desc: Assembler and disassembler for DEX bytecode: decode framework and system app code, patch small runtime checks, and reassemble for re-signing tests.
tools.when: Analyzing preinstalled or framework APKs on devices you own, or patching a specific smali check and rebuilding the APK.
tools.install: Download smali-2.x.jar and baksmali-2.x.jar from GitHub releases

tools.name: class-dump
tools.desc: Dumps Objective-C class interfaces from a Mach-O binary, exposing the app's object graph and method signatures for review.
tools.when: Mapping an app's Objective-C surface from a decrypted IPA you are authorized to test before deeper reversing.
tools.install: Download class-dump from the project page and place it in /usr/local/bin

tools.name: frida-ios-dump
tools.desc: Dumps the decrypted IPA from a jailbroken device using Frida, turning App Store-encrypted slices into analyzable binaries.
tools.when: Get a decryptable binary from your own jailbroken test device before starting static analysis.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/AloneMonkey/frida-ios-dump && cd frida-ios-dump && pip install -r requirements.txt && python3 dump.py <AppName>

tools.name: ipatool
tools.desc: Downloads IPAs directly from the App Store using your own Apple ID, enabling analysis of publicly available apps you lawfully retrieve.
tools.when: Pulling an IPA for review where you hold a valid Apple ID and authorization for the app.

tools.name: Frida (iOS)
tools.desc: frida-server on a jailbroken device hooks and swizzles classes and traces methods for runtime inspection of your test apps.
tools.when: Tracing iOS app runtime behavior, bypassing cert pinning, and dumping decrypted classes on a device you control.
tools.install: Install frida-server via Sileo/Cydia and keep the version matched to the host pip install of frida-tools

tools.name: objection (iOS)
tools.desc: objection on iOS: disable SSL pinning, browse Keychain and UserDefaults, and explore classes from a single console without custom Frida JS.
tools.when: Fast runtime checks on your own jailbroken test device when writing Frida scripts is overkill.

tools.name: cycript
tools.desc: Runtime REPL mixing Objective-C and JavaScript to poke live processes and objects on jailbroken devices.
tools.when: Interactive in-process class inspection and object manipulation during authorized iOS testing.
tools.install: Download the binary/dylib from cycript.org and launch with cycript -p <pid>

tools.name: Sileo
tools.desc: Modern package manager for jailbroken devices and the clean way to install frida-server, debuggers, and testing tweaks on your test device.
tools.when: Bootstrap a jailbroken lab device: install Frida, ldid, and testing utilities from one UI.
tools.install: Install Sileo from its GitHub release on a jailbroken device

tools.name: OWASP MASTG & UnCrackable Apps
tools.desc: The Mobile Security Testing Guide plus the UnCrackable APPv1-v4 challenge apps with documented solutions — the reference mobile CTF syllabus.
tools.when: Learning or validating a technique on trusted challenge apps before applying it to an authorized engagement.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/OWASP/MASTG && run the UnCrackable APKs under Frida/objection on your test device

tools.name: DVIA (Damn Vulnerable iOS App)
tools.desc: Deliberately vulnerable iOS app for practicing jailbreak-based runtime testing around keychain, transport security, and privacy.
tools.when: Controlled iOS practice that mirrors real runtime vulnerabilities before touching your own production-grade apps.
tools.install: Build it from source in Xcode and deploy to a device you own

tools.name: Frida CodeShare
tools.desc: Community hub of reusable Frida scripts (pinning bypasses, trace templates, dexdump variants) for accelerating script authoring.
tools.when: Find a proven hooking pattern before writing your own custom script for an authorized app.
tools.install: Browse codeshare.frida.re and run a script with frida -l script.js

domains.name: Network Attacks & Analysis
domains.tagline: Host discovery, port scanning, pivoting, packet capture, on-path interception, and network service auditing for understanding and testing traffic on networks you operate.

tools.name: Nmap
tools.desc: The reference network mapper: full- and half-open TCP/UDP scans, service/version detection, OS fingerprinting with -O, and a 600+ script engine (NSE) for targeted checks.
tools.when: Every assessment starts here — run a -sV service audit on hosts you own after a broad port sweep, then drill into specific services with scripts.

tools.name: masscan
tools.desc: Asynchronous TCP port scanner that sweeps entire CIDRs at line rate; its results pipe directly into Nmap or naabu for follow-up.
tools.when: Scan very large ranges fast — your whole lab estate or an entire /8 you operate — before focused Nmap work.

tools.name: RustScan
tools.desc: Rust port scanner that finds open ports across a /16-class range in seconds, then hands the results to Nmap automatically.
tools.when: Fast all-ports sweeps where speed beats verbosity; pair with -- -sV to keep Nmap's service-detection depth.

tools.name: naabu
tools.desc: ProjectDiscovery's fast SYN scanner focused on top-N port lists with parallel host/port batching; the port layer of the httpx/nuclei pipeline.
tools.when: Quick broad discovery feeding a recon pipeline: naabu --top-ports 1000 then export JSON to httpx.

tools.name: p0f
tools.desc: Passive OS fingerprinting via TCP/IP stack quirks (TTL, window size, DF) and HTTP signatures; needs no packets of its own, only observed traffic.
tools.when: Identify OSes on a network you operate without direct scans — feed it a capture or live traffic mirrored from your switch.

tools.name: nbtscan
tools.desc: Scans NetBIOS name services for hostnames, logged-in users, MAC addresses, and shared-disk hints across a Windows LAN.
tools.when: On an authorized Windows segment, census machine names and shares quickly when ICMP and ARP answers are filtered.

tools.name: Nmap NSE
tools.desc: Nmap's scripting engine ships 600+ community scripts (smb-*, ssl-*, dns-*, vuln-*) that interrogate services after a scan; run category- or name-filtered sets.
tools.when: After port discovery, run safe script categories (--script default,safe) or a specific script like smb-enum-shares against hosts you own.

tools.name: nmap-vulners
tools.desc: NSE script set that queries the Vulners API with detected CPE/service versions and annotates scan output with matching advisories and exploit links.
tools.when: Fast triage of version-fatigued service lists: run -sV --script vulners on your own hosts to surface known-CVE matches to patch.

tools.name: arp-scan
tools.desc: ARPs whole subnets and lists live hosts with MAC/OUI vendor — the most reliable L2 census, answered even where ICMP is filtered.
tools.when: First step on any network you operate: enumerate every physical host on the LAN before scanning services.

tools.name: netdiscover
tools.desc: Active and passive ARP discovery with a live table of IP, MAC, and vendor; passively learns hosts from traffic without sending a packet.
tools.when: A visual live view of your LAN, or passive L2 discovery when you want to stay quiet while monitoring your own segment.

tools.name: fping
tools.desc: Parallel ICMP pinger that sweeps ranges and prints alive/dead hosts in script-friendly output.
tools.when: Fast liveness check of large or off-subnet ranges where ARP-based tools cannot reach.

tools.name: massdns
tools.desc: High-performance DNS resolver that resolves and brute-forces huge name lists at tens of thousands of queries per second, emitting A/AAAA/CNAME results.
tools.when: Resolve or brute candidate subdomain lists on your own estate in minutes instead of hours of single-threaded dig.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/blechschmidt/massdns && cd massdns && make

tools.name: chisel
tools.desc: Single-binary TCP/UDP tunnel over HTTP(S) with reverse and SOCKS5 modes; one client, one server, no special privileges.
tools.when: Run a chisel client on a host you own and forward ports back through an HTTP egress that filters plain SOCKS.

tools.name: frp
tools.desc: Fast reverse proxy that exposes local services behind NAT via a public server; config-driven with TLS, auth, and load balancing.
tools.when: Stable exposure of lab services or a pivot point behind restrictive NAT you control.

tools.name: stowaway
tools.desc: Multi-hop proxy chain builder (agent/admin model) supporting TCP/UDP and dynamic forwards chained across several hops.
tools.when: Build long multi-hop chains across several hosts you control when a single tunnel is insufficient.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/ph4ntonn/Stowaway && cd Stowaway/Client && go build

tools.name: rpivot
tools.desc: SOCKS4 reverse proxy: a client on an internal host you own connects out through your listening server, opening a tunnel into that internal network.
tools.when: When the internal host can egress only toward your server; lightweight Python, no agent install beyond the script.

tools.name: ligolo-ng
tools.desc: TUN-based tunneling: the agent builds an encrypted tunnel to your proxy, which routes full IP traffic into the agent's network as if you had a real VPN.
tools.when: Full network pivoting across a host you own — route arbitrary hosts/subnets without per-port forwarding.

tools.name: proxychains
tools.desc: Forces any TCP client through a chain of HTTP/SOCKS proxies by shimming its socket calls via LD_PRELOAD.
tools.when: Route existing CLIs through your tunnel(s) without rewriting them — proxychains nmap <target>.

tools.name: sshuttle
tools.desc: Transparent VPN over SSH that forwards arbitrary TCP/UDP/DNS for whole subnets through an SSH connection without per-port forwards.
tools.when: Pivot your whole routing table through a jump host you administer using just an SSH key.

tools.name: socat
tools.desc: Bidirectional relay between TCP, UDP, UNIX sockets, and files, with SSL and FORK support — the byte-plumbing workhorse.
tools.when: Expose or forward services between hosts, wrap TLS around a plaintext target, or daemonize a listener in controlled lab setups.

tools.name: Ncat
tools.desc: Nmap's netcat with TLS, proxy chaining, IPv6, and connection brokering built into a MIT-licensed binary.
tools.when: Read/write test a service, grab a banner, or relay a plaintext session without extra tooling.

tools.name: Wireshark
tools.desc: Graphical packet analyzer decoding hundreds of protocols with stream following, session reassembly, and deep dissection.
tools.when: Investigate a specific conversation or replay a .pcap from your network — the closest thing to seeing the bytes yourself.

tools.name: tshark
tools.desc: Wireshark's terminal sibling: captures and dissects live or file traffic with the full dissector set and JSON/CSV field output.
tools.when: Capture or parse on a headless host and pipe structured output into scripts.

tools.name: tcpdump
tools.desc: Command-line packet capture with Berkeley Packet Filter expressions; the standard for headless and rolling capture.
tools.when: Capture on a server you administer or dump to files with -w for later analysis — trivially scriptable.

tools.name: tcpflow
tools.desc: Reassembles TCP sessions from captures into per-connection files, reconstructing transferred content instead of packet fragments.
tools.when: Pull actual payloads (files, HTTP bodies, plaintext credentials) out of a .pcap you own.

tools.name: bettercap
tools.desc: Modular MITM framework — ARP/DNS/DHCP spoofing, sniffing, HTTP proxies — with an interactive shell, caplets, and a REST API.
tools.when: Full-featured on-path testing on a network you operate: spoof, sniff, and log plaintext from clients you control.

tools.name: ettercap
tools.desc: Classic MITM suite with ARP poisoning, sniffing, filters, and plugin-based interception of plaintext protocols.
tools.when: Traditional LAN MITM lab work when you want the legacy plugin and filter ecosystem.

tools.name: mitmproxy
tools.desc: Interactive HTTPS interception proxy with a terminal UI and Python addons for rewriting and scripting flows.
tools.when: Inspect or rewrite HTTP(S) from an app or device you control, with mitmproxy's CA explicitly trusted on that device.

tools.name: Responder
tools.desc: LLMNR/NBT-NS/mDNS poisoner that answers resolution queries on a segment you operate and logs the Net-NTLMv1/v2 hashes clients send to it.
tools.when: Validate whether your own Windows clients leak credentials when their resolver goes quiet — to justify disabling LLMNR/NBT-NS.

tools.name: mitm6
tools.desc: Poisons DNS via IPv6 router advertisements so Windows clients look up WPAD and other names through your server on the v6 network.
tools.when: Test IPv6 spoofing of your own dual-stack Windows clients to confirm mitigations (WPAD removal, RA filtering) are in place.

tools.name: hping3
tools.desc: Crafts custom TCP/UDP/ICMP packets via raw sockets with hand-tuned flags, timing, payloads, and fragmentation.
tools.when: Probe how your own firewalls treat malformed or flagged packets, or test a service on non-standard ports.

tools.name: Scapy
tools.desc: Python packet library for crafting, forging, and dissecting virtually any protocol; can send, sniff, capture, and fuzz from a REPL or scripts.
tools.when: Build bespoke probes or protocol fuzzers for your own services when off-the-shelf tools cannot express the exact packet.

tools.name: snmpwalk
tools.desc: Net-SNMP's tree walker: pulls entire OID subtrees (sysDescr, interfaces, processes, routing) when a community string is read-accessible.
tools.when: Dump as much SNMP-visible detail as possible from one of your managed devices using the read community after discovery.

tools.name: snmp-check
tools.desc: Perl enumerator that turns SNMP walks into human-readable reports — system, network, routing, and listening ports in one shot.
tools.when: Quick presentation-ready SNMP summary of a device you manage without memorizing OIDs.

tools.name: onesixtyone
tools.desc: Fast SNMP scanner that blasts sysDescr requests across a range with multiple community strings and logs responders.
tools.when: Discover which of your own network devices run SNMP with default or weak read communities across a whole estate.

tools.name: ldapsearch
tools.desc: OpenLDAP's query client: filters, attribute selection, base DN control, and search limits for directory interrogation.
tools.when: Query directory objects (users, groups, OUs, attributes) on a directory you administer or are authorized to audit.

tools.name: ldapdomaindump
tools.desc: Dumps Active Directory users, computers, groups, nested memberships, GPOs, and more from a single LDAP query with any valid account.
tools.when: One-shot AD network object dump for analysis and reporting during an authorized directory audit.

tools.name: smbclient
tools.desc: Samba's SMB/CIFS client for browsing, listing, and transferring files against Windows and Samba shares with full auth options.
tools.when: Test share access and anonymous or null listings on hosts you operate before deeper tooling.

tools.name: enum4linux-ng
tools.desc: Maintained Python successor to enum4linux; automates SMB/RPC null-session enumeration of users, shares, password policy, and sessions.
tools.when: Complete legacy SMB enumeration (users, shares, policy) in one command against an assessed host.

tools.name: NetExec
tools.desc: Successor to CrackMapExec: multi-protocol (SMB, LDAP, MSSQL, WinRM, RDP) credential-validated enumeration of shares, users, sessions, and policy across fleets.
tools.when: Credentialed health-check across many Windows hosts at once during an authorized assessment — who is admin where, which shares are open.

tools.name: Impacket
tools.desc: Fortra's Python implementations of Windows network protocols with ~100 example scripts — smbclient, secretsdump, psexec, wmiexec, getTGT, and more.
tools.when: Protocol-level SMB/RPC/directory work from Linux when you need scriptable, low-level control over the wire.

tools.name: showmount
tools.desc: Queries the NFS mount daemon for exported filesystems (showmount -e) on NFS servers, listing paths and export flags.
tools.when: Enumerate which NFS exports a host you operate offers, and with what flags — first step before any mount testing.

tools.name: rpcclient
tools.desc: Samba's RPC client that interrogates MS-RPC endpoints — user, domain, SID, and session lookups, often over null sessions.
tools.when: Legacy SMB/RPC enumeration (SID and user queries) when standard SMB clients are blocked on a network you're authorized to test.

tools.name: xfreerdp
tools.desc: FreeRDP's client: connects over RDP from the CLI with drive and clipboard forwarding, screenshots, and full NLA support.
tools.when: Access a Windows RDP host you manage for GUI testing, session capture, or share-mount tests.

tools.name: rdesktop
tools.desc: Veteran open-source RDP client with single-session support and configurable codec and bitmap options.
tools.when: Lightweight RDP client for older Windows services where FreeRDP is overkill.

tools.name: ssh-audit
tools.desc: Actively probes an SSH server and scores its configuration — kex, ciphers, MACs, key types — against known weaknesses and current advisories.
tools.when: Audit the SSH policy of your own hosts; ships CI-friendly JSON and HTML report output.

tools.name: lftp
tools.desc: Feature-rich FTP/FTPS/SFTP/HTTP client with mirroring, resuming, scripting, and batch transfers.
tools.when: Poke an FTP service you run: anonymous-login checks, recursive listing, and large recursive mirrors.

domains.name: OSINT — People, Infrastructure & Metadata
domains.tagline: Passive intelligence on people, exposed infrastructure, and document metadata — for authorized recon and for auditing your own digital footprint.

tools.name: Sherlock
tools.desc: Checks a username across 400+ platforms using HTTP status/pattern heuristics and returns every profile that exists; the reference CLI for username enumeration, actively maintained.
tools.when: Confirm which sites a username you own is registered on so you can harden or clean up your own footprint.

tools.name: Maigret
tools.desc: Collects a username dossier across 3000+ sites with account-type tags (social, dating, code) and exports HTML/PDF/JSON reports; picks up a fresh site list on each run.
tools.when: When Sherlock's pass/fail list is not enough and you want an exportable report of everywhere a handle you control appears.

tools.name: Blackbird
tools.desc: Blazing-fast username enumerator that checks 500+ services with thread pools and color-coded existence results; built as a speed-focused companion to Sherlock and Maigret.
tools.when: Bulk-check many candidate usernames over a short window, limited to handles and accounts you are authorized to investigate.

tools.name: WhatsMyName
tools.desc: A community-maintained dataset of 700+ sites with exact fingerprints (URI patterns and success/not-found heuristics); the data engine underlying most username checkers.
tools.when: Audit a checker result or drive your own authorized username sweep against a curated, up-to-date site list.

tools.name: HaveIBeenPwned
tools.desc: Definitive breach and password-exposure checker: search any email or domain across a huge corpus of leaked datasets; free web search plus a documented API, with Pwned Passwords openly downloadable.
tools.when: Check whether addresses or domains you control appeared in known breaches, and enforce password-exposure checks on your own estate.

tools.name: IntelligenceX
tools.desc: Dark-web and public-data search engine indexing leaks, paste sites, forums, and code over a 10-year retention window; free tier with API and Telegram bots.
tools.when: Check if your emails, domains, or phone numbers surface in dark-web and paste archives you are authorized to monitor.

tools.name: LeakCheck
tools.desc: Commercial breach aggregator with billions of entries supporting email, username, phone, and live-keyword search; paid tiers unlock full records.
tools.when: Correlate breach hits across emails and passwords, but only on credentials you hold or are authorized to test.

tools.name: Holehe
tools.desc: Checks which 120+ sites an email is registered on by replaying password-recovery flows without mailing the target, so the address is never alerted.
tools.when: Find which platforms a breached or owned email is tied to, so stale accounts you control can be closed or secured.

tools.name: emailrep.io
tools.desc: Hosted API that scores email reputation, flags breach exposure and disposable providers, and lists the mainstream profiles tied to an address; free tier needs no key.
tools.when: Triage a suspicious inbound sender or audit your own addresses as part of a defensive OSINT review.

tools.name: theHarvester
tools.desc: Passive harvester of emails, employee names, subdomains, and reported API keys for a domain across many open sources; the reference domain reconnaissance CLI.
tools.when: Map every email and subdomain publicly linked to a domain you own before hardening mail and DNS.

tools.name: PhoneInfoga
tools.desc: Phone-number OSINT framework that attributes country, area, carrier, and line type and gathers scattered footprint data via configurable scanners; stable but slowly maintained.
tools.when: Resolve a number you own or are authorized to analyze into provider facts before deeper carrier-level checks.

tools.name: Instaloader
tools.desc: Downloads Instagram profiles, posts, hashtags, highlight stories, and their metadata (captions, likes, comments) without an API key; scriptable and actively maintained.
tools.when: Archive a public profile you own, or collect hashtag and post metadata for evidence preservation.

tools.name: Osintgram
tools.desc: Interactive shell that pulls public Instagram profile info, captions, followers, tag lists, and bio-contact strings using a scratch session or a free Hiker API token (educational-use disclaimer included).
tools.when: Relationship analysis on a public profile you operate — who tags, who comments, what contact strings appear in bios.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/Datalux/Osintgram && pip3 install -r requirements.txt

tools.name: snscrape
tools.desc: Python library/CLI that scrapes public posts and profiles to JSONL from several platforms; X/Twitter and Reddit backends are dead behind logins, but Telegram, Weibo, and some Mastodon instances still work.
tools.when: Programmatic retrieval and archiving of public posts on platforms snscrape still supports, e.g. Telegram channels you monitor.

tools.name: ExifTool
tools.desc: Reads, writes, and edits EXIF/GPS/IPTC/XMP metadata across images, PDFs, and Office files; the metadata workhorse behind most document-forensics pipelines.
tools.when: Forensic-grade tag extraction from local files — geolocation, author, generator, timestamps — before release or after acquisition.

tools.name: FotoForensics
tools.desc: Web tool that runs Error Level Analysis (ELA), panel scans, EXIF review, and JPEG quantization analysis to spot digital tampering in an uploaded image.
tools.when: Check whether an image you own or are authorized to examine was edited, and inspect residual metadata block by block.

tools.name: Metagoofil
tools.desc: Dork-driven harvester that finds indexed documents (.pdf, .docx, .xlsx) for a domain and downloads them for metadata stripping; the maintained opsdisk fork ships on Kali.
tools.when: Collect every publicly indexed document on a domain you own so metadata and hidden information can be scrubbed.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/opsdisk/metagoofil && pip3 install -r requirements.txt

tools.name: FOCA
tools.desc: Windows GUI (C# with SQL Server backend) that fingerprints documents across search engines and extracts users, folders, and software into a browsable metadata project.
tools.when: When you have a Windows workstation and want a point-and-click metadata project view for documents you control.

tools.name: VirusTotal
tools.desc: Industry-standard crowdsourced engine for hashes, samples, URLs, and IP/domain reputation with 90+ AV engines, plus passive DNS and threat-signal context.
tools.when: Check a file hash, URL, or IP you are investigating against years of crowdsourced detections during authorized analysis.

tools.name: ipinfo.io
tools.desc: IP address datasets and API for location, ISP, ASN, company, and privacy-risk signals; free lookup tier covers geolocation and network attribution.
tools.when: Resolve an IP address you are investigating into location, provider, and ASN context.

tools.name: ipapi.co
tools.desc: Free IP geolocation API returning country, city, ISP, timezone, and currency for any address; also offers bulk and commercial JSON/CSV plans.
tools.when: Script location lookups for lists of IPs appearing in your own logs.

tools.name: Google Maps
tools.desc: Global mapping, Street View, and satellite imagery search; the core visual geolocation and place-lookup surface for OSINT.
tools.when: Correlate landmarks, signage, or geotagged imagery against the physical world during authorized investigations.

tools.name: Yandex Maps
tools.desc: Alternative globe with strong coverage of Eastern Europe, Russia, and CIS regions plus street-level panoramas; a useful cross-check for place and imagery comparison.
tools.when: Cross-check locations and side-by-side imagery with Google Maps when coverage hints at CIS or Eurasian regions.

tools.name: Shodan
tools.desc: The reference internet device and service search engine indexing banners, ports, vulnerabilities, and exposure history for any IP or domain; also exposes free InternetDB lookups.
tools.when: See exactly which ports and services your public IP ranges expose right now — and how long that exposure has existed — before closing them.

tools.name: Censys
tools.desc: Internet-wide scan platform over hosts, services, and certificates with structured query language and host/cert/web-property APIs; free tier includes search and lookups.
tools.when: Certificate-centric inventory and pivots — find every host presenting a given cert — or query structured service data beyond free Shodan limits.

tools.name: Netlas
tools.desc: Scanning platform over billions of indexed hosts supporting IPv4/IPv6, full response-body regex, DNS, WHOIS, and certificate search with a REST API; free tier capped near 50 requests/day.
tools.when: Lucene/regex search across full HTTP response bodies when Shodan banners are too shallow for your authorized query.

tools.name: DNSDumpster
tools.desc: One-page passive DNS mapping tool that enumerates subdomains, MX/TXT/SPF records, and hosts onto an interactive network map for a domain.
tools.when: Fast visual pass over the subdomain and mail infrastructure of a domain you own before deeper enumeration.

tools.name: SecurityTrails
tools.desc: Commercial passive DNS and subdomain intelligence with historical DNS records, certificate timelines, and connected-domain data via REST API.
tools.when: Retrieve DNS history and subdomain changes over time for a domain you operate, straight into scripts.

tools.name: crt.sh
tools.desc: Open certificate-transparency log search; returns every issued certificate — and therefore every hostname — for a domain, sorted by issue date.
tools.when: Enumerate all hostnames that ever had a public certificate for domains you own, including retired staging hosts.

tools.name: Hurricane Electric BGP
tools.desc: Global BGP, IPv6, and routing intelligence: AS numbers, prefixes, IXP membership, route announcements, and peer relationships in a browsable web database.
tools.when: Attribute an IP or prefix to its ASN and understand routing relationships for infrastructure you analyze.

tools.name: RIPEstat
tools.desc: RIPE NCC's data API for IP/ASN attribution, route history, geolocation, and abuse contacts; queryable over REST with ready-made widgets.
tools.when: Programmatic WHOIS/ASN and routing lookups for lists of IPs or prefixes you are researching.

tools.name: DomainTools
tools.desc: Commercial WHOIS and domain-intel suite (WhoIs, reverse whois, registration history, DNSHistory, Iris) maintained for 20+ years; priced via API/subscription tiers.
tools.when: Full WHOIS history and reverse-ownership pivots on domains involved in authorized investigations.

tools.name: OpenCorporates
tools.desc: Open database of millions of companies worldwide extracted from public registries; unique API for entities, officers, and filings across many jurisdictions.
tools.when: Discover corporate structure, officers, and cross-jurisdiction registrations behind a company you are authorized to research.

tools.name: Companies House (UK)
tools.desc: UK government registry of companies, officers, people with significant control (PSC), and filings, exposed through a free public API.
tools.when: Company, director, and beneficial-owner lookups for UK-registered entities.

tools.name: SEC EDGAR
tools.desc: US SEC's full-text filings database (10-K, 8-K, S-1, proxies) exposing financials, executives, and subsidiaries; free API with fair-use limits.
tools.when: Pull US-listed company filings for financial and personnel intelligence.

tools.name: Crunchbase
tools.desc: Venture and funding profile database with financing rounds, acquisitions, growth-stage signals, and key-people digests for startups and private companies.
tools.when: Sketch the funding trajectory, investors, and key people of a private company you analyze.

tools.name: GitHub Code Search
tools.desc: GitHub's built-in search over the public code index with operators for language, path, and extension; also surfaces users, commits, and leaked-token suspects.
tools.when: Find public code, configs, and secrets that mention an identifier you own, and review your own repositories' exposure.

tools.name: Sourcegraph
tools.desc: Public-code search engine with regex, literal, and symbol-aware queries across open repositories; good for finding leaked patterns and re-used infrastructure.
tools.when: Regex-wide sweep of public code for a credential prefix, domain, or package name you are attributing.

tools.name: GitDorker
tools.desc: Automates GitHub 'dork' queries from a 3000+-entry dork list through the search APIs to surface exposed files, keys, and configs in public repositories.
tools.when: Glob for suspicious files and secrets across public repos related to your own organization or authorized targets.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/obheda12/GitDorker && pip3 install -r requirements.txt

tools.name: Nosey Parker
tools.desc: Fast secret-scanner that extracts API tokens and credentials from git histories with high-precision regex and entropy rules; written in Rust for large corpora.
tools.when: Scan cloned public repositories (e.g., ones you own) for historic secrets before they are abused.

tools.name: Blockchain.com Explorer
tools.desc: Bitcoin block explorer with address, transaction, and pending-mempool views plus webhooks and an authenticated explorer API.
tools.when: Trace bitcoin addresses and transaction flows connected to a case you are authorized to investigate.

tools.name: Etherscan
tools.desc: Reference Ethereum block explorer with address, token, contract-code, and event-log analysis and a free API; covers other EVM chains via sibling explorers.
tools.when: Analyze EVM addresses, token transfers, and smart-contract interactions you are investigating.

tools.name: WalletExplorer
tools.desc: Clusters bitcoin addresses into services where possible, letting you see a wallet's whole activity — including market aggregation endpoints.
tools.when: View a bitcoin address in service context and reveal associated addresses during authorized tracing work.

tools.name: BitcoinAbuse
tools.desc: Public API and searchable database of bitcoin addresses reported for scams and fraud, with user-submitted evidence and descriptions.
tools.when: Check whether an address you are investigating carries attached abuse reports.

tools.name: Wayback Machine
tools.desc: The Internet Archive's store of hundreds of billions of web snapshots; view any URL as it existed historically, with CDX listings and full-text site search.
tools.when: Recover removed pages, track historical site changes, and capture evidence before content disappears.

tools.name: waybackpy
tools.desc: Python client for the Wayback and CDX APIs: save snapshots, query availability, and stream archive listings programmatically.
tools.when: Scripted archival and CDX queries to build change-history timelines for URLs you monitor.

tools.name: Archive.today
tools.desc: Independent web snapshot service that mirrors pages on demand and blocks most crawlers; a useful second capture layer parallel to the Wayback Machine.
tools.when: Save a live page as evidence through an independent archive when you want redundancy across capture providers.

tools.name: Common Crawl
tools.desc: Petabyte-scale open crawl corpus refreshed monthly (WARC/WAT/WET files) with a URL index API; reconstruct what a site published even without per-page snapshots.
tools.when: Pull historical page versions or URL-level index data for content you have permission to analyze.

tools.name: Ahmia
tools.desc: Ethical search engine for the Tor network with support for .onion and I2P; continuously indexes dark-web pages and filters illegal content.
tools.when: Index and discover .onion pages relevant to a monitoring program you are authorized to run.

tools.name: Dark.fail
tools.desc: Trusted, hand-verified directory of live .onion marketplaces and services with uptime status; a safe entry index rather than an in-depth search engine.
tools.when: Locate legitimate .onion services and verify their current uptime during authorized dark-web research.

tools.name: DeHashed
tools.desc: Commercial breach database covering email, username, phone, IP, and password hashes with fuzzy search and cross-referencing across billions of records; subscription required for full records.
tools.when: Correlate leaked credentials and keys across datasets — only for accounts you own or are contracted to test.

tools.name: Pastebin Search
tools.desc: Pastebin's own search across public pastes, combinable with search engines via site: dorks; useful for monitoring dropped credentials and dumps.
tools.when: Monitor public paste dumps that mention an organization or domain you are authorized to defend.

tools.name: SpiderFoot
tools.desc: Automated OSINT correlation engine with 200+ modules and a YAML correlation engine, surfaced through a web UI, CLI, and API; built to map an attack surface and connect entities.
tools.when: A broad sweep of a domain, IP, or email you own to correlate entities across many free data sources in a single scan.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/smicallef/spiderfoot && pip3 install -r requirements.txt

tools.name: Maltego
tools.desc: Commercial graph-based link-analysis platform (desktop and browser) whose transforms reach identity, breach, and infrastructure datasets; free Community Edition exists with result limits.
tools.when: Investigative link analysis where a visual graph of who connects to whom beats raw JSON output.

tools.name: Google Hacking Database (GHDB)
tools.desc: Canonical reference catalog of search-engine operators and example queries that surface exposed files, login panels, and misconfigurations in public indexes.
tools.when: Compose and reuse proven dorks to audit what public indexes expose about domains you own.

domains.name: Password Attacks & Cracking
domains.tagline: Recover and test credentials you are authorized to attack: offline GPU/CPU hash cracking, hash identification, wordlists and rules, VPN PSK recovery, and lab-only NTLM relay, pass-the-hash and LSASS dumping chains.

tools.name: Hashcat
tools.desc: World's fastest password recovery utility: GPU-optimized OpenCL/CUDA kernels for 590+ hash modes across dictionary (-a 0), mask (-a 3), hybrid (-a 6/7), PCFG and rule-based (-a 0 -r) attacks, with a slow-hash tuning engine for salted/costed formats.
tools.when: The default for offline hashes you hold (dumps, configs, SAM/NTDS extract): benchmark, run wordlist + rules, then mask; benchmark against your own GPUs before buying cloud time.

tools.name: hashcat-utils
tools.desc: MIT-licensed stdin/stdout pipeline utilities (cap2hccapx, combipow, len, cutb, rulegen…) that pre-process captures and wordlists into exactly the candidate and hash formats hashcat expects.
tools.when: Convert WPA captures or normalize custom wordlists before a hashcat run; the companion tools to a serious cracking pipeline.

tools.name: John the Ripper
tools.desc: The classic Unix password cracker with dictionary, incremental (Markov), and rule modes; runs on CPU out of the box, and on OpenCL/hosted hardware in jumbo builds.
tools.when: First port of call for /etc/shadow-style hashes and any environment without working GPU drivers; pairs with your own .conf rules.

tools.name: John the Ripper jumbo
tools.desc: Community 'bleeding-jumbo' branch adding hundreds of extra hash/cipher formats (NTLM, macOS, PDF, RAR, KeePass, FortiGate, IKE-PSK) plus the *2john converters used to package encrypted files before cracking.
tools.when: Whenever your hash or file format is not covered by stock John or hashcat — the widest offline-format coverage available.

tools.name: Hashtopolis
tools.desc: Self-hosted client/server platform that distributes hashcat workloads across many GPUs on your own fleet, with task queues, chunking, and a web UI for assigning hash lists and attack modes.
tools.when: Fill a lab or rented cloud-GPU rack with crack work: a Hashtopolis server dishes out chunks to each agent and consolidates results for your authorized recovery jobs.

tools.name: GoCrack
tools.desc: FireEye's manager/worker framework written in Go for managing password-cracking tasks across a cluster of GPU hashcat workers, with a web panel for task packaging and result retrieval.
tools.when: An alternative to Hashtopolis when you want a Go-native manager for a reclaimed GPU cluster; archived but still runnable for lab workflows.

tools.name: hcxtools
tools.desc: Converts Wi-Fi captures (pcapng) and probe/eapol frames into the PMKID and PBKDF2 hashes that hashcat and John crack directly — the modern replacement for binary service packs.
tools.when: Process a 4-way-handshake or PMKID capture from your own access point on the way to an offline WPA2/WPA3 Purge PSK attack.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/ZerBea/hcxtools && make && sudo make install

tools.name: aircrack-ng
tools.desc: The de-facto Wi-Fi suite: airodump-ng for capture, aireplay-ng for handshake injection, and aircrack-ng for dictionary/PTW attacks against WEP and WPA/WPA2 across your own networks.
tools.when: Authorized wireless testing of infrastructure you operate: capture the handshake, verify the client, then hand the hash to hashcat for the heavy lifting.

tools.name: hashid
tools.desc: Python regex identifier for 220+ hash types that prints the matching hashcat mode (-m) and John format, so the correct cracking command is chosen before the first run.
tools.when: The moment you collect a hash (dump, config, CTF): identify it before picking -m/--format to avoid wrong-mode and line-length failures.

tools.name: Name-That-Hash
tools.desc: Friendly command-line and web-identifying hash analyst that recognizes her way through common formats and prints the matching hashcat and John modes with sample hashes.
tools.when: A zero-friction second opinion on ambiguous hashes (e.g. distinguishing NTLM from MD4/NDSS) before you commit to a cracker.

tools.name: hashes.com sample hashes
tools.desc: Online database documenting sample hashes and lookup methods for a wide range of algorithms (MD5, NTLM, bcrypt, Argon2, Joomla, …) useful for confirming a suspect format.
tools.when: Cross-check an unusual hash against documented samples, or eyeball expected lengths/salt formats before choosing an engine.

tools.name: Hashcat example hashes
tools.desc: Official table with one valid sample hash per hashcat mode (password is always 'hashcat'), including VPN PSK (5300/5400/2500) and firewall (7000) formats; also embedded via hashcat --example-hashes.
tools.when: Confirm your hash formatting and attack command offline before a live run, or label unknown samples in your own CTFs.

tools.name: SecLists
tools.desc: The security tester's companion collection: passwords (10k/1M/rockyou-derived), usernames, default router credentials, and discovery/fuzzing payloads in one tree.
tools.when: First stop in any authorized recovery or login test — reach for its dictionaries before generating anything custom.

tools.name: rockyou.txt
tools.desc: The 2009 RockYou leak (~14M real-world passwords) that remains the standard baseline dictionary for fast-hash testing; shipped with Kali and mirrored in SecLists.
tools.when: Quick first-pass dictionary sweep against fast hashes you own before rule/mask work, exactly as Kali documents it.

tools.name: OneRuleToRuleThemAll
tools.desc: Community-curated single hashcat .rule file merging the best of popular rule sets (NSAKEY, d3ad0ne, etc.) so one base wordlist yields high-coverage candidate mutations.
tools.when: A proven default ruleset for the dictionary+rule phase (-a 0 -r) when you don't want to hand-tune your own .rule file.

tools.name: hashcat best64.rule
tools.desc: The stock best64.rule ships in the hashcat repo and applies 64 high-yield mangles (append digit, toggle case, leetspeak, suffix) — the quickest low-cost rule win.
tools.when: A fast, predictable ruleset that is safe to run on the default pool before heavier custom rules.

tools.name: Openwall John rules
tools.desc: John's rule engine and wiki-documented preset rules (dumb, wordlist, KoreLogic, single) mutate base words with case, suffix, prefix and substitution pipelines.
tools.when: Applying John-side rule sets in jumbo-supported formats, especially when you are already cracking with john rather than hashcat.

tools.name: Pipal
tools.desc: Wordlist statistics analyzer that reports password length, character set, repeated digits, baseword frequency and pattern bias so you can shape the right attack.
tools.when: Analyze your own leaked/test wordlist before building rules: learn the shape (e.g. 'capitalized word + 2 digits') and pick efficient masks.

tools.name: statsprocessor
tools.desc: Hashcat's position-based password generator that derives per-position character frequencies from a wordlist and emits statistically weighted masks for -a 3 attacks.
tools.when: Turning observations from your wordlist scans into a frequency-driven mask attack that outperforms naive charsets.

tools.name: Mentalist
tools.desc: Graphical wordlist builder centered on human password paradigms: case mangling, keyboard walks, year/digit insertion, exporting full lists or ready-made hashcat/John rules.
tools.when: Visually profile a candidate password space (vocab + year + symbol) when you prefer a GUI over hand-editing rule files.

tools.name: kwprocessor
tools.desc: Hashcat-team keyboard-walk generator producing passwords that follow adjacent-key routes and basechars/config surprises for PINs and passphrases typed on keyboards.
tools.when: Target PINs and passphrases your own devices generate along keyboard patterns, where walk-derived guesses beat pure randomization.

tools.name: crunch
tools.desc: Character-set wordlist generator enumerating all combinations/permutations with @,%^ pattern placeholders plus output splitting, resume and gzip/7z output.
tools.when: Generate bounded, pattern-shaped candidate lists (known prefixes/suffixes, specific charsets) to feed hashcat or John.

tools.name: CeWL
tools.desc: Ruby spider that crawls a site to a depth and emits the unique words (plus author/email metadata) it finds — a vocabulary completely specific to that target.
tools.when: Build organization-specific dictionaries (your own web app, a CTF) where site vocabulary beats generic lists.

tools.name: CrackStation
tools.desc: Free online hash cracker (MD5, SHA1, NTLM, and 220+ other algorithms) that matches your hashcat modes against massive precomputed tables.
tools.when: A quick single-hash sanity lookup during analysis; treat as a confirmation aid, never as your primary recovery path for sensitive data.

tools.name: Kerbrute
tools.desc: Go-based userenum/passwordspray tool that walks Kerberos pre-authentication: it discovers valid users from KDC error codes and tests one password against many accounts without lockouts.
tools.when: Authorized domain testing where you need lockout-safe spraying via AS-REP pre-auth and user enumeration against your own KDC.
tools.install: Download release binary from the repo, or go install github.com/ropnop/kerbrute@latest

tools.name: NetExec
tools.desc: The fork-lifted successor to CrackMapExec; its kerberos module performs password spraying and user enumeration across your SMB/Kerberos estate with clean protocol handling.
tools.when: Office-wide spray validation when you already carry a NetExec install and want one client for SMB, LDAP, Kerberos and SSH checks.

tools.name: Spray
tools.desc: Small Python sprayer that takes a forged inventory of usernames and a handful of passwords, sleeps between attempts, and reports hits plus failed-auth stats.
tools.when: Lockout-conscious spraying against your own AD from a Linux attack box with randomized delays.

tools.name: TREVORspray
tools.desc: Python sprayer against Microsoft 365/Azure AD and AD with strong anti-lockout controls (seasonable delays, account randomization, MFA-threshold guardrails).
tools.when: Azure AD/Office 365 authorized spray testing where you must respect MFA lockout and per-account backoff.

tools.name: DomainPasswordSpray
tools.desc: The canonical community PowerShell sprayer: enumerates domain users from AD, tests one password across them, detects lockdown policies and can pass an existing password.
tools.when: Classic AD password-spray validation in your own estate with built-in user enumeration and graceful exit on failure.

tools.name: MSOLSpray
tools.desc: Python sprayer for Azure Active Directory / Microsoft 365: validates tenant, tests credentials via MSOL endpoints and reports valid user texture plus lockout status.
tools.when: Authorize-and-run check of Azure AD accounts in your own tenant without tripping global lockout thresholds.

tools.name: o365spray
tools.desc: Username enumeration and password spraying against Microsoft 365 / Azure AD with built-in rate limiting, module-based spraying and user check against MSOL open endpoints.
tools.when: Coverage of M365 as the primary cloud sprayer when you need mature lockout-safe logic built in.

tools.name: Responder
tools.desc: LLMNR/NBT-NS/mDNS poisoner in a lab: it answers name-resolution queries and captures NTLMv1/v2 challenge-response hashes from clients that voluntarily submit them.
tools.when: Lab/pentest only: run it to demonstrate why your own network filters these protocols, and feed captured that to a relay or cracker.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/lgandx/Responder && cd Responder && sudo proxychains4 -i tcp -v python3 responder.py -I eth0

tools.name: mitm6
tools.desc: IPv6 abuser for labs: advertises a rogue DHCPv6 server so Windows clients register DNS and hand over WPAD traffic that can feed NTLM credential relaying.
tools.when: Building a relaying pipeline against your own IPv6-enabled lab where clients trust rogue DHCPv6 — pair with ntlmrelayx, lab only.

tools.name: impacket ntlmrelayx
tools.desc: The relay half of the chain: accepts captured NTLM authentications and replays them to SMB/LDAP on targets you control, enabling hash history recording or relayed logins without knowing the plaintext password.
tools.when: The canonical lab relay server after a poisoning daemon harvests NTLM; keep every target in your own lab scope.
tools.install: pip install impacket; python3 ntlmrelayx.py -t smb://<lab-target>

tools.name: impacket psexec / wmiexec
tools.desc: Impacket's psexec and wmiexec use an NTLM hash directly to open an administrative service/exec on a Windows host — no password needed, lab authors' flagship use case for hash validation.
tools.when: After you hold a hash for a machine in-scope: psexec for a service-metered shell, wmiexec for a cleaner WMI-backed execution.

tools.name: NetExec (pass-the-hash)
tools.desc: Netexec smb/winrm handles pass-the-hash logins (-H) at scale, checks admin rights and executes commands — replacing CrackMapExec workflows with an active fork.
tools.when: Sweep several lab hosts with one hash to map who accepts admin hash logins; identical protocol coverage keeps it a natural psexec alternative.
tools.install: pipx install netexec; nxc smb 127.0.0.1 -u admin -H :NTHASH

tools.name: evil-winrm
tools.desc: WinRM shell client that authenticates with a password or NTLM hash and gives an interactive PowerShell session for post-hash validation.
tools.when: Clean, HTTP-bound lab session when WinRM is open and you prefer a stable PowerShell interactive to service-write tricks.

tools.name: Mimikatz
tools.desc: The lab-standard post-exploitation credential extractor: reads LSASS memory to dump plaintext passwords, NTLM hashes, Kerberos tickets and DPAPI keys on systems you administer.
tools.when: Authorized lab/engagement 'logonpasswords' runs on endpoints you own to prove how cached secrets age; always on-lab, never stealth marginal.
tools.install: Download release from the repo and run sekurlsa::logonpasswords on your own host

tools.name: lsassy
tools.desc: Python library that grabs and parses LSASS memory via WMI/remote scripts without landing a binary on the target, returning parsed credentials for lab review.
tools.when: Remote-to-itself lab extraction on Windows endpoints you operate, minimizing artefact noise compared to writing a standalone dump.

tools.name: DonPAPI
tools.desc: DPAPI-centric credential dumper that walks LSASS and protected-store databases plus DPAPI master keys on remote machines, carving secrets and their derivation chains.
tools.when: Lab DPAPI-focused extraction where you want the credential chain laid out and don't need a full interactive shell.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/login-securite/DonPAPI && pip install -r requirements.txt

tools.name: firepwd
tools.desc: Pure-Python decryptor for Mozilla Firefox/Thunderbird logins.json driven by the derived master-password key; recovers saved site credentials from a copy you own.
tools.when: Inspect the saved logins of your own Firefox profile (e.g. a forgotten master password) on a copy, never someone else's browser data.

tools.name: SharpDPAPI
tools.desc: C# DPAPI toolkit from the GhostPack family that decrypts Chrome/Edge vaults, DPAPI master keys and credential files on Windows — the standard for authorized browser-store recovery.
tools.when: Recover Chrome/Edge saved credentials on machines you administer, using your own user context/master key.
tools.install: Download the compiled release or build from source, run from your own session

tools.name: LaZagne
tools.desc: Python credential-store dumper that walks browsers, WiFi profiles, mail clients, SSH keys and many desktop apps, recovering stored logins and passwords from your own machine.
tools.when: One-shot sweep of every local credential store on a system you own for DR/hygiene or lab inventory.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/AlessandroZ/LaZagne && cd LaZagne && python3 laZagne.py all

tools.name: hashcat VPN PSK modes (IKE-PSK 5300/5400, Cisco-IPSEC 2500)
tools.desc: Dedicated hashcat modes crack IKE pre-shared keys (5300/5400) and Cisco IPSEC VPN hashes (2500/500) captured from phase-1 handshakes, alongside FortiGate (7000) formats for firewall admin hashes.
tools.when: Recover a PSK for a VPN you administer when the key was mis-remembered; pair with ike-scan for the phase-1 capture first.

tools.name: ike-scan
tools.desc: IKE discovery and testing tool that sends phase-1 negotiation to a VPN gateway and captures the responder's hash — the handshake you feed straight into hashcat's IKE-PSK modes.
tools.when: Grab a legitimate IKE PSK exchange from a VPN endpoint you own, then crack it offline with hashcat for key-hygiene validation.

tools.name: John *2john archive converters
tools.desc: zip2john, rar2john and 7z2john turn encrypted ZIP/RAR/7z archives into $zip$/$rar$/$7z$ hashes that john jumbo or hashcat crack by password.
tools.when: Recover a forgotten password on your own archive: convert once, then crack with john -jumbo or hashcat after wordlist+rule passes.

tools.name: fcrackzip
tools.desc: Fast zip password cracker with dictionary and brute-force modes (libzip-based fork runs far faster than the unzip-spawning original).
tools.when: A quick direct brute/dictionary check of a small single ZIP without standing up a John pipeline; superseded by *2john for real workloads.

tools.name: pdf2john
tools.desc: John/jumbo converter that extracts the hash from password-protected PDFs (RC4 and AES variants) and feeds it to john or hashcat for offline recovery.
tools.when: Open a PDF you own whose password was lost: convert to the $pdf$ format and crack on your own CPU/GPU.

tools.name: keepass2john
tools.desc: John jumbo converter that packages a sealed .kdbx KeePass vault into a $keepass$ hash crackable by John or hashcat, covering the current PBKDF2 runtime cost.
tools.when: Unlock your own KeePass vault after the master password drifted; always work on the copy you own, never a database you don't control.

tools.name: pdfcrack
tools.desc: Dedicated GPL tool recovering owner/user passwords from PDFs using the classic security handler (rev 2-4) via wordlist or brute force with state save/restore.
tools.when: Recover legacy (pre-AES-256 rev 5) PDFs you own; on modern AES R4/R6 documents prefer pdf2john's formats instead.

domains.name: Phishing & Social Engineering
domains.tagline: Simulating the human factor: phishing campaigns, cloned logins, credential harvesting, and MFA-phishing proxies — all framed for authorized security-awareness testing.

tools.name: GoPhish
tools.desc: Open-source, self-hosted campaign engine: compose email templates, landing pages, target groups, and SMTP profiles, then track opens, clicks, and submitted credentials per recipient via web UI and REST API.
tools.when: The standard engine for authorized organizational awareness campaigns — schedule simulations against your own employees, export per-recipient results, and measure click-rate improvement over time.

tools.name: King Phisher
tools.desc: Python client/server phishing toolkit (SecureState) with parallel campaigns, page cloning, credential-harvesting landing pages, geo-location of clickers, and SPF checks. Declared no longer maintained — treat as legacy.
tools.when: Self-hosted client-plus-server workflows in legacy environments; otherwise prefer Gophish for new authorized programs.

tools.name: PhishSpark
tools.desc: Commercial self-hostable phishing-simulation platform with SPF/DKIM/DMARC setup wizard, HMAC-signed tracking links, prebuilt templates (Microsoft 365, payroll portals), and per-department risk scoring. Sends only to your own users with written approval.
tools.when: Teams that want a lighter-weight, guided simulation workflow with built-in authorization guardrails without standing up Gophish infrastructure.
tools.install: Sign up at https://phishspark.com (free tier) or follow the Docker quick-start in /docs for self-host.

tools.name: Evilginx2
tools.desc: Go-based reverse-proxy that fronts a real site over a domain you control, captures post-login session cookies, and demonstrates why legacy 2FA alone does not protect a session. The reference tool for authorized MFA-phishing and passkey-migration exercises.
tools.when: When authorized red-team scope includes proving session-token exposure or comparing legacy 2FA against phishing-resistant FIDO2/passkeys in your own environment.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/kgretzky/evilginx2 && cd evilginx2 && make

tools.name: Modlishka
tools.desc: Go reverse proxy that transparently proxies a whole multi-domain HTTPS site through one phishing domain and captures credentials and session tokens. Pioneered the modern AitM technique in research; author restricts use to authorized testing and defensive awareness.
tools.when: Authorized engagements that need whole-domain transparent proxying without client-side certificates, or historical demos of the AitM technique.

tools.name: EvilGophish
tools.desc: Combines the Gophish campaign engine with an evilginx2-class reverse proxy in one toolchain, letting an authorized red team schedule phishing emails and capture session tokens from a single console.
tools.when: When you want token capture plus Gophish-style campaign scheduling and reporting in one self-hosted deployment.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/fin3ss3g0d/EvilGophish && cd EvilGophish && sudo bash setup.sh

tools.name: Social-Engineer Toolkit (SET)
tools.desc: TrustedSec's menu-driven Python framework bundling page cloning, credential harvesters, email mass-mailers, and SMS vectors behind one guided interface. Preinstalled on Kali; built for running authorized awareness campaigns.
tools.when: Guided multi-vector campaigns on a Kali box — a single menu covers credential-harvest, phishing, and SMS exercises entirely inside your own scoped environment.

tools.name: BeEF
tools.desc: Browser Exploitation Framework: serves a JavaScript hook that, once a consenting user's browser loads it, gives the operator a live inside view of that browser session with modules including fake login prompts and environment probing.
tools.when: Training that shows employees the inside of a compromised browser session live, or to check whether your org notices browser-hook indicators.

tools.name: Wifiphisher
tools.desc: Rogue-access-point toolkit that drives nearby clients to a captive-portal page to collect Wi-Fi credentials — a physical testing and awareness tool for demonstrating lookalike Wi-Fi portals on scoped, consenting networks.
tools.when: On-site authorized assessments where the goal is showing how easily a lookalike Wi-Fi portal harvests credentials; never on networks you do not own or lack written consent for.

tools.name: zphisher
tools.desc: Automated login-page cloning kit with 30+ ready templates, served over localhost/cloudflared/ngrok links with submissions logged locally. Widely used for building credential-phishing awareness demos — strictly in authorized labs or against your own organization.
tools.when: Entry-level awareness demos or in-house training where a ready-made lookalike login page is enough and no full campaign engine is needed.
tools.install: git clone --depth=1 https://github.com/htr-tech/zphisher && cd zphisher && bash zphisher.sh

tools.name: CredSniper
tools.desc: Flask/Jinja2 framework serving cloned multi-step login pages (username → password → 2FA token) with Let's Encrypt SSL and a results API. Unmaintained since 2020; use only in authorized test campaigns and labs.
tools.when: Small scoped engagements that want a page-only collector with a results API; prefer the AitM proxes for session-level testing.

tools.name: PhishMailer
tools.desc: Generates realistic HTML and plain-text email messages with attachments for in-house phishing simulations, including per-recipient personalization and SMTP sending. Fills the content-creation step of authorized awareness campaigns.
tools.when: When you need convincing message and attachment content to feed into Gophish or your own SMTP as part of an approved simulation.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/BiZken/PhishMailer && cd PhishMailer && pip install -r requirements.txt

tools.name: MXToolbox
tools.desc: Suite of free web lookups covering SPF, DKIM, DMARC, BLACKLIST, and email header analysis plus spam-score checks — the de-facto starter kit for validating whether your own domain records are spoof-proof and readable by receivers.
tools.when: First stop when you deploy or audit your org's email authentication; also useful pre-/post-campaign to confirm your simulation sender domain isn't bouncing.

tools.name: Google Admin Toolbox Check MX
tools.desc: Google's lookup service that checks MX, SPF, and DMARC records for a domain and flags common misconfigurations from a Google-managed mail perspective.
tools.when: Quick monthly self-checks of your domain's mail authentication plus loopbacks against Gmail's parser behavior.

tools.name: Mail-Tester
tools.desc: Generates a test address and scores an actual emailed message against SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and content heuristics (0-10), including which records Gmail/Outlook see when your message arrives.
tools.when: Verifying that a simulation or real marketing message passes authentication before you trust email-deliverability reports.
tools.install: Send a test email to the address shown at https://www.mail-tester.com/.

tools.name: dmarcian
tools.desc: DMARC-focused platform with free record inspectors and DMARC aggregate-report parsing that shows which senders are failing authentication against your own domain. A core tool for the defense side of spoofing.
tools.when: Parsing DMARC aggregate reports, planning policy progression (none → quarantine → reject), and proving to leadership that typosquatting mail is being rejected.

tools.name: EasyDMARC
tools.desc: Free DNS records lookup for SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and BIMI with visual health reports; also offers continuous monitoring and report parsing on paid tiers.
tools.when: Self-service DNS-stack validation and monthly health snapshots across many domains at once.

tools.name: DKIMValidator
tools.desc: Free web validator that checks a public DKIM record for a given domain and selector, verifying RFC 6376 correctness before rollout.
tools.when: Confirming a specific DKIM selector publishes correct records during signing deployment.
tools.install: Open https://www.dkimvalidator.com/ and enter the domain/selector.

tools.name: Google Message Header Analyzer
tools.desc: Google's free raw-header decoder that maps each Received hop, SPF/DKIM/DMARC verdict, and authentication results into a consumable timeline — great for teaching how spoofed look-alikes get flagged (or slip through).
tools.when: Post-campaign forensics and training walkthroughs where you show employees exactly which header tells a phish from a real sender.

tools.name: Microsoft Message Header Analyzer
tools.desc: Free Microsoft header decoder that parses authentication results (SPF/DKIM/DMARC) and delivery path from raw outlook.com/Exchange messages, including spam-confidence and EOP verdict lines.
tools.when: Investigating how a message behaved inside Microsoft 365, or inside table-top exercises where defenders trace a reported phish end to end.

tools.name: Canarytokens
tools.desc: Thinkst's free drop-in tokens — a unique URL, document, or credential cred that alerts your team the moment it is visited or submitted. Uses any arbitrary token in an email so a single interaction is logged and correlated.
tools.when: Defensive phishing-awareness tracking: embed a custom URL token in an awareness email or lure-bearing document and get alerted when anyone (attacker or trainee) interacts with it.
tools.install: Generate a token at https://canarytokens.org/generate (self-host via github.com/thinkst/canarytokens).

tools.name: PhishTool
tools.desc: Web-based phishing analysis workspace (with a Chrome extension) that decodes emails, auto-extracts headers, URLs, and indicators, and routes findings to case-management/email-security tools. Also offers click-through analytics for reporting.
tools.when: Turning employee reports into vetted phishing cases, or running analytics on how reported phish relate to your authorized campaign metrics.
tools.install: Sign up at https://www.phishtool.com/ (web app + Chrome extension).

tools.name: urlscan.io
tools.desc: Screenshots and inventories full page loads — every request, redirect, domain, script, and certificate — for a submitted URL. The reference tool for dissecting phishing landing pages and look-alike domains.
tools.when: Analyzing a reported phish's full resource pattern, comparing a look-alike against the real login site, and sharing a sandboxed screenshot in incident write-ups.

tools.name: VirusTotal
tools.desc: Aggregates dozens of antivirus and URL-blocker verdicts plus domain reputation for a submitted URL or file. Fast triage when deciding whether a link is attacker infrastructure.
tools.when: Quick triage of a reported URL against multi-vendor verdicts before escalation to your SOC.
tools.install: Submit a URL at https://www.virustotal.com/ (APIs via account).

tools.name: CheckPhish
tools.desc: Bolster's AI URL scanner that renders pages in isolation and classifies phishing/brand-impersonation attempts with a screenshot and intelligence score, exposed as a web dashboard and REST API.
tools.when: Automated triage of suspected brand-impersonation and look-alike domains inside awareness campaigns or hunt queues.
tools.install: Submit a URL at https://checkphish.ai/ (API key required).

tools.name: PhishTank
tools.desc: Community-run phishing URL database (operated by Cisco Talos) you can query to see whether a domain/URL is already classified as phishing, and where defenders and vendors submit new sightings.
tools.when: Defensive lookup of reported URLs against a maintained community blocklist, and submitting confirmed phish from your campaign analysis.

tools.name: OpenPhish
tools.desc: Automated phishing intelligence engine that curates active phishing URLs and feeds them through API and free/demo endpoints, with per-campaign and per-region details.
tools.when: Feeding confirmed phishing URLs from your analysis into this feed to inform downstream detectors, and researching active campaigns your org may have been targeted by.
tools.install: Browse or pull feeds at https://openphish.com/.

tools.name: PhishDetect
tools.desc: Open-source service (client + self-hosted node) that clusters phishing pages by SHA-1 hash of page content and exposes an API for lookups, letting an org build its own look-alike detector.
tools.when: Self-hosted phishing-pattern detection where you want clustering and a private lookup API for your own authorized-scope pages.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/phishdetect/phishdetect && cd phishdetect && docker-compose up -d

tools.name: URLhaus
tools.desc: abuse.ch's malware-URL sharing platform that tracks URLs used for phishing, drive-by downloads, and C2, with free API and hourly CSV/JSON feeds for defensive enrichment.
tools.when: Checking whether a reported URL is already tracked as malicious and pulling machine-readable feeds into your detection stack.

tools.name: PhishStats
tools.desc: Real-time database of active phishing domains with public dashboards, IP/URL/domain/RDNS queries, and an API — useful for validating whether host indicators are known-phishing infrastructure.
tools.when: Enriching an I/O indicator from a reported phish against a live phishing-activity database.

tools.name: Google Safe Browsing Transparency
tools.desc: Google's Safe Browsing status checker that reveals whether a given web property is being flagged as deceptive or socially engineered, plus the local Lookup API for programmatic checks.
tools.when: Checking whether a reported URL is actively defanged in Chrome/Firefox user bases, and automating dangerous-site checks.
tools.install: https://transparencyreport.google.com/safe-browsing/search or the Safe Browsing Lookup API.

tools.name: KnowBe4
tools.desc: Leading commercial security-awareness platform combining simulated phishing campaigns, template libraries, and training modules with per-user risk scoring, plus reporting that ties click rates to training completion.
tools.when: Enterprise-scale awareness programs needing turnkey campaign templates, LMS-style training, and board-ready reports on phishing risk.

tools.name: Hoxhunt
tools.desc: Commercial continuous-training platform built around real-world threat reporting: employees report suspicious mail, the service validates it and dispatches micro-learnings while feeding behavioral data to security teams.
tools.when: Organizations that want reporting-led training that blends real user reports with simulations and automated follow-up.

tools.name: Cofense PhishMe
tools.desc: Commercial phishing-defense platform that mixes simulated phishing, template management, and automation that ingests the precise phish employees report — with the Cofense Reporter add-in pushing sightings straight to the SOC.
tools.when: Teams coupling simulation with a strong 'report the phish' culture and automated triage of what users actually receive.

tools.name: Microsoft 365 Report Message Add-in
tools.desc: Free Microsoft add-in for Outlook/OWA that gives users a 'Report' button to flag phishing, junk, or not-junk straight to Microsoft and (with a user-reporting policy) to your security team's mailbox.
tools.when: Giving every employee a zero-friction way to report suspected phish, then mining those submissions in table-top exercises and campaign post-mortems.
tools.install: Deploy from M365 admin → Settings → Integrated apps; docs at https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/submissions-users-report-message-add-in-configure

tools.name: Cofense Reporter
tools.desc: Outlook/heb browser reporting add-in that forwards a reported email, with attachments and headers intact, to the organization's phishing mailbox and auto-prepends a standardized template for triage.
tools.when: Structuring free-form employee reports so analysts receive complete headers/attachments from day one of an awareness program.
tools.install: Deploy via https://cofense.com/ (Outlook add-in / browser toolbar).

tools.name: SANS OUCH! Newsletter
tools.desc: Free monthly, non-technical security awareness newsletter from SANS covering phishing, social engineering, and reporting habits; can be licensed for redistribution to staff and reused as tabletop discussion material.
tools.when: A pre-written, vetted security-awareness cadence for employees and a ready-made reading list before table-top exercises.

tools.name: Jigsaw Phishing Quiz
tools.desc: Free interactive quiz from Jigsaw by Google that walks participants through tricky real-world email screenshots and explains each phishing tell with instant feedback.
tools.when: A low-stakes, engaging lter for kickoff of a training meeting or a fresh-start activity right after a failed simulation click.

domains.name: Privilege Escalation (Linux & Windows)
domains.tagline: Local audit of Linux & Windows privilege boundaries: lax permissions, exposed SUID/sudo surface, scheduler jobs, and unpatched escalations — on systems you own.

tools.name: LinPEAS
tools.desc: Runs hundreds of privilege-boundary checks — SUID/GUID binaries, writable PATHs, cron entries, capabilities, credentials in files, known-vuln hints — on Linux/Unix/MacOS and color-codes findings by severity.
tools.when: First pass on any Linux host you are authorized to assess; `-s` for a faster/stealthier run, `-e` to enable extra checks before you dig into anything manually.

tools.name: LinEnum
tools.desc: Single-shell-script Linux enumeration collecting user, sudo, cron, SUID, PATH, and file-permission checks into one grep-able report; still ships as the Kali/BlackArch `linenum` package.
tools.when: A quick, dependency-free sweep when you want a portable .sh you can drop on a box and read results calmly offline.

tools.name: linux-smart-enumeration (lse)
tools.desc: Ranked Linux enumerator that reveals findings progressively by importance level (-l0..-l2) and can watch for recurring cron/process activity while it runs.
tools.when: When you want signal-first output instead of a full dump; escalate verbosity only if the default level comes up empty.

tools.name: SUID3NUM
tools.desc: Standalone Python SUID enumerator that separates default binaries from custom ones, cross-matches custom binaries against GTFOBins, and can auto-exploit non-destructive cases.
tools.when: After LinPEAS flags SUID binaries: use it to distinguish vanilla OS binaries from operator-installed ones and jump straight to the GTFOBins-relevant entries.

tools.name: SudoKiller
