tools.desc: Sudo-focused escalation auditor that checks for misconfigured sudo rules, sudo-version CVEs with prerequisites, dangerous GTFOBins entries, environment-variable abuse, and missing scripts referenced by sudoers.
tools.when: A host where `sudo -l` reveals a non-trivial rule set and you want a catalog of candidate commands plus CVE-flagged sudo versions to try manually.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/TH3xACE/SUDO_KILLER && cd SUDO_KILLER && ./SUDO_KILLERv3.sh -c -a -e -r report.txt -p /tmp

tools.name: GTFOBins
tools.desc: Reference site (not a tool): documents how standard Unix binaries — when sudo, SUID, or capability-misconfigured — can escape restricted contexts, read/write files, or escalate.
tools.when: Look up every SUID binary and sudo rule your enumeration surfaced; if the binary is listed, the page shows the exact boundary you wrongly granted.

tools.name: GTFOBLookup
tools.desc: Offline command-line lookup utility that mirrors GTFOBins, LOLBAS, WADComs, and HijackLibs to disk so you can search abuse vectors without a browser or internet.
tools.when: Air-gapped hosts or terminal-only workflows where you need to query GTFOBins/LOLBAS by executable name and category from the CLI.

tools.name: linuxprivchecker
tools.desc: Python script that enumerates base system info and hunts world-writable files, misconfigurations, and cleartext passwords; written to suggest investigation targets rather than run exploits.
tools.when: An OSCP-friendly second opinion after LinPEAS when you want a leaner, Python-based cross-check on the same host.

tools.name: unix-privesc-check
tools.desc: PentestMonkey's classic shell script for weak file permissions and simple escalation vectors (world-writable files, exposed .netrc/.ssh), packaged in Kali; mature but only lightly maintained.
tools.when: A conservative, read-only check on aged Unix boxes (also Solaris/AIX/HP-UX) where you want a second, low-noise opinion on file-permission drift.
tools.install: sudo apt install unix-privesc-check && unix-privesc-check standard

tools.name: pspy
tools.desc: Unprivileged process snooper: uses /proc scans triggered by inotify events to catch short-lived processes (cron jobs, root scripts, and the arguments they carry) that a normal `ps` sweep never sees.
tools.when: Park it for a couple of minutes after enumeration on a Linux host; timing-dependent scheduler jobs that static scans miss appear as they fire.

tools.name: inotifywait
tools.desc: inotify-based file/directory event watcher (create/modify/access/delete) from the inotify-tools package; the building block for precise, pattern-able watching scripts.
tools.when: Point it at a specific writable directory or config file (e.g. a scheduler-owned path) and see exactly when and which files change on boxes you own.

tools.name: fatrace
tools.desc: fanotify-based system-wide file-access reporter (read/write/open/close per PID and path) — useful when a scheduled job touches files too briefly for process listing to catch.
tools.when: Wide-surface file watching on your own host where inotify recursion gets unwieldy; narrow it with `--dir` to a single directory of interest.
tools.install: sudo apt install fatrace && sudo fatrace --dir /var/spool

tools.name: WinPEAS
tools.desc: Windows counterpart to LinPEAS from the same PEASS suite: scans services, scheduled tasks, unquoted paths, AlwaysInstallElevated, stored credentials, and patch gaps; ships as winPEAS.exe (x64/x86) and winPEAS.bat in one release.
tools.when: First pass on any Windows host you are authorized to assess; run as a low-integrity user, then re-run elevated to compare the privilege surface.

tools.name: Seatbelt
tools.desc: GhostPack C# host-survey tool bundling dozens of 'safety-check' modules (token privileges, services, autoruns, credential stores, scheduled tasks) runnable in grouped or single-command mode.
tools.when: Focused follow-up enumeration when you need a specific answer (e.g. only TokenPrivileges, Services, or the LOLBAS module); supports clean txt/json output.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/GhostPack/Seatbelt && cd Seatbelt && dotnet build -c Release

tools.name: PrivescCheck
tools.desc: itm4n's PowerShell-only enumeration script covering Windows privesc vulnerabilities and configuration issues, with Base/Extended/Audit check tiers and HTML/TXT/CSV report formats.
tools.when: A single PowerShell script where you want consolidated, report-ready output without artifacts touching disk; use `-Extended` when the base run comes up empty.

tools.name: windows-privesc-check
tools.desc: PentestMonkey's standalone executable (Python via PyInstaller) that audits securable objects for weak ACLs: services, service executables, %ProgramFiles% DLLs, %PATH%, registry RunOnce, and FAT installs.
tools.when: Older/legacy Windows images where you want a misconfig-focused audit (not a patch check) runnable as a single portable .exe, ideally as Administrator.

tools.name: LOLBAS
tools.desc: Windows sibling of GTFOBins: catalogs living-off-the-land binaries, scripts, and libraries that legitimate shipped Windows components can be coerced into doing beyond their intended job.
tools.when: Cross-check any signed binary or allowlisted script your enumeration surfaces on a Windows host — each entry lists the exact abuse command and MITRE mapping.

tools.name: linux-exploit-suggester
tools.desc: Off-host Linux audit tool (LES): reads kernel/distro fingerprints and cross-references them against current public exploit/PoC sets to rank exposure to known local privilege-escalation bugs.
tools.when: After enumeration, when you want a ranked, CVE-linked shortlist of which kernel-era exploits are plausibly worth testing on your own lab or CTF hosts.

tools.name: linux-exploit-suggester-2
tools.desc: Perl-based next-gen suggester that matches kernel/package versions against an exploit-db-derived list and can pull matching PoCs for review.
tools.when: A second candidate shortlist when LES disagrees, or old-style searching where you want the actual exploit source downloaded into your lab to read first.

tools.name: Watson
tools.desc: .NET tool that enumerates missing KBs on a Windows host and suggests exploits for applicable local privilege-escalation CVEs, with exploit links per finding.
tools.when: On lab Windows 10 (1507–2004) / Server 2016–2019 builds to map a CVE-to-exploit table fast; superseded for newer builds by WES-NG, which tracks the live MSRC feed.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/rasta-mouse/Watson && cd Watson && dotnet build -c Release

tools.name: WES-NG (wesng)
tools.desc: Windows Exploit Suggester - Next Generation: takes a `systeminfo` dump (or missing-patch list) and maps it against a continuously updated MSRC/NVD dataset to list missing patches and known exploits.
tools.when: Grab `systeminfo` from your Windows lab host, run wes.py on your workstation, and correlate patches offline for any supported OS from XP to Windows 11.
tools.install: pip install wesng && wes.py --update && wes.py systeminfo.txt

tools.name: Windows-Exploit-Suggester (legacy)
tools.desc: The 2014 original that coined the term; now archived because it depends on Microsoft's Security Bulletin Excel dump, which has been frozen since Q1 2017 — it can only address XP/Vista-era systems.
tools.when: Only retro lab images from before 2017; for any current Windows host use WES-NG, which reads the live MSRC feed instead.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/GDSSecurity/Windows-Exploit-Suggester && cd Windows-Exploit-Suggester && python windows-exploit-suggester.py --update

tools.name: Dirty Pipe (CVE-2022-0847)
tools.desc: Root POC for CVE-2022-0847 (Linux 5.8–5.16.x): abuses an uninitialized pipe_buffer flag to overwrite read-only page-cache data; this build overwrites /etc/passwd and restores it after popping a shell.
tools.when: On lab or CTF kernels inside the affected range when no misconfiguration path exists; expect it to fail cleanly on 5.16.11+ or backported-fix kernels.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/Arinerron/CVE-2022-0847-DirtyPipe-Exploit && cd CVE-2022-0847-DirtyPipe-Exploit && gcc -o exploit exploit.c && ./exploit

tools.name: PwnKit (CVE-2021-4034)
tools.desc: Qualys-reported pkexec (polkit) memory-corruption exploit giving a one-command root shell on unpatched systems; technically a setuid userspace flaw, not the kernel, but near-unrivaled in reliability when present.
tools.when: Applies to many distros of 2009–2022 vintage; `make dry-run` tests whether your own host is vulnerable without popping a shell.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/berdav/CVE-2021-4034 && cd CVE-2021-4034 && make && ./cve-2021-4034

tools.name: dirtycow (CVE-2016-5195)
tools.desc: The archived Dirty COW race-condition family (CVE-2016-5195) for kernels roughly up to 4.8.3: PoCs write into read-only mappings, e.g. splicing a new root account into /etc/passwd.
tools.when: Only legacy or sandboxed images that still run pre-2016-fix kernels; treat it as a historical exercise — modern distros are not exposed.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/firefart/dirtycow && cd dirtycow && gcc -pthread dirty.c -o dirty -lcrypt && ./dirty

tools.name: Rubeus
tools.desc: C# Kerberos abuse toolkit covering kerberoast, AS-REP roast, S4U constrained/unconstrained delegation, and golden/silver/diamond ticket forgery from any domain-joined host.
tools.when: Escalation inside Active Directory when you own an SPN-bearing or delegation-active account: request service tickets for offline cracking or impersonate users through s4u.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/GhostPack/Rubeus && cd Rubeus && dotnet build -c Release

tools.name: Impacket (GetUserSPNs.py)
tools.desc: Python Kerberos suite whose GetUserSPNs.py requests TGS tickets for services running under user accounts (Kerberoasting) and GetNPUsers.py hunts pre-auth-disabled accounts (AS-REProasting).
tools.when: Roasting from a Linux attack box (or WSL) where you have valid domain credentials but no Windows shell; also handles delegation-related ticket replay.
tools.install: python3 -m pipx install impacket && GetUserSPNs.py -request -dc-ip 10.0.0.1 corp.local/user

domains.name: Reconnaissance & OSINT
domains.tagline: Passive + active discovery: subdomains, DNS, historical data, people, leaks, and exposed assets.

tools.name: crt.sh
tools.desc: Search engine over public Certificate Transparency logs; finds every subdomain that ever appeared in an issued TLS certificate.
tools.when: Zero-setup first pass: instant historical subdomain list from issued certificates, no API keys required.

tools.name: Cert Spotter
tools.desc: SSLMate's certificate-transparency monitor with a JSON API; returns certificate-linked subdomains plus issuance history.
tools.when: Watch a domain for newly issued certificates over time and script the subdomain results.

tools.name: Subfinder
tools.desc: Fast passive subdomain discovery from 25+ sources (certificates, DNS, archives, APIs); runs well keyless and better with free API keys.
tools.when: The daily driver for breadth: batch-enumerate subdomains from many passive sources in seconds.

tools.name: Chaos
tools.desc: ProjectDiscovery's continuously updated subdomain dataset fed by bug-bounty programs, queried through the chaos-client CLI.
tools.when: Pull an up-to-date subdomain dataset for a listed asset instead of brute-forcing from scratch.

tools.name: VirusTotal
tools.desc: Huge passive-DNS and resolution graph; the domain 'Relations' tab exposes related hosts, resolutions, and SSL-cert domains.
tools.when: Correlate a domain's infrastructure graph and pull historical resolutions when an API key is at hand.

tools.name: Puredns
tools.desc: Pipeline-focused brute-forcer that mass-resolves candidates through validated public resolvers and filters wildcard responses automatically.
tools.when: Run a strong wordlist through trusted resolvers when you only want real, wildcard-free hits as pipeline output.

tools.name: Gobuster
tools.desc: Multi-mode brute-forcer whose DNS mode guesses subdomains from a wordlist and resolves each candidate.
tools.when: Quick DNS wordlist run when full resolver management is overkill for the scope.

tools.name: altdns
tools.desc: Generates wordlist-based permutations of known subdomains (prefixes, suffixes, number swaps) to rediscover forgotten hosts.
tools.when: Expand an existing host list into thousands of plausible neighbor names before resolving.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/infosec-au/altdns && cd altdns && pip3 install -r requirements.txt

tools.name: dnsgen
tools.desc: Pipes known domains through smart permutation rules (word insertion, affixing, number manipulation) to produce candidate subdomains.
tools.when: Compose with massdns (cat list | dnsgen - | massdns) for a fast generate-then-resolve enumerator.

tools.name: Amass
tools.desc: OWASP's one-stop subdomain engine: passive source scraping plus active brute forcing woven into an asset relationship graph.
tools.when: Long-running, full-scope enumeration where breadth and cross-asset correlation matter most.

tools.name: dnsx
tools.desc: High-performance DNS toolkit that resolves thousands of candidates and returns A/AAAA/CNAME/TXT with wildcard filtering.
tools.when: Filter a huge candidate list down to live hosts and fetch their records in a single pass.

tools.name: massdns
tools.desc: Extremely fast bulk resolver built to validate millions of candidates over UDP against a list of public resolvers.
tools.when: Feed permutation output at internet scale when normal resolver throughput rate-limits you.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/blechschmidt/massdns && cd massdns && make

tools.name: dig
tools.desc: BIND's universal DNS interrogation client: any record type, AXFR/IXFR zone transfer attempts, and scripting-friendly output.
tools.when: Verify individual records and try authorized zone transfers on targets you are cleared to test.

tools.name: DNSRecon
tools.desc: Python DNS recon kit: standard records, cache snooping, wildcard testing, brute force, and AXFR checks in one pass.
tools.when: Automate the full DNS interrogation checklist on a scope where hand-rolled dig commands get tedious.

tools.name: dnstwist
tools.desc: Permutation engine for typo-squatting and homograph lookalikes of a domain; resolves each variant to flag impersonation risk.
tools.when: Authorized brand-protection reviews: find lookalike domains that could phish or impersonate your organization.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/elceef/dnstwist && cd dnstwist && make all

tools.name: WHOIS
tools.desc: Standard registrar/registry client returning registration, owner, and nameserver records for domains and IP blocks.
tools.when: Pull registration dates and registrant metadata for a domain or range during authorized investigations.

tools.name: RDAP
tools.desc: openrdap's Go client for the modern RDAP protocol: structured JSON instead of loose text, with paging and entity linking.
tools.when: Script structured WHOIS-like lookups and follow registrant/registrar entities programmatically.

tools.name: ViewDNS.info
tools.desc: Free web aggregator for historical DNS, reverse IP, IP history, ASN/netblock maps, and WHOIS, with no API key.
tools.when: Cross-check old IPs, nameservers, or reverse lookups without pulling out heavy tooling.

tools.name: SecurityTrails
tools.desc: Full passive-DNS history plus subdomain and associated-domain APIs; the free tier works without keys.
tools.when: Reconstruct a domain's historical IP infrastructure to find withdrawn dev or staging servers.

tools.name: DNSDumpster
tools.desc: Visual subdomain, MX, and hostname map with optional on-page screenshots of discovered hosts.
tools.when: A graphical first look at a domain's DNS layout without signing up for anything.

tools.name: Rapid7 Open Data
tools.desc: Massive historical forward-DNS, reverse-DNS, and SSL scan datasets published as downloadable snapshots.
tools.when: Power offline historical enumeration across full internet snapshots with your own tooling.

tools.name: Wayback Machine
tools.desc: Internet Archive's snapshot library exposing old pages, removed endpoints, and historical response bodies for any URL.
tools.when: Recover deleted pages or inspect the evolution of login/config URLs during authorized historical research.

tools.name: urlscan.io
tools.desc: Renders and archives pages with full DOM, request log, and IP metadata; searchable by domain across every scan.
tools.when: See what a page actually loaded (networks, frameworks, subresources) without touching the target yourself.

tools.name: naabu
tools.desc: ProjectDiscovery's fast SYN scanner sweeping the top-N ports and handing live hosts to httpx/nuclei.
tools.when: Broad-but-quick port sweep across a large host list as pipeline input.

tools.name: masscan
tools.desc: Internet-scale SYN scanner (millions of packets/sec) that emits results in a format nmap can consume.
tools.when: Full-CIDR or internet-range sweeps when naabu's port sets are too small.

tools.name: RustScan
tools.desc: Sweeps all 65,535 ports in seconds and auto-pipes open ports into nmap service detection.
tools.when: Complete all-port coverage with minimal effort, letting nmap take over the fine details.

tools.name: Nmap
tools.desc: The canonical suite: stealth/connect scans, OS and service fingerprinting, version detection, and the NSE scripting engine.
tools.when: Deep service identification and low-rate version scans on a focused host set.

tools.name: httpx
tools.desc: Probes host lists for live web services, returning status, title, tech, CDN, and TLS fingerprints in one pass.
tools.when: Turn DNS/noise results into a clean inventory of live, web-facing hosts.

tools.name: WhatWeb
tools.desc: Signature-based fingerprint scanner matching headers, cookies, and HTML against 1,800+ technology definitions.
tools.when: Per-URL technology attribution across a moderately sized authorized target list.

tools.name: Retire.js
tools.desc: Scans page JavaScript for known-vulnerable library versions using DOM signatures.
tools.when: Fingerprint front-end dependencies and their exact versions on pages you are authorized to review.

tools.name: wafw00f
tools.desc: Sends harmless, identifiable probes to classify which WAF (if any) fronts a site, with vendor-specific signatures.
tools.when: Understand a target's defensive layer before deeper authorized testing.

tools.name: Feroxbuster
tools.desc: Rust-based recursive content discovery with smart filtering, auto-tuning, and server-config thesaurus support.
tools.when: Recursive directory/file brute force that stays fast on large authorized targets.

tools.name: dirsearch
tools.desc: Python content scanner with a large bundled dictionary, recursion, and multiple filter options.
tools.when: Quick wordlist-driven directory hunting with minimal setup.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/maurosoria/dirsearch && cd dirsearch && python3 dirsearch.py

tools.name: ffuf
tools.desc: Blazing-fast Go fuzzer for directories, virtual hosts, parameters, and headers via FUZZ placeholders.
tools.when: Flexible content, vhost, or parameter fuzzing where wordlists and matcher filters need fine control.

tools.name: Katana
tools.desc: ProjectDiscovery's crawler with headless and standard modes, strict scope control, and JS-rendered page crawling.
tools.when: Deep crawl restricted to in-scope hosts while capturing files, parameters, and tech hints.

tools.name: gospider
tools.desc: Crawler focused on discovering subdomains, paths, buckets, and endpoints across seed URLs, with optional JS scraping.
tools.when: Link newly found subdomains to their content and gather link graphs across many seeds.

tools.name: hakrawler
tools.desc: Simple, fast link-crawler emitting unique URLs, forms, and script references from the pages it visits.
tools.when: A lightweight URL harvest with zero configuration before heavier crawling kicks in.

tools.name: LinkFinder
tools.desc: Regex and JS-parser-based endpoint miner that extracts URLs and hidden API paths from JavaScript bundles.
tools.when: Map the API surface hidden inside a site's JavaScript bundles.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/GerbenJavado/LinkFinder && cd LinkFinder && pip3 install -r requirements.txt

tools.name: SecretFinder
tools.desc: Scans JS files for hardcoded keys, tokens, and credentials using cloud/API-specific signature patterns.
tools.when: Authorized audits: surface API keys or credentials accidentally shipped in client-side bundles.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/m4ll0k/SecretFinder && cd SecretFinder && pip3 install -r requirements.txt

tools.name: Shodan
tools.desc: The canonical search engine for exposed services: banners, ports, TLS certs, and device fingerprints across the internet.
tools.when: Find every internet-facing service an organization exposes, by banner, org, or certificate query.

tools.name: Censys
tools.desc: Continuous internet-scan dataset with faceted search over hosts, certificates, and services, plus ASN/hosting attribution.
tools.when: Correlate exposed services with certificates and hosting metadata at scale.

tools.name: FOFA
tools.desc: Cyberspace search engine indexing services, assets, and applications with powerful expression-based queries.
tools.when: Get an overlapping, independent view of your exposed asset surface from different data sources.

tools.name: BuiltWith
tools.desc: Maps the technology stack of any site and can reverse-search for other sites sharing the same tech footprint.
tools.when: Per-URL tech attribution and finding related deployments through shared vendor footprints.

tools.name: PublicWWW
tools.desc: Source-code search engine matching any snippet (analytics IDs, tracking pixels, specific JS) across indexed sites.
tools.when: Find other properties sharing the same tracking or CDN code to expand the authorized asset footprint.

tools.name: Sherlock
tools.desc: Checks 400+ sites for a username in seconds and maps social/forum presences back to one identity.
tools.when: Correlate an individual's handle across platforms during authorized persona research.

tools.name: WhatsMyName
tools.desc: Open-source username-presence database with auditable per-service detection patterns.
tools.when: When you need a maintained, inspectable detection database you can extend for niche platforms.

tools.name: theHarvester
tools.desc: Multipurpose passive gatherer of emails, subdomains, hosts, and employee names from search engines, PGP, and GitHub.
tools.when: First-pass sweep that combines the human and asset surface in a single command.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/laramies/theHarvester && cd theHarvester && pip3 install -r requirements.txt

tools.name: Hunter.io
tools.desc: Web and API domain email finder with address patterns, verification, and per-domain counts (rate-limited free tier).
tools.when: Discover and verify an organization's email address pattern during authorized intel gathering.

tools.name: holehe
tools.desc: Checks whether an email address is registered on hundreds of online services without sending any mail.
tools.when: Map which platforms an address is active on during an authorized investigation, minding service rate limits.

tools.name: Have I Been Pwned
tools.desc: Canonical breach-correlation service checking emails and password ranges against aggregated breached datasets.
tools.when: Identify which breaches an address appears in via the authenticated API during incident response.

tools.name: DeHashed
tools.desc: Searchable breach database with rich filtering by username, email, IP, and password hash.
tools.when: Structured correlation across breaches with exportable results for authorized investigations.

tools.name: Intelligence X
tools.desc: Search engine for documents, leaks, dark-web content, PGP keys, and historical web data, with a public API.
tools.when: Broadly triangulate a domain, email, or identity across leaks and scraped datasets.

tools.name: asnmap
tools.desc: ProjectDiscovery CLI mapping domains/IPs to ASNs and returning organization plus CIDR blocks from multiple sources.
tools.when: Expand scope correctly by pulling every org-owned netblock for a target.

tools.name: bgp.he.net
tools.desc: Hurricane Electric's BGP board showing ASN graphs, prefix announcements, and peering for any network.
tools.when: Visualize an organization's routing footprint, upstreams, and IPv4/IPv6 prefixes.

tools.name: ipinfo.io
tools.desc: IP metadata API providing geolocation, ASN, organization, hosting/cloud detection, and per-range domain lists.
tools.when: Attach location and hosting context to discovered IPs and enrich bulk results from the CLI.

domains.name: Red Team Infrastructure & Operations
domains.tagline: Authorized red team tooling: offensive toolkits, operations & reporting, emulation replays, objectives, pivoting, and practice labs.

tools.name: Impacket
tools.desc: Fortra's Python suite for network protocols: SMB/RPC/DCOM/WinRM/Kerberos plus the canonical example scripts (secretsdump, psexec, wmiexec, ntlmrelayx, GetADUsers) for credential harvesting and lateral movement.
tools.when: The workhorse of Windows-lab lateral movement and credential extraction during authorized tests — and the tooling blue teams build artifacts for.

tools.name: NetExec
tools.desc: The maintained successor to CrackMapExec: multi-protocol (SMB/WinRM/LDAP/MSSQL/SSH) networked exploitation toolkit with a plugin system and MCP integration.
tools.when: Fast credential-spraying and share/deployment outreach across a Windows estate in an authorized engagement or AD lab.

tools.name: Responder
tools.desc: lgandx's LLMNR/NBT-NS/mDNS responder that answers name-resolution queries on a test segment to reveal legacy protocol reliance and gather hashes for offline cracking.
tools.when: In a lab or scoped internal test with an explicit rule of engagement, to demonstrate why legacy name-resolution protocols must be disabled.

tools.name: PowerSploit
tools.desc: PowerShellMafia's PowerShell post-exploitation framework (CodeExecution, Recon, Exfiltration, Persistence, Privesc modules). Archived since 2021, yet it remains the canonical documented corpus of PowerShell tradecraft and a rich set of well-known signatures to exercise.
tools.when: Studying classic PowerShell post-exploitation module patterns and testing AMSI/logging detections against well-known tool output.

tools.name: SharpSploit
tools.desc: cobbr's C# post-exploitation library — the compiled mirror of PowerSploit-style tradecraft (execution, persistence, lateral movement, credentialing) for .NET agents.
tools.when: Reference for .NET-based post-exploitation modules and for training why compiled tooling changes the detection story.

tools.name: Nishang
tools.desc: samratashok's collection of PowerShell scripts (reverse shells, keylogging, persistence, scanners) that has historically driven entry-level and small-scope authorized testing.
tools.when: Quick PowerShell payload/auxiliary scripts in a Windows lab without dragging in a full framework.

tools.name: PoC-in-GitHub
tools.desc: nomi-sec's curated index tracking the latest public proof-of-concept exploits by CVE, with cross-references to Exploit-DB, Metasploit, and Nuclei templates.
tools.when: Keep a lab exploitation pipeline current: pull fresh, citation-tracked PoCs to evaluate and adapt in authorized testing.

tools.name: ired.team
tools.desc: The 'red team notes & experiments' GitBook by @spotheplanet — a structured walkthrough of offensive techniques (code execution, injection, persistence, lateral movement) with tool usage and detection notes, documented for education.
tools.when: Read-and-try technique references while building your own lab; the notes pair each experiment with what to look for from a defender's seat.

tools.name: HackTricks
tools.desc: The community wiki of pentesting techniques across web, Windows, Linux, AD, and cloud with tooling recipes and methodology — now maintained as the HackTricks-wiki GitBook project, runnable locally via Docker.
tools.when: Look up a technique or methodology in seconds; the most current single reference for esoteric protocol abuse and tool recipes.

tools.name: RedEye
tools.desc: CISA + PNNL's visual analytic for red-team operations: parses Cobalt Strike and other C2 logs, renders the multi-host attack graph, and supports 'campaign' export for blue-team handoff. Archived to maintenance mode — still the reference for C2 log visualization.
tools.when: Turn raw C2 logs into a shareable, annotated attack-path visualization to debrief stakeholders after an assessment.

tools.name: Ghostwriter
tools.desc: SpecterOps' open-source web application for red-team operations: client tracking, report writing, engagement documents (report templates, infographics), and evidence storage in one place.
tools.when: Run the operational/admin side of a red-team engagement — consistent client documentation, task tracking, and report generation.

tools.name: netdiscover

tools.name: ZMap
tools.desc: High-performance network scanner built for internet-wide research on services you own; the engine behind the ZMap project ('there are no secrets on the internet').

tools.name: AutoRecon

tools.name: Nettacker
tools.desc: OWASP scanner framework that scans layers of your network (ports, services, subdomains), correlates results, then runs follow-up module checks.

tools.name: WhatWeb

tools.name: Nikto

tools.when: Fast baseline sweep of a web server's exposed surface before deeper application testing.

tools.name: wafw00f
tools.desc: Identifies whether and which WAF (Cloudflare, ModSecurity, AWS WAF, etc.) fronts a web property, and fingerprints its version where detectable.
tools.when: Checking what edge protection sits in front of your applications before sending scan traffic through it.

tools.name: OWASP ZAP

tools.name: Wapiti

tools.name: Nuclei
tools.desc: ProjectDiscovery's template engine running thousands of YAML checks against web, network, and infrastructure targets to confirm known CVEs and misconfigurations.

tools.name: dalfox

tools.name: WPScan
tools.desc: WordPress scanner that fingerprints core, theme, and plugin versions against the WPScan vulnerability database and does user and weak-password checks.

tools.name: droopescan

tools.name: Nessus

tools.name: OpenSCAP

tools.name: Pacu

tools.name: Prowler

tools.when: Read-only posture reviews of your cloud subscriptions summarized into one report.

tools.name: Trivy

tools.name: Clair

tools.name: osv-scanner

tools.desc: Official NIST vulnerability feed and web UI; the reference source for CVE metadata, CPE mappings, and CVSS metrics.

tools.desc: Google's hosted query engine that flags weak Content-Security-Policy directives that allow XSS to slip through.
tools.when: When the target sends a CSP and you want to quickly grade its effectiveness and find bypassable directives.
tools.install: Open the hosted checker at https://csp-evaluator.withgoogle.com

tools.name: SecurityHeaders.com
tools.desc: Scans a URL's response headers against the OWASP Secure Headers Project and scores the hardening state.
tools.when: When you want an instant, shareable header hardening report for a site you own or administer.

tools.name: headers.dev
tools.desc: Simple API/website that returns all response headers of a URL for quick inspection from the terminal.
tools.when: When you want a fast, no-install way to pull and eyeball a target's response headers.

tools.name: httpx
tools.desc: ProjectDiscovery's fast HTTP toolkit that fingerprints hosts, technologies, status codes, and response headers at scale.
tools.when: When you need to bulk-collect status codes, headers, and tech fingerprints across hundreds of in-scope hosts.

domains.name: Wireless & Bluetooth Security
domains.tagline: WiFi capture and cracking, PMKID and precomputed tables, RF spectrum analysis, WPS auditing, and Bluetooth — all framed for labs and gear you own or are authorized to audit.

tools.name: airmon-ng
tools.desc: Script from the aircrack-ng suite that flips a supported chipset into monitor mode (and back), kills interfering processes, and reports adapter capabilities.
tools.when: First step of any authorized Wi-Fi test: enable monitor mode on the adapter you own and confirm chipset/driver support before capture or injection.

tools.name: iw
tools.desc: The nl80211 wireless CLI: lists radios and phy capabilities and sets interface modes (monitor/managed) without legacy wrapper scripts.
tools.when: When airmon-ng's heuristics stall, set mode=monitor by hand on an interface you control and verify the phy supports injection.

tools.name: macchanger
tools.desc: Spoofs a wireless interface's MAC address so lab captures originate from an anonymized, disposable local address.
tools.when: Before a capture or wifite run in your lab when you want a clean identity that is trivially reset between tests.

tools.name: tcpdump
tools.desc: Classic packet capture tool; on a monitor interface it proves the card actually sees 802.11 beacons, probe requests, and management frames.
tools.when: Smoke-test the adapter: run tcpdump on mon0 and confirm frames before starting a long airodump or Kismet session on your own hardware.

tools.name: airodump-ng
tools.desc: Channel-by-channel capture of BSSIDs, clients, signal, and encryption; logs raw PCAPc and collects probe requests and association traffic from nearby APs you can hear.
tools.when: Start discovery here on hardware you control: target channels, capture beacon/probe data, and note handshake material for later offline work.

tools.name: horst
tools.desc: Lightweight ncurses 802.11 monitor with channel scanning, signal histograms, and per-client statistics, no daemon or web UI required.
tools.when: A minimal TUI for quick signal and channel-noise checks mid-test in your lab when Kismet is overkill.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/br101/horst && cd horst && make && sudo make install

tools.name: Kismet
tools.desc: Multi-protocol passive detector with server + web UI; tracks 802.11, Bluetooth, and SDR sources and logs probe traffic for long-running surveys.
tools.when: Long-running passive mapping of your authorized airspace, or intrusion-detection-style monitoring over your own test environment.

tools.name: Wireshark
tools.desc: Universal dissector with deep 802.11 and EAPOL support; supply the PMK to decrypt WPA traffic you captured from your own APs.
tools.when: Post-capture dissection of handshakes, probe requests, and Bluetooth frames from gear you own.

tools.name: wifite2
tools.desc: Automated lab auditor: scans, lets you pick a target you own, then drives deauth, handshake capture, and cracking (or WPS work via reaver/bully) from one menu.
tools.when: Repeatable capture-to-crack runs against your own APs where one command replaces a long manual chain.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/derv82/wifite2.git && cd wifite2 && sudo python3 setup.py install

tools.name: aireplay-ng
tools.desc: Frame injection and replay from aircrack-ng: sends deauthentication frames and replays captured packets to force a fresh 4-way handshake from an idle station.
tools.when: In your lab, deauth a stationary test client to accelerate handshake capture and PSK policy validation on APs you manage.

tools.name: mdk4
tools.desc: Multi-purpose 802.11 tool with aggressive deauthentication, probe-testing, and fuzzing modes (mdk4 w / m / f) for validating client and AP reactions.
tools.when: Stress the deauth resistance of APs you own and verify clients reconnect cleanly and re-associate after interference.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/aircrack-ng/mdk4 && cd mdk4 && make && sudo make install

tools.name: hcxdumptool
tools.desc: Raw PCAPNG capture of PMKID and EAPOL material using a single adapter; PMKID needs no connected client and no deauthentication.
tools.when: On APs you own that expose PMKID, grab the token passively and skip the whole deauth-and-reassociate dance.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/ZerBea/hcxdumptool.git && cd hcxdumptool && make && sudo make install

tools.name: hcxtools
tools.desc: Converts hcxdumptool PCAPNG captures into hashcat/john-ready hash formats (mode 22000), filtering duplicates and invalid entries.
tools.when: After capture, normalize EAPOL/PMKID material into 22000 format so GPU testing can start on your own hashes.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/ZerBea/hcxtools.git && cd hcxtools && make && sudo make install

tools.name: aircrack-ng
tools.desc: The suite's cracking core validates WPA/WPA2 handshakes against wordlists (and PTW for WEP), verifying recovered keys against the captured material.
tools.when: Offline verification of PSK strength from captures taken against your own access points.

tools.name: hashcat
tools.desc: GPU password cracker with native WPA-PBKDF2-PMKID+EAPOL kernels (mode 22000) for turning captured handshake hashes into keys at high speed.
tools.when: When masks/rules outgrow aircrack-ng and you have a GPU available for faster PMK derivation in your lab.

tools.name: cowpatty
tools.desc: Wordlist PSK verifier that confirms candidate passphrases against captured handshake material without extra dependencies.
tools.when: Clean no-frills confirmation that a candidate passphrase matches your capture before moving on.

tools.name: airolib-ng
tools.desc: Builds precomputed PMK tables keyed by (ESSID, password) from wordlists and serves hashes to aircrack-ng for instant reuse.
tools.when: Repeatedly audit the same ESSID: precompute its PMK table once, then crack many captured handshakes instantly in your lab.

tools.name: genpmk
tools.desc: cowpatty's companion that precomputes the per-ESSID PMK seed file from a wordlist for fast later handshake verification.
tools.when: One-off ESSID precompute when you do not want the full airolib database machinery.

tools.name: wash
tools.desc: Passive scanner for WPS-enabled access points: reports WPS state and lockout status without launching an active registrar exchange.
tools.when: Recon your own estate for WPS-enabled APs before deciding a PIN audit is even worthwhile.

tools.name: Reaver
tools.desc: The reference WPS registrar brute-forcer: probes PIN transaction logic and, on vulnerable lab routers, recovers the WPS PIN and derived WPA-PSK.
tools.when: Confirm your lab AP's WPS lockout and PIN policy — most modern routers lock out after failures, which is the outcome you want to verify.

tools.name: Bully
tools.desc: C reimplementation of the WPS PIN attack with more forgiving association handling and clearer logging than reaver.
tools.when: When reaver stalls against your own AP, bully's retry logic often completes the audit where reaver cannot.

tools.name: pixiewps
tools.desc: Offline WPS computation tool (R1/R2/RB) that takes the e-S1/e-S2 nonces captured by reaver/bully and recovers the PIN without brute force.
tools.when: On older WPS APs you own with predictable RNG, run pixiewps over a reaver capture to recover the PIN in seconds instead of hours.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/wiire/pixiewps && cd pixiewps && make && sudo make install

tools.name: airbase-ng
tools.desc: Creates 802.11 software access points from a monitor-mode card; the primitive behind most fake-AP tests, including WEP/WPA emulation and injection.
tools.when: Stand up a disposable simulated AP in your own lab for behavior tests and client-device compatibility checks.

tools.name: hostapd-wpe
tools.desc: Patched hostapd that adds WPA enterprise (PEAP/MSCHAPv2) credential capture for controlled authentication tests in your lab.
tools.when: Building an enterprise authentication test rig against client configs you control, capturing challenge/response pairs for offline review.
tools.install: git clone https://gitlab.com/kalilinux/packages/hostapd-wpe && cd hostapd-wpe && sudo make -C hostapd install

tools.name: wifiphisher
tools.desc: Carries out evil-twin attacks with a real captive portal: clones a target AP you own, then serves phishing templates to harvest credentials and PMKID.
tools.when: Demo rogue-AP and social-engineering tradecraft only against APs and clients you own or explicitly control in the lab.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/wifiphisher/wifiphisher && cd wifiphisher && sudo python3 setup.py install

tools.name: fluxion
tools.desc: Evil-twin toolkit that deauths a target you own, runs a cloned fake AP, and feeds a captive-login page to collect passphrases.
tools.when: Scripted WPA2 capture plus captive-portal phishing against your own APs and test accounts.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/FluxionNetwork/fluxion && cd fluxion && sudo ./fluxion.sh

tools.name: eaphammer
tools.desc: Targeted evil-twin and enterprise attack tool with WPA/WPA2 enterprise automation, KARMA, and credential-database harvesting for lab demos.
tools.when: Enterprise (802.1X) test scenarios against your own lab RADIUS and client fleets before touching production gear.

tools.name: bettercap
tools.desc: Host-side network and monitoring framework whose BLE module runs recon, sniffs, and offers a ble.proxy that can pose as a peripheral for lab devices.
tools.when: Scriptable, host-based BLE enumeration and proxy testing of your own peripherals without dedicated sniffing hardware.

tools.name: Ubertooth
tools.desc: Open 2.4 GHz radio plus host software for Bluetooth capture and injection; follows Classic BT hopping patterns and BLE channels on the Ubertooth One dongle.
tools.when: Hardware-level analysis of hop patterns, advertising data, and pairing behavior of peripherals you own.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/greatscottgadgets/ubertooth && cd ubertooth/host && mkdir build && cd build && cmake .. && make && sudo make install

tools.name: btlejack
tools.desc: Sniffs and interacts with BLE connections via nRF24-family USB dongles; supports jamming and session recovery from previously captured keys.
tools.when: Low-cost BLE session auditing of your own accessories — map advertising channels and check for key reuse across connections.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/virtualabs/btlejack && cd btlejack && make && sudo make install

tools.name: BlueZ
tools.desc: Linux's Bluetooth stack: bluetoothctl, btmon, hcitool, and gatttool expose controller state, HCI packets, and GATT services.
tools.when: Free host-side visibility before reaching for RF hardware; btmon gives clean pairing and connection traces for your own adapters.

tools.name: bt_audit (BTSD)
tools.desc: The BTSD Bluetooth audit suite: psm_scan maps L2CAP PSM services and rfcomm_scan enumerates RFCOMM channels on local or paired devices.
tools.when: A quick authorized inventory of services your own BT peripherals expose before deeper hardware testing.
tools.install: Download bt_audit-0.1.1.tar.gz from betaversion.net, extract, and run make in the src directory

tools.name: Proxmark3 (Iceman)
tools.desc: Proxmark3 hardware plus the Iceman project firmware: read, clone, and analyze low- and high-frequency tags including MIFARE, ISO14443, and iCLASS.
tools.when: Physical badge and tag auditing of assets you own — sniff reader/tag sessions and validate card copy resistance.

tools.name: libnfc
tools.desc: Portable NFC library with CLI tools (nfc-list, nfc-read, nfc-mfclassic) for enumerating and reading tags through USB readers.
tools.when: With an ACR122U-class reader, enumerate and read blocks on cards you own without dedicated hardware.

tools.name: mfoc
tools.desc: The classic MIFARE Classic hardnested tool: exploits leaked (weak) keys to recover the full key set of a card you own.
tools.when: Recover all sectors of a weak-key MIFARE Classic card in your lab for badge cloning and access-control red-team tests.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/nfc-tools/mfoc && cd mfoc && ./autogen.sh && ./configure && make && sudo make install

tools.name: mfcuk
tools.desc: MIFARE Classic dark-side attack tool that recovers keys on cards whose PRNG hands out predictable nonces.
tools.when: When mfoc's hardnested path fails against a card you own, mfcuk's dark-side vector is the fallback.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/nfc-tools/mfcuk && cd mfcuk && ./autogen.sh && ./configure && make && sudo make install

tools.name: RTL-SDR
tools.desc: Cheap USB software-defined radio receiver: drivers plus rtl_test, rtl_fm, and rtl_tcp for raw IQ sampling and streaming.
tools.when: The base RF capture hardware and tooling: stream IQ captures into gqrx or inspectrum for analysis of signals in your own environment.

tools.name: gqrx
tools.desc: GNU Radio-based desktop receiver that demodulates and displays spectrum and waterfall from an SDR dongle.
tools.when: Interactively scan ISM bands and identify transmitters or interference sources before blaming your own Wi-Fi gear.

tools.name: inspectrum
tools.desc: Offline analysis of recorded IQ or audio: renders interactive water-falls to identify modulation, timing, and packet structure.
tools.when: After recording bursts with rtl_sdr, step through symbols to identify the modulation type before deeper decoding.

tools.name: GNU Radio
tools.desc: Flow-graph framework for designing and running custom demodulators and decoders; the engine underneath gqrx and many SDR toolchains.
tools.when: When you must decode a custom protocol from captured samples of signals you are authorized to receive.

domains.name: Application Security (SAST, DAST, Secrets & SCA)
domains.tagline: Product-security gates for the code and recipes you ship: SAST, DAST, secrets detection, dependency (SCA), fuzzing, and threat modeling — nested by technique for dev and DevProd teams.

tools.name: Semgrep
tools.desc: Lightweight app-sec static analyzer for 30+ languages: YAML rules that read like the code they match, bundled security packs (p/security-audit, p/owasp-top-ten), and pre-commit/CI/IDE hooks.
tools.when: The default SAST layer for any dev team: run it per-PR in CI or in the editor to catch injection, dangerous-API misuse, and hardcoded secrets before merge.

tools.name: CodeQL
tools.desc: GitHub's query-based analysis engine that databases your code and runs QL queries to find vulnerability classes; the CLI is free and the strongest maintained rule sets ship through GitHub code scanning.
tools.when: High-signal coverage on GitHub-hosted repos: enable code scanning on schedules and PRs, then drop into the CodeQL CLI to run or author bespoke queries on a local database.
tools.install: Download the CodeQL CLI bundle from github.com/github/codeql-action/releases

tools.name: SonarQube
tools.desc: Self-hosted code-quality and security platform: the Community Edition runs hundreds of static rules over 30+ languages with dashboards, quality gates, and trended security reports.
tools.when: When an org needs a shared, dashboard-visible quality gate and SAST history instead of per-commit CLI output.

tools.name: Bandit
tools.desc: PyCQA's AST-based Python analyzer flags common first-party mistakes — SQLi, shell injection, pickles, eval, weak crypto, and path permissions — with a low-noise report you can tune.
tools.when: A no-config SAST pass for Python services: pip-install, point it at the package directory, and wire into CI.

tools.name: gosec
tools.desc: SecureGo's Go static analyzer walking ASTs and data flow to find hardcoded creds, weak TLS configs, unsafe sql/exec sinks, and integer-overflow risk in first-party Go code.
tools.when: The quick Go-specific SAST gate in CI, alongside or before a language-agnostic scanner like Semgrep.

tools.name: Brakeman
tools.desc: The reference Ruby on Rails scanner: static analysis tuned to Rails patterns (SQL injection, XSS, mass assignment, unsafe deserialization) with actionable remediation notes.
tools.when: Any Rails/Ruby codebase in CI: one command and the framework-aware findings are worth more than generic engines.

tools.name: SpotBugs + FindSecBugs
tools.desc: SpotBugs is the Java bytecode static analyzer; the FindSecBugs plugin adds 120+ security patterns (path traversal, XXE, weak crypto, injection sinks) to its findings.
tools.when: Java/JVM builds that need bytecode-level findings beyond a pattern scanner — wire the Maven/Gradle plugin into the build.

tools.name: Security Code Scan (.NET)
tools.desc: An open-source Roslyn analyzer that adds taint-tracking security rules for C#: SQL injection, deserialization, path traversal, and cryptographically weak constructs.
tools.when: .NET solutions in CI: install the NuGet analyzer and let it run inline with the build for zero extra infra.

tools.name: eslint-plugin-security
tools.desc: Node.js Security's ESLint plugin that flags hardcoded credentials, unsafe regex, non-literal require/child_process, and other JS security smells directly in lint output.
tools.when: Node/JS repos already on ESLint: enable the security ruleset for the fastest in-editor security feedback.

tools.name: Psalm
tools.desc: PHP static analysis with a taint-check mode (`--taint-analysis`) that traces untrusted input to sinks for SQLi, XSS, file access, and more.
tools.when: PHP projects wanting first-party vulnerability detection in CI without a managed SaaS.

tools.name: OWASP ZAP
tools.desc: Full web/API security scanner: intercepting proxy, spider, passive + active scanning, and a programmable REST API; ships zap-baseline.py and Docker images ready for automated CI DAST.
tools.when: Stand up per-app DAST: run the baseline scan against a staging build nightly or per-PR, then use the proxy for manual testing of tricky auth flows.

tools.name: Nuclei
tools.desc: ProjectDiscovery's template-driven vulnerability scanner with 8,000+ community YAML templates (CVEs, exposures, misconfigs) and fast protocol-level scanning.
tools.when: Broad templated coverage across an app inventory — feed it URLs/HTTP inputs in CI and get CVE-check results without bespoke rules.

tools.name: Wapiti
tools.desc: Python black-box web scanner performing GET/POST parameter fuzzing for OWASP classes (SQLi, XSS, file inclusion, command injection) with a DAST REST API.
tools.when: Scriptable scan of internal apps where you want a ZAP alternative with no Docker dependency and easy output automation.

tools.name: Burp Suite
tools.desc: PortSwigger's leading web application testing platform: Community gives the intercepting proxy, history, and Repeater/Decoder manual tools free; the automated scanner is paid.
tools.when: Manual pentest-style review of your own apps: drive the app through the proxy, then replay, tamper, and fuzz individual requests by hand.

tools.name: Arachni
tools.desc: Ruby-based web scanner with a rich modular architecture and REST/WebSocket APIs; unmaintained for several years but deployable standalone or embedded.
tools.when: Legacy stacks that ship its browser-based grid, or when you want its fingerprinting modules self-hosted — otherwise prefer ZAP or Nuclei.

tools.name: RESTler
tools.desc: Microsoft's stateful REST API fuzzer: ingests your OpenAPI spec, infers producer-consumer request dependencies, then fuzzes request sequences to surface 5xx crashes, resource leaks, and security-checker violations.
tools.when: API-only DAST beyond the HTML UI: after a ZAP baseline, point RESTler at the schema to grind through every endpoint and parameter combination.
tools.install: Download the RESTler release archive from github.com/microsoft/restler-fuzzer/releases

tools.name: Schemathesis
tools.desc: Property-based API testing against OpenAPI/GraphQL schemas: generates edge-case and adversarial requests and can run its built-in security checks against each response.
tools.when: Shift-left API testing in CI where you want schema-driven request generation plus explicit security assertions, with a GiHub Action.

tools.name: OWASP Dependency-Check
tools.desc: OWASP's SCA utility that fingerprints declared dependencies (Java, .NET, Python, Node, Ruby, Go, Rust, and more) against NVD and other feeds, emitting CVSS-scored known-CVE reports.
tools.when: The reference dependency gate for build output: run on release builds to block known-vulnerable libraries before they ship; the first run downloads the full NVD feed.

tools.name: OSV-Scanner
tools.desc: Google's open-source vulnerability scanner (the engine behind GitHub Dependabot) that matches lockfiles and SBOMs against the OSV.dev database — fast, quiet, and free of NVD feed friction.
tools.when: Snappy per-lockfile check in CI (package-lock.json, go.sum, requirements, poetry, etc.) when you want OSV-only coverage without a heavyweight feed.

tools.name: pip-audit
tools.desc: Python Packaging Authority's scanner audits direct and transitive PyPI requirements against OSV/advisory feeds, and can auto-fix vulnerable packages installed locally (--fix).
tools.when: Python-only repos: the smallest honest way to keep requirements.txt/pyproject dependency lists clean as part of pre-commit or CI.

tools.name: npm audit
tools.desc: Bundled npm command that checks the installed dependency tree against the npm advisory database and can auto-downgrade (`npm audit fix`) where a patched version exists.
tools.when: Zero-setup Node dependency gate: run in CI after install and block on high/critical findings.
tools.install: Bundled with npm — no install needed

tools.name: govulncheck
tools.desc: The Go team's vulnerability scanner: uses static analysis of function call graphs to report only findings that are actually reachable from your code, not every transitive dependency.
tools.when: Go modules in CI: `govulncheck ./...` gives call-reachable CVEs with far less noise than generic SCA.

tools.name: cargo-audit
tools.desc: RustSec's lockfile auditor (cargo.lock) reporting known vulnerabilities from the RustSec Advisory Database, with `cargo audit fix` for auto-updates.
tools.when: Rust projects in CI: run against the committed Cargo.lock every PR.

tools.name: Grype + Syft
tools.desc: Anchore's pair: Syft generates SPDX/CycloneDX SBOMs from images and filesystems, Grype matches them against multiple vulnerability feeds with reachability-aware reporting in some modes.
tools.when: Container-first SCA inside the build: generate the SBOM, scan it with Grype, and attach it as a build attestation.

tools.name: Gitleaks
tools.desc: Fastest OSS secret scanner: a single Go binary that sweeps full git history or plain directories with 200+ regex rules for API keys, tokens, and passwords, exporting JSON/SARIF with pre-commit and GitHub Action hooks.
tools.when: Gate every repo and pipeline: full-history sweep when onboarding, then pre-commit/PR scans from then on; the default before anything heavier.

tools.name: TruffleHog
tools.desc: Secret scanner with 600+ credential detectors that actively verify matches against vendor APIs to separate live credentials from noise; scans git, GitHub/GitLab orgs, S3, Docker, and filesystems.
tools.when: Org-wide sweeps where knowing which leaked credentials still work matters more than raw match counts.

tools.name: detect-secrets
tools.desc: Yelp's Python scanner that audits a repo once into a .secrets.baseline then diffs only new lines in pre-commit/CI, so only genuinely new secrets get flagged instead of the same approved ones on every run.
tools.when: Teams worn out by re-flagged false positives: do the one-time audit + baseline review, then let it police new commits.

tools.name: ggshield
tools.desc: GitGuardian's open-source CLI that scans commits, PRs, and CI output for secrets with pre-commit hooks and does live-verification checks; the hosted dashboard beyond it is commercial.
tools.when: Pre-commit + CI hook coverage when you already use GitGuardian's engine conventions and want its detectors locally.

tools.name: AFL++
tools.desc: The maintained successor of American Fuzzy Lop: coverage-guided in-process fuzzing with QEMU and Frida modes, custom mutators, and calibration for both source and pure-binary targets.
tools.when: Fuzz any C/C++ parser or binary you own: compile with afl-clang-fast, seed a corpus, and let parallel instances grind for crashes and hangs.

tools.name: libFuzzer
tools.desc: Clang's in-process, coverage-guided fuzzing library: link a fuzz target function, enable -fsanitize=fuzzer,address, and get corpus minimization plus sanitizer-detected crashes for free.
tools.when: C/C++ libraries in LLVM builds where in-process fuzzing with ASan/UBSan finds more per second than fork-based engines.

tools.name: Honggfuzz
tools.desc: Google's coverage-guided fuzzer with hardware-based performance counters (Intel PT), persistent mode, and simple configuration; strong on Linux for network and file-parsing targets.
tools.when: When you want hardware-assisted coverage on Linux or a fast standalone alternative to AFL++ for your parsers.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/google/honggfuzz.git && cd honggfuzz && make

tools.name: Jazzer
tools.desc: CodeIntelligence's JVM coverage-guided fuzzer built on libFuzzer: fuzzes Java/Kotlin through a JNI agent with sanitizer-like detection of OOM, stack overflow, and exception-based failures.
tools.when: Grab your @FuzzTest hooks and parse untrusted Java input (JSON, XML, protobuf) to find exceptions, hangs, and memory issues.
tools.install: Download the Jazzer release archive from github.com/CodeIntelligenceTesting/jazzer/releases

tools.name: OSS-Fuzz
tools.desc: Google's open-source continuous fuzzing service for critical OSS: builds your project with sanitizers, runs libFuzzer/AFL++/Honggfuzz at scale, and files issues when new bugs are found.
tools.when: You maintain a widely-used open-source library with a C/C++/Golang/Rust surface and want Google-scale fuzzing with zero infra of your own.
tools.install: Follow google/oss-fuzz quickstart (Docker + build.sh) — no direct install

tools.name: ProFuzzBench
tools.desc: TU Delft's highly-configurable benchmark for stateful protocol fuzzing: 8 real network protocols with reproducible AFLNet/AFL++/libFuzzer harnesses and Docker-based campaigns.
tools.when: Evaluate or compare protocol fuzzers, or learn stateful fuzzing against realistic targets before applying it to your own servers.

tools.name: OWASP Threat Dragon
tools.desc: OWASP's open-source threat-model tooling for STRIDE/LINDDUN workflows with a browser-based or desktop diagram UI that exports models to JSON for CI review automation.
tools.when: Teams that want a shared, reviewable threat model per service without forcing every engineer to learn a coding DSL.

tools.name: pytm
tools.desc: OWASP's Pythonic framework: define your system as Python objects and generate data-flow diagrams, STRIDE threat lists, and mitigations — diffs cleanly in git and runs in CI.
tools.when: When the threat model must live in the repo and be code-reviewed like any other artifact, or is derived from your IaC definitions.

tools.name: Threagile
tools.desc: Agile threat-modeling toolkit driven by a YAML architecture description: auto-generates STRIDE-based risks, diagrams, and reports via CLI or Kubernetes operator, with a rules engine.
tools.when: Organizations that standardize on YAML-first threat modeling and want automated risk catalogs from the same source of truth.

domains.name: Blue Team — Defense & Detection
domains.tagline: Tools defenders run to detect, hunt, and respond on their own estate: SIEM, endpoint and network telemetry, detection engineering, response automation, and hostile edge hardening.

tools.name: Elastic Stack (ELK)
tools.desc: Reference open-core free SIEM: ships logs via Elastic Agent/Beats into Elasticsearch, renders detections and dashboards in Kibana, and runs the detection engine on EQL/ES|QL, Sigma, and YARA rule content.
tools.when: Your first-stop free SOC when you want one cluster for full-text log search plus security detections and can absorb Elasticsearch operations.
tools.install: docker run -d -p 9200:9200 -e discovery.type=single-node docker.elastic.co/elasticsearch/elasticsearch:9.5.1 (then add Kibana + Elastic Agent via the docs)

tools.name: Wazuh
tools.desc: Open-source XDR/SIEM pairing an Elastic/OpenSearch backend with a unified agent delivering file-integrity monitoring, security configuration assessment, vulnerability detection, active response, and compliance dashboards.
tools.when: When you want SIEM plus an endpoint agent in one cohesive open bundle with built-in compliance reporting (PCI-DSS/HIPAA/SOC 2) and less manual Elasticsearch plumbing.

tools.name: Security Onion
tools.desc: Turnkey NSM distribution bundling Suricata (detection + full packet capture), Zeek metadata, Elastic/Kibana dashboards, osquery host visibility, and alert/case management into a single guided install.
tools.when: Fastest way to stand up a whole detection-and-response platform on one box when you don't want to assemble SIEM, IDS, and ingestion yourself.
tools.install: Download the ISO from https://securityonion.com, install, then run: sudo so-setup-network (guided wizard)

tools.name: Graylog
tools.desc: Open-source log management and SIEM on Elasticsearch/OpenSearch storage, with flexible extraction pipelines (streams + pipeline rules) for parsing, enrichment, GEOIP, and threat-intel tagging.
tools.when: Log centralization when you want clean server-side pipelines to poll, enrich, and route messages — without running a fleet of endpoint agents or Wazuh-style XDR.
tools.install: curl -L -o graylog-repo.deb https://packages.graylog2.org/repo/packages/graylog-7.1-repository_latest.deb && sudo dpkg -i graylog-repo.deb && sudo apt-get install graylog-server

tools.name: Velociraptor
tools.desc: Open-source DFIR + endpoint-monitoring framework (Rapid7): fleet-wide hunts over VQL, live evidence collection across thousands of hosts, and a monitoring engine running Sigma detections against ETW/eBPF events in real time.
tools.when: Endpoint hunt and incident response at scale — triage every host, collect volatile evidence, then keep them watched with live detections; often the 'endpoint SIEM' half of a free SOC.

tools.name: Splunk Free
tools.desc: Free perpetual tier of the commercial SIEM incumbent: SPL search over indexed events and mature dashboards/alerts, capped at 500 MB/day ingest; a full license scales past the cap.
tools.when: When you want enterprise SIEM UX and Splunk's integration ecosystem at zero cost for a lab or small estate, or as the benchmark when evaluating an all-open stack.

tools.name: Velociraptor
tools.desc: Open-source endpoint visibility and collection platform: deploy lightweight agents, run prebuilt forensic artifacts and fleet-wide VQL hunts, push live Sigma/EQL detections, and pull processes, disk, and registry data to a central server.
tools.when: Hunt across every host you own in one place: stand up the server, enroll agents, and answer 'what happened here' with fleet-wide queries and persistent monitoring.

tools.name: osquery
tools.desc: SQL-powered agent exposing OS state — processes, sockets, files, users, listeners — as queryable tables; fire fleet-wide queries instantly and schedule packs, managed via Fleet (FleetDM).
tools.when: Lightweight cross-platform telemetry when you want to 'SELECT' answers from every host and ship results to SIEM; the armchair-friendly complement to Velociraptor.

tools.name: Sysmon
tools.desc: Windows Sysinternals driver that logs high-fidelity process creation, network connections, and file writes beyond default auditing; pair with the SwiftOnSecurity or Modular config for a solid hunting baseline.
tools.when: On every Windows host where you need attacker-action visibility and can ship its event log to your SIEM — no heavy agent required.

tools.name: LimaCharlie
tools.desc: Cloud-native SecOps platform: an EDR sensor streams verbose endpoint telemetry over TLS in real time, and a YAML-based Detection & Response engine runs the full open Sigma ruleset with automated response actions.
tools.when: When you want EDR plus detection-as-code in the cloud without running a SIEM or agent server yourself; the free Community org covers small estates and labs.
tools.install: preinstalled (cloud SaaS) — create a free Community org at limacharlie.io, run the per-OS sensor installer, and enable the Sigma ruleset

tools.name: RITA
tools.desc: Active Countermeasures' open-source network-traffic analysis framework that ingests Zeek logs and scores beaconing, long connections, DNS tunneling, and threat-intel hits for hunting C2.
tools.when: Turn passive Zeek metadata into C2 hunting: run it against captured or rolling Zeek logs to surface beacons and suspicious external connections a normal SIEM query would miss.
tools.install: Download the installer from https://github.com/activecm/rita/releases, then: tar -xf rita-<version>-installer.tar.gz && sudo ./rita-*/install_rita.sh

tools.name: Zeek
tools.desc: Passive network-analysis framework (formerly Bro) feeding rich protocol metadata, file hashes, and events to hunting and SIEM pipelines via 70+ log types — the data source RITA and BZAR consume.
tools.when: The metadata layer for hunt stacks: deploy the sensor, let its conn/dns/http logs flow into Elastic or RITA, and never push raw packets for every question.
tools.install: sudo apt-get install zeek (zeek.org apt repo) or docker pull zeek/zeek

tools.name: Suricata
tools.desc: OISF's multi-threaded open-source IDS/IPS engine inspecting traffic with Snort-compatible rules at multi-Gbps speeds and emitting structured EVE JSON alerts (plus PCAP) straight into your SIEM.
tools.when: High-throughput signature detection at your network edge or segmentation points; the default self-managed NIDS with an IPS fallback.
tools.install: sudo add-apt-repository ppa:oisf/suricata-stable && sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install suricata && sudo suricata-update

tools.name: Snort 3
tools.desc: Cisco's next-generation open-source NIDS/IPS: multi-threaded, Lua-based policy language, faster pattern matching than 2.x, tuned with Talos rules.
tools.when: When you prefer Cisco's Talos rule ecosystem, are migrating an existing Snort 2 deployment, or want SnortML-driven engine tuning.
tools.install: sudo apt-get install snort3 (Ubuntu 22.04+; otherwise build from the source tarball on snort.org)

tools.name: Zeek
tools.desc: Passive network-analysis framework (formerly Bro) that logs rich protocol metadata, file hashes, and events across 70+ log types for later forensics instead of blocking in real time.
tools.when: Deep protocol visibility feeding a SIEM or full-packet archive — run it beside Suricata/Snort because Zeek answers 'what happened' while the IDS engine answers 'alert'.
tools.install: sudo apt-get install zeek (zeek.org apt repo) or docker pull zeek/zeek

tools.name: tshark
tools.desc: Wireshark's terminal sibling: captures, decrypts, and prints live or offline traffic with the full dissector set and CSV/JSON/raw output for scripted analysis.
tools.when: Get Wireshark-grade dissection piped into grep, jq, or detection pipelines without a GUI — the workhorse for carving answers out of PCAP on servers and sensors.

tools.name: tcpdump
tools.desc: Command-line packet capture using Berkeley Packet Filter (BPF) expressions; the standard for headless logging and scripted sniffing on any host.
tools.when: Rolling capture on a sensor, router, or lab box where no GUI exists, or when you need a quick BPF-filtered sniff to confirm what is on the wire.

tools.name: Auditd
tools.desc: Linux Audit framework userspace (auditd, auditctl, ausearch) recording privileged actions, file access, and security-relevant events to an immutable log across reboots.
tools.when: Build the audit trail that CIS/STIG rules require on Linux hosts and answer 'who accessed what, when' during a response with ausearch.

tools.name: Logstash
tools.desc: Data-shaping pipeline (the 'L' in ELK) that pulls logs and metrics, parses, enriches, filters, and routes them to Elasticsearch or any other output.
tools.when: The parsing/enrichment middle layer when an agent's native handling is not enough for messy or appliance-shaped log sources heading into Elastic.

tools.name: Sigma
tools.desc: The generic, SIEM-agnostic detection format: YAML rules describing log semantics; sigma-cli compiles them to Splunk, Elastic, Loki, MS Sentinel, and dozens of query languages from the SigmaHQ public rule set.
tools.when: Author one detection and ship it everywhere: port a SigmaHQ rule, run sigma convert --target <siem>, and validate the query against live logs before tuning.
tools.install: pipx install sigma-cli && git clone https://github.com/SigmaHQ/sigma

tools.name: CAR
tools.desc: MITRE's Cyber Analytics Repository: a knowledge base of validated analytics that pair each ATT&CK technique with a hypothesis, pseudocode, and concrete implementations (Splunk, EQL, Zeek).
tools.when: Harvest battle-tested analytic ideas to port into Sigma or your SIEM — read the operating theory and data model before writing new rules from scratch.

tools.name: Atomic Red Team
tools.desc: Red Canary's adversary-simulation library mapping hundreds of ATT&CK techniques to executable test definitions; each atomic documents the exact procedure and the telemetry a detection should fire on.
tools.when: Prove a Sigma/SIEM rule actually fires by running the matching atomic test and watching your alert pipeline — the purple-team workflow lives in the purpleteam domain.

tools.name: YARA
tools.desc: Binary pattern-matching rule engine for malware families and byte-level IOCs; complements SIEM rules when the evidence is a dropped file, not a log (fuller coverage in the malware domain).
tools.when: Match captured samples or suspicious files against signature rules, or encode a family signature your log-query team can't express in Sigma.

tools.name: Shuffle
tools.desc: Open-source SOAR platform: drag-and-drop workflow builder wiring apps, triggers, and actions to automate alert triage, enrichment calls, and response playbooks against your SIEM and intel tools.
tools.when: Automate repeatable analyst actions (enrich an IOC, quarantine a host, open a ticket) with a free self-hosted SOAR instead of hand-scripted glue.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/shuffle/shuffle && cd shuffle && docker compose up -d

tools.name: n8n
tools.desc: Fair-code workflow automation platform with 400+ integrations and a visual editor; a flexible general engine for chaining webhooks, email, HTTP APIs, and internal tools.
tools.when: Lighter-weight automation when Shuffle feels security-specific but you still want playbooks, schedules, and HTTP-triggered workflows in one self-hosted box.

tools.name: TheHive
tools.desc: Open-source security incident-response platform (TheHive 5) for collecting, sharing, and analyzing alerts as collaborative cases with tasks, observables, and full audit history.
tools.when: Track active incidents and alerts with structured cases, then close the loop by pushing findings back into detection tuning.

tools.name: Cortex
tools.desc: Open-source analyzer engine (TheHive companion): responders and analyzers run one-shot enrichments — DNS, hash lookups, intel feeds, quarantines — from TheHive, MISP, or its REST API.
tools.when: Standardized IOC enrichment as analyzers you can call from TheHive cases, MISP, or your SOAR playbooks without wiring each vendor API yourself.

tools.name: CISA Incident Response Playbooks
tools.desc: CISA's Federal Government Cybersecurity Incident and Vulnerability Response Playbooks: role-by-role, phase-by-phase response guidance with ready-to-copy templates for incident handling.
tools.when: Start with these when writing your own playbooks — lift the phases, roles, and communications plan, then adapt the details to your estate.

tools.name: NIST SP 800-61r3
tools.desc: NIST Special Publication 800-61 revision 3: incident-response recommendations and considerations for cybersecurity risk management — organizing IR, handling evidence, and coordination guidance.
tools.when: A defensible framework for how response teams should be structured and measured, whether you are building a small SOC or a whole CSIRT.

tools.name: Canarytokens
tools.desc: Thinkst's free hosted (or self-hosted Docker) tripwire factory generating DNS, URL, document (PDF/Word), AWS-key, QR-code, and Slack tokens that alert instantly when touched.
tools.when: When a full honeypot is overkill: sprinkle fake DNS names, URLs, or documents across AD, share drives, and public infra for cheap, near-instant detection of unauthorized access.
tools.install: preinstalled (canarytokens.org) — self-host: git clone https://github.com/thinkst/canarytokens-docker && cd canarytokens-docker && docker compose up

tools.name: OpenCanary
tools.desc: Thinkst's open-source multi-protocol honeypot daemon (SSH, telnet, HTTP, FTP, SNMP, SMB, RDP, MySQL) firing syslog, email, Slack, and webhook alerts on any probe; the OSS sibling of commercial Thinkst Canary.
tools.when: Drop a near-zero-footprint daemon on a jump host, file server, or DMZ for alerting on unexpected interaction — richer coverage lives in the honeypots domain.

tools.name: rspamd
tools.desc: Fast open-source mail filter scoring incoming message content with Bayesian/spamassassin rules, and signing outbound mail with DKIM plus DMARC/SRS support via its own Milter interface.
tools.when: Harden your own postfix/exim MTA: filter inbound spam and authenticate outbound with DKIM signing and SPF/DMARC alignment in one service.
tools.install: sudo add-apt-repository ppa:rspamd/rspamd && sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install rspamd

tools.name: checkdmarc
tools.desc: Python module/CLI validating SPF and DMARC DNS records end-to-end, including SPF lookup counts and void lookups, DMARC effectiveness warnings, MTA-STS, DANE/TLSA, and BIMI checks.
tools.when: Audit your own domain's email authentication posture before or after publishing records — run it defensively to catch a policy an attacker or vendor broke.

tools.name: swaks
tools.desc: Swiss Army Knife for SMTP: crafts arbitrary test messages with full control over sender, headers, attachments, and TLS to verify mail relays and backend behavior on hosts you administer.
tools.when: Verify an MTA or relay does what it should — test who can relay, check headers and SPF/DKIM passing, or reproduce a delivery issue from your own mail server.

tools.name: CrowdSec
tools.desc: Open-source crowd-sourced IPS (Suricata-aware): watches logs and events locally, bans offending IPs via bouncers at the firewall/nginx/cloud level, and shares signals through the community blocklist.
tools.when: Active response at the edge — replace dumb fail2ban-style blocking with attack-originated, shareable banishment backed by community signals.
tools.install: curl -s https://install.crowdsec.net | sudo sh && sudo cscli collections install crowdsecurity/linux && sudo systemctl start crowdsec

tools.name: Fail2ban
tools.desc: Classic log-scrape intrusion-prevention daemon that watches services (ssh, nginx, postfix) and bans repeat offenders through the host firewall or iptables backends.
tools.when: Simple, well-understood scoring-based banning on a single host — perfect when CrowdSec's community-signal model is more than you need.

tools.name: ModSecurity
tools.desc: The OWASP open-source WAF engine (an OWASP Production project) inspecting HTTP and enforcing SecRule policies on Apache/nginx; load the OWASP CRS on top for real attack coverage.
tools.when: Inline HTTP-layer defense when you want the battle-tested rule ecosystem and can commit to tuning false positives against your own apps.
tools.install: sudo apt-get install libapache2-mod-security2 (Apache; for nginx compile the module with --with-compat --add-dynamic-module=../ModSecurity-nginx)

tools.name: Coraza
tools.desc: OWASP WAF written in Go with near-full ModSecurity compatibility — runs CRS v4 without the legacy C engine as a library or middleware for Caddy, Traefik, APISIX, and API gateways.
tools.when: Cloud-native stacks (Go services, containers, Caddy/Traefik/APISIX) where ModSecurity's build model is awkward but you still want CRS protection.
tools.install: xcaddy build --with github.com/corazawaf/coraza-caddy/v2 (then add the coraza_waf block to the Caddyfile)

tools.name: OWASP CRS
tools.desc: The OWASP flagship Core Rule Set — a community-maintained rule layer detecting SQLi, XSS, scanners, and OWASP Top 10 attacks that runs on both ModSecurity and Coraza engines; a ruleset, not a standalone tool.
tools.when: The rule layer to load onto any WAF engine so a bare install actually detects web attacks; tune via the anomaly-scoring exclusions to cut false positives.
tools.install: git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/coreruleset/coreruleset.git (then Include the CRS config in your WAF engine)

tools.name: Cloudflare WAF
tools.desc: Commercial managed edge WAF (SaaS) filtering traffic on Cloudflare's CDN with managed rulesets (including OWASP CRS coverage) plus bot and rate controls — no servers to run.
tools.when: When your apps already sit behind Cloudflare and you want managed rules, DDoS/bot defense, and zero self-hosting in one panel.
tools.install: preinstalled (SaaS) — enable in the dash.cloudflare.com Security panel, pick a managed ruleset, and tune via custom rules

domains.name: Cloud Security — AWS, Azure & GCP
domains.tagline: Posture audits, scoped offense, and public-bucket checks across AWS, Azure, and GCP — nested by provider and by function for your own accounts and sanctioned assessments.

tools.name: Prowler
tools.desc: Runs 1,000+ read-only checks across AWS, Azure, and GCP against CIS Benchmarks and 70+ compliance frameworks, with remediation guidance per finding.
tools.when: Kick off every posture review with it — the default for CIS/NIST alignment on any provider, driven via CLI, Docker, or the API.

tools.name: Scout Suite
tools.desc: NCC Group's multi-cloud auditor pulls configuration from provider APIs and renders a browsable point-in-time HTML report of risk areas for AWS, Azure, and GCP.
tools.when: Grab a clean visual report of config risk as a second opinion alongside Prowler; expect a quiet repo — last major release was 2022.

tools.name: CloudSploit (Trivy Cloud)
tools.desc: Aqua's Node.js CSPM scanner covering AWS, Azure, GCP, OCI, and GitHub with CIS/PCI/HIPAA modes; actively developed as the open-source half of the hosted Aqua Trivy Cloud / Wave platform.
tools.when: Broad self-hosted multi-cloud config checks in CI; know that the maintained commercial route is Aqua Trivy Cloud.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/aquasecurity/cloudsploit.git && cd cloudsploit && npm install

tools.name: Steampipe
tools.desc: Run SQL queries over live AWS, Azure, GCP, and 200+ other APIs, then reuse the same queries for compliance benchmarks (CIS) and ad-hoc posture checks.
tools.when: When you want scriptable, queryable posture evidence: SQL across your accounts beats shell-script loops and feeds reporting directly.

tools.name: Pacu
tools.desc: The AWS exploitation framework: modular post-compromise attacks covering IAM privilege escalation, Lambda backdoors, log tampering, and EC2 RCE, with a session database for clean reporting.
tools.when: After you hold valid-but-least-privilege AWS keys and want to demonstrate what an attacker could escalate to — lab/own-account use only.

tools.name: CloudFox
tools.desc: Bishop Fox's situational-awareness enumerator maps exploitable attack paths across AWS (34 commands) plus early Azure/GCP coverage, writing loot files for other tools.
tools.when: Run `cloudfox aws --profile X all-checks` first on any fresh scope to learn the estate and spot privesc paths before deeper exploitation with Pacu.

tools.name: Prowler (AWS)
