tools.desc: Prowler pinned to AWS (`-p aws`): 300+ AWS-specific checks across CIS 1.x/2.x, NIST 800-53, and Well-Architected focus areas, with per-finding remediation and CSV/JSON/SARIF output.
tools.when: The primary AWS compliance gate in CI or on a schedule; run alongside GuardDuty-focused triage for config findings.

tools.name: Scout Suite (AWS)
tools.desc: Scout Suite run with AWS credentials: point-in-time dumps of IAM, S3, EC2, and Security Group posture into a navigable HTML report annotated with risk rules.
tools.when: Fast visual sweep of one AWS account when you want a self-contained report artifact to share, not another CLI table.
tools.install: pip3 install scoutsuite && scout aws --profile prod

tools.name: cloud-inquisitor
tools.desc: Riot Games' config-audit and incident-response platform: scans accounts against custom rules, auto-remediates (e.g., open S3 buckets), and ships a web dashboard; only lightly maintained since 2021.
tools.when: When you want rule-driven auto-remediation on legacy AWS estates and accept a quiet project — otherwise prefer Prowler or Steampipe.

tools.name: AWS CLI & Batch Scripts
tools.desc: The built-in `aws` CLI plus shell one-liners and jq pipelines for service inventory, bucket ACL listing, unused IAM keys, and cross-account drift — endless and dependency-free.
tools.when: Quick targeted checks while Prowler/Steampipe are overkill: `aws iam list-access-keys --no-user-paginate`, `aws s3api get-bucket-acl`, etc.

tools.name: PMapper
tools.desc: NCC Group's Principal Mapper builds a graph of IAM users/groups/roles and their effective permissions, then computes shortest privilege-escalation and takeover paths.
tools.when: Model least-privilege drift: generate the graph in minutes and query for principals reaching admin via any path.

tools.name: enumerate-iam
tools.desc: Brute-forces every read-only AWS API call against a credential set to print exactly which IAM permissions it holds.
tools.when: You recovered AWS keys of unknown privilege and need the permission list fast, before choosing an escalation path.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/andresriancho/enumerate-iam.git && cd enumerate-iam && pip3 install -r requirements.txt

tools.name: IAMActionHunter
tools.desc: Collects and queries AWS IAM policy statements to surface users and roles holding privesc-relevant permissions (iam:create*, iam:put*...) and exports CSV; also ships as a Pacu module.
tools.when: Hunt least-privilege violations and privilege-escalation levers across a large account in minutes, then review the CSV.

tools.name: S3Scanner
tools.desc: Scans lists of bucket names across AWS and S3-compatible stores (GCP, DigitalOcean, Linode, Scaleway) for existence, tests every permission path for misconfigurations, and can enumerate or dump objects.
tools.when: Find your own exposed buckets at scale: feed candidate names, get back which are public, listable, or readable.

tools.name: S3audit
tools.desc: NCC Group's small Go tool checks S3 bucket permissions via the public ListObjects/GetObject/Acl APIs against a given bucket or custom wordlist.
tools.when: Single-target bucket permission triage and wordlist-driven scan of buckets you own, without standing up a full scanner.

tools.name: Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark (docs)
tools.desc: Microsoft's authoritative Azure security baseline: control families (identity, network, storage, data protection) with CSPM tooling guidance and mapping to NIST/CIS regulatory frameworks.
tools.when: Your reference before running scanners — know which controls the tool checks and which ones Azure Policy/Defender must enforce, since no scanner covers a benchmark alone.
tools.install: Reference guide — no install; mapped controls ship as built-in Azure Policy initiatives

tools.name: Azure Threat Research Matrix (ATRM)
tools.desc: MSTIC's community threat matrix documenting Azure/AWS/GCP attack vectors (reconnaissance, persistence, privilege escalation) with real examples and KQL hunting queries.
tools.when: Understand how attackers actually move in a tenant so your posture checks and MicroBurst-style simulations target the realistic paths.

tools.name: Prowler (Azure)
tools.desc: Prowler pinned to Azure (`-p azure --az-cli-auth`): 100+ read-only checks over Entra ID, subscriptions, storage, key vault, and network config against CIS Microsoft Azure 1.x/2.x.
tools.when: The main automated Azure compliance pass in CI or on a schedule; complements but does not replace Azure Policy assignments.

tools.name: Scout Suite (Azure)
tools.desc: Scout Suite's Azure provider: one-command dump of subscription posture (ARM resources, RBAC, storage, NSGs) into an HTML report with risk annotations.
tools.when: A point-in-time visual Azure report that mirrors your AWS workflow and is easy to archive as an evidence artifact.

tools.name: MicroBurst
tools.desc: NetSPI's PowerShell toolkit for attacking Azure: service discovery, weak-config auditing, credential dumping (AzPasswords), and post-exploitation on VMs, Key Vault, and Automation accounts.
tools.when: The default Azure toolkit in authenticated engagements on your own tenant; Windows-only, so run it from a PowerShell host with the Az modules installed.

tools.name: Stormspotter
tools.desc: Microsoft Azure Red Team's attack-graph tool: collects subscription and ARM resources into Neo4j and renders the attack surface with pivot opportunities.
tools.when: Map a large tenant visually and find cross-resource pivot paths once you hold reader-level access in a sanctioned assessment.

tools.name: ATEAM
tools.desc: NetSPI's unauthenticated reconnaissance tool probes name permutations across App Services, Key Vault, Storage, DevOps, SharePoint, and Databricks to discover Azure resources and attribute tenant IDs.
tools.when: From outside, discover forgotten Azure resources whose names leak a tenant — ideal for attack-surface checks on your own domains before logging in.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/NetSPI/ATEAM.git && cd ATEAM && pip3 install -r requirements.txt

tools.name: Scout Suite (GCP)
tools.desc: Scout Suite's GCP provider: gathers project posture across IAM, GCE, GCS, GKE, and Cloud SQL into a browsable HTML risk report, including Org-level IAM.
tools.when: The quickest visual read of GCP config risk in one project — pair with Prowler for covered CIS controls.
tools.install: pip3 install scoutsuite && scout gcloud --project-id PROJECT

tools.name: Prowler (GCP)
tools.desc: Prowler pinned to GCP (`-p gcp`): 100+ read-only checks against the Google Cloud CIS 1.x benchmark covering IAM, logging, networking, and storage.
tools.when: The compliance-first GCP pass in CI; best paired with its AWS/Azure siblings for org-wide reporting.

tools.name: Forseti (retired)
tools.desc: Google's old inventory-and-policy engine for detecting GCP misconfigurations; officially retired by the Google Cloud team and no longer developed.
tools.when: Only revisit for legacy estates already running it — for new work use Prowler/Scout Suite plus Policy Controller and Assured workloads.

tools.name: gcloud CLI & Scripted Audits
tools.desc: The `gcloud` CLI plus `gcloud asset`, IAM recommender, and `gcloud projects get-iam-policy` pipelines for fast targeted checks and drift reporting.
tools.when: Quick focused questions — who can do what in a project, which buckets changed, logging disabled — without a full scanner run.

tools.name: gcp-scanner
tools.desc: Google's scanner determines what a compromised credential can reach across GCE, GCS, GKE, Cloud SQL, BigQuery, KMS, and more, pulling from VM metadata, SA keys, or OAuth tokens.
tools.when: Assess blast radius after a leaked service account key or compromised VM, without needing gcloud installed.

tools.name: gcpwn
tools.desc: NetSPI's GCP and Workspace pentesting framework: enumerates and downloads project data, builds BloodHound OpenGraph models, and bundles credential and exploit tooling.
tools.when: Deep GCP/Workspace engagements where you want structured enumeration feeding BloodHound-style attack-path analysis.

tools.name: GCP IAM Privilege Escalation Toolkit
tools.desc: Rhino's documented GCP IAM privesc methods plus a scanner (enumerate_member_permissions.py then check_for_privesc.py) that flags principals able to escalate.
tools.when: Audit who in your projects could privilege-escalate to org ownership and validate hardened role design.

tools.name: GCPBucketBrute
tools.desc: Enumerates Google Storage buckets from keyword permutations and reports per-bucket access, flagging public, writable, and privilege-escalation-prone (storage.buckets.setIamPolicy) buckets.
tools.when: Check which of your GCS buckets are reachable or writable without auth, including escalations visible from a service account.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/RhinoSecurityLabs/GCPBucketBrute.git && cd GCPBucketBrute && pip3 install -r requirements.txt

tools.name: Checkov
tools.desc: Prisma Cloud-maintained IaC static analyzer with 1,000+ built-in policies for Terraform (incl. plan output), CloudFormation, Kubernetes, Helm, Dockerfile, Bicep, ARM, and Serverless; graph-based and multi-resource aware.
tools.when: The default IaC gate: scan Terraform/K8s/Dockerfile in CI and on terraform plan to catch exposed resources and weak IAM before apply.

tools.name: tfsec
tools.desc: Fast Terraform-specific static scanner with 400+ rules and custom Rego/policy support; development has wound down as scanning moved into Trivy (trivy config).
tools.when: Lightweight, human-friendly Terraform warnings in pre-commit; for maintained updates run the same checks via Trivy config.

tools.name: Terrascan (archived)
tools.desc: Tenable's Rego-policy IaC scanner for Terraform, CloudFormation, ARM, K8s, Helm, and Docker; the repository was archived November 2025 and is read-only.
tools.when: Only for aligning with existing Terrascan policy sets on frozen pipelines — new IaC work should use Checkov or KICS.

tools.name: cfn-guard
tools.desc: AWS's official CloudFormation policy-as-code tool: validates templates and yes, live stacks, against declarative rules written in a purpose-built Guard DSL; ships AWS managed rule collections.
tools.when: Enforce organizational CloudFormation rules (allowlists, encryption, tag policies) in CI against templates before deploy.

tools.name: cfn-nag
tools.desc: Stelligent's rule-based CloudFormation linter that flags over-permissive IAM wildcards, plaintext secrets, and open security groups across templates.
tools.when: Fast, opinionated CloudFormation warnings with zero configuration; a solid first pass before cfn-guard rules.

tools.name: kube-bench
tools.desc: Aqua's CIS Kubernetes benchmark runner that checks control-plane nodes (kube-apiserver, etcd) and workloads against the CIS K8s Benchmark 1.9+ sections.
tools.when: Baseline your clusters against CIS on install and after upgrades; run from the node or via the official image.

tools.name: kube-score
tools.desc: Opinionated static analysis of Kubernetes object manifests scoring against best practices: resource requests, probes, securityContext, network policies.
tools.when: Per-manifest linting in CI for the small, common mistakes — complements policy-heavy gatekeepers like Kyverno and kube-bench.

tools.name: KICS
tools.desc: Checkmarx's open-source IaC scanner (Keeping Infrastructure as Code Secure) running thousands of queries across 20+ platforms — Terraform, K8s, Docker, Helm, CloudFormation, Ansible — with SARIF output and OPA/Rego custom queries.
tools.when: A complementary cross-check on IaC after Checkov, or the pick when you want OPA/Rego policy authoring (the slot archived Terrascan used to fill).

tools.name: Trivy
tools.desc: Aqua's all-in-one scanner: OS/library package CVEs in images and filesystems, SBOM generation, IaC misconfigs (absorbed tfsec), Kubernetes scanning, and registry CI — one binary, zero daemon.
tools.when: The single tool to add to a container build: `trivy image`, `trivy fs --scanners vuln,secret,misconfig`, and `trivy sbom` cover images to source in one install.

domains.name: Container & Kubernetes Security
domains.tagline: Defending your own clusters: image scanning, SBOM, runtime detection, CIS posture, admission policy, Sigstore signing, and offensive lab checks.

tools.name: Trivy
tools.desc: Aqua Security's comprehensive scanner covering container images, filesystems, git repos, VMs, and Kubernetes; detects CVEs, misconfigurations, secrets, and licenses from one binary.
tools.when: Gate every image build in CI and scan at push time; add trivy-operator (or Kubescape) for in-cluster image monitoring.

tools.name: Grype
tools.desc: Anchore's fast vulnerability scanner for images, filesystems, and SBOMs; pairs with Syft and adds EPSS, KEV, and OpenVEX filtering to prioritize real risk.
tools.when: Speed-first CI scans, or scan an SBOM you already generated instead of re-pulling and re-analyzing the image.

tools.name: Clair
tools.desc: Quay/Red Hat's v4 vulnerability database server for registries: ingests manifests and exposes a gRPC API that clairctl, clair-hook, or admission controllers query for container-layer CVE data.
tools.when: Deploy next to Quay (or your own registry) for server-side scanning of every pushed image instead of one-off CI scans.

tools.name: Anchore (Enterprise)
tools.desc: Commercial policy-and-compliance platform built on the Grype/Syft engine with admission control (anchore-admission-controller) and scheduled registry scanning; the legacy open-source anchore-engine CLI is deprecated.
tools.when: When you need continuous registry posture, feeds/webhooks, and audited policy gates as a platform rather than a single binary.
tools.install: helm repo add anchore https://charts.anchore.io && helm install anchore anchore/anchore-enterprise

tools.name: Docker Scout
tools.desc: Docker's image analyzer for CVEs, provenance, and supply-chain compliance; highlights CISA KEV reachability and suggests base-image/model upgrades, integrated into Docker Desktop and CI.
tools.when: Fastest starting point for teams already on Docker — compare images, audit a registry, and enforce policies without another platform.

tools.name: Snyk Container
tools.desc: Snyk's container scanning CLI ('snyk container test') covering images plus Kubernetes/IaC config, with base-image upgrade paths and registry/workspace integration.
tools.when: Teams already using Snyk for SCA/app-sec want container coverage in the same console and policy engine.

tools.name: hadolint
tools.desc: Haskell Dockerfile linter that parses the Dockerfile AST and applies best-practice rules, delegating inline shell checks to ShellCheck (DL- and SC-prefixed findings).
tools.when: Lint Dockerfiles in CI to catch untagged images, root users, and unsafe RUN commands before the image is ever built.

tools.name: dockle
tools.desc: Container image linter that audits the built image against CIS Docker image checkpoints and best practices (non-root user, HEALTHCHECK, setuid/setgid files, content trust).
tools.when: Audit the built image itself, complementing Dockerfile lint, right before pushing to a production registry.

tools.name: Syft
tools.desc: Generates SBOMs for container images, filesystems, and archives in CycloneDX, SPDX, and Syft JSON; feeds Grype directly and supports signed in-toto attestations.
tools.when: Produce a machine-readable dependency inventory at build time and ship it with the image to prove supply-chain provenance.

tools.name: CycloneDX CLI
tools.desc: OWASP CycloneDX CLI to validate, merge, diff, convert, sign, and verify CycloneDX and SPDX BOMs; exits non-zero on invalid input for CI gating.
tools.when: Normalize third-party vendor SBOMs into one format, diff releases to catch dependency drift, or enforce schema-valid BOMs in the pipeline.

tools.name: sbomqs
tools.desc: Interlynk's SBOM quality & compliance scorer: grades SPDX/CycloneDX BOMs on completeness, licensing, relationships, and format correctness, then filters by quality score.
tools.when: Score vendor-supplied and generated SBOMs in CI so you can reject 'good enough' BOMs and see which tooling produces trustworthy output.

tools.name: Cosign
tools.desc: Sigstore CLI to sign and verify images, blobs, and SBOM attestations with keyless (OIDC) or key-based signatures stored as OCI artifacts, backed by the Rekor transparency log.
tools.when: Sign every image in CI and verify at admission time (Kyverno, Gatekeeper, or the sigstore policy controller) to stop unsigned/mutated image pulls.

tools.name: Notation
tools.desc: CNCF Notary Project CLI (OCI 1.1 signatures) for signing and verifying artifacts with X.509/SPIFFE certificates; keeps signatures as native OCI artifacts and integrates with Azure/AWS KMS signers.
tools.when: Enterprise environments that already run X.509 PKI/KMS and want cert-managed signing rather than Sigstore's ephemeral, keyless model.

tools.name: Sigstore Policy Controller
tools.desc: Sigstore's admission controller that verifies signatures and attestations on every pod creation, mutating the request to enforce trust policies cluster-wide.
tools.when: Cluster-wide 'only signed/attested images run here' enforcement as an image-policy layer, complementary to schema-style admission policies like Kyverno.
tools.install: helm repo add sigstore https://sigstore.github.io/helm-charts && helm install policy-controller sigstore/policy-controller -n cosign-system --create-namespace

tools.name: Rekor CLI
tools.desc: Query and verify entries in the Rekor transparency log (DSSE/tekton/blob/cosign types): confirm a signature was logged at a point in time and detect tampered/duplicate entries.
tools.when: Forensic checks that complement signature verification — prove an artifact existed in the log, correlate with incident timelines, or audit your own signing records.

tools.name: Distroless
tools.desc: Google's minimal base images with no shell, package managers, or runtimes — static, cc, and Debian variants with nonroot tags that slash attack surface and image size.
tools.when: Production images that never need a shell: shift all debugging to the builder stage or sidecars and run the runtime stage as non-root by default.

tools.name: Wolfi
tools.desc: Chainguard's apk-based, no-glibc-bloat OS purpose-built for containers — the upstream of hardened Chainguard images, reproducibly assembled with apko into slim distroless-style images.
tools.when: Teams needing a lean, fully open-source base where you still install apk packages and build tools inside multi-stage builds without bloating the runtime image.

tools.name: kube-bench
tools.desc: Aqua's Go tool that runs the CIS Kubernetes Benchmark against control plane, etcd, and worker node configuration, matched to the running Kubernetes version.
tools.when: Validate a specific hardened baseline after cluster upgrades, node onboarding, or as a scheduled per-node job.

tools.name: docker-bench-security
tools.desc: Docker's CIS Docker Benchmark script auditing the Docker/containerd host, daemon, and running containers against dozens of best-practice checks.
tools.when: Harden and periodically re-audit the container host on worker nodes after workloads are deployed; quick compliance readout for a single host.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/docker/docker-bench-security.git && cd docker-bench-security && sudo sh docker-bench-security.sh

tools.name: Kubescape
tools.desc: CNCF-incubating Kubernetes security platform scanning clusters, manifests, Helm charts, git repos, and images against CIS, NSA-CISA, and MITRE ATT&CK; operator mode adds continuous posture and eBPF runtime.
tools.when: First full-posture sweep of a cluster and as a CI gate on manifests; install the operator for continuous compliance monitoring.

tools.name: Popeye
tools.desc: Read-only live-cluster sanitizer that lints deployed workloads for misconfigurations, dead resources, port mismatches, and missing probes, scoring overall cluster health.
tools.when: Periodic 'wide-open' sweep to catch drift and operational debt that static manifest review misses.

tools.name: kube-linter
tools.desc: StackRox (Red Hat) static analyzer for Kubernetes YAML and Helm charts with 40+ built-in checks (privileged containers, insecure service types, missing resource limits) and SARIF output for CI.
tools.when: Pre-deploy linting in CI — catch risky manifests before apply, complementing runtime posture and admission checks.

tools.name: kubeaudit
tools.desc: Audits manifests and live clusters against security controls (privileged, hostNetwork, capabilities, allowPrivilegeEscalation) and can auto-fix them; repo is archived and the brew formula deprecated as of 2025.
tools.when: Only where an existing pipeline integrates its autofix mode; otherwise prefer kube-linter + kube-bench for actively maintained coverage.

tools.name: OPA Gatekeeper
tools.desc: CNCF policy controller that enforces Rego-based policy through constraint templates and constraints, with admission webhooks, audit, and mutation support.
tools.when: Enforce registry allowlists, required labels, and security-context rules at admission when you already know Rego or want the largest policy ecosystem.

tools.name: Kyverno
tools.desc: CNCF-graduated Kubernetes-native policy engine using YAML (no new language) to validate, mutate, generate, and clean up resources; verifies image signatures via cosign.
tools.when: Teams that prefer familiar YAML and want mutation, image verification, and policy-as-a-resource without learning Rego.
tools.install: helm repo add kyverno https://kyverno.github.io/helm-charts && helm install kyverno kyverno/kyverno -n kyverno --create-namespace

tools.name: Polaris
tools.desc: Fairwinds policy-as-code with 30+ built-in checks across security, networking, reliability, and efficiency; runs as a dashboard, CI CLI, or mutating admission webhook.
tools.when: Drop-in baseline enforcement with a visible compliance dashboard when full OPA or Kyverno is overkill.

tools.name: Conftest
tools.desc: Tests Kubernetes manifests, Helm values, Terraform, and CUE against Rego policies from the CLI; CI-friendly and shares the same policy language as OPA Gatekeeper.
tools.when: Control-plane-free policy checks in pre-commit/CI, or validate the exact Rego you will enforce with Gatekeeper before installing anything.

tools.name: Cilium
tools.desc: eBPF-based CNI enforcing Kubernetes NetworkPolicy and extended CiliumNetworkPolicy with identity-based rules (no IP juggling), plus Hubble for policy-aware flow observability.
tools.when: Strict workload micro-segmentation with per-L4/L7 rules and visibility; it replaces your CNI, so plan a rollout, not a drop-in patch.
tools.install: helm repo add cilium https://helm.cilium.io && helm install cilium cilium/cilium --namespace kube-system

tools.name: Calico
tools.desc: Project Calico/Tigera CNI delivering the Kubernetes NetworkPolicy API plus GlobalNetworkPolicy and host-endpoint policy for traffic entering/leaving nodes.
tools.when: Clusters already on Calico, or when you need global (not just namespace-scoped) network policy that covers host endpoints.

tools.name: kube-hunter
tools.desc: Legacy Aqua pen-test tool that finds cluster weaknesses from an attacker's perspective (exposed dashboards, leaked secrets, weak RBAC); officially no longer under active development.
tools.when: Offense-style spot check on a cluster you own; treat findings as a starting list since it is not actively maintained.

tools.name: Falco
tools.desc: CNCF-graduated kernel monitoring agent (eBPF or driver) that watches syscalls enriched with container and Kubernetes metadata, alerting via a flexible rules engine.
tools.when: Deploy on every production node for real-time detection of shells in containers, privileged pods, and sensitive-file access.
tools.install: helm repo add falcosecurity https://falcosecurity.github.io/charts && helm install falco falcosecurity/falco

tools.name: Tetragon
tools.desc: Cilium's eBPF-based runtime security and observability with no userspace for traffic paths: policy-driven tracing of syscalls and network events, plus kubectl-level enrichment.
tools.when: High-throughput, eBPF-first detection with built-in network insights and lower operational moving parts than a driver-based agent.
tools.install: helm repo add cilium https://helm.cilium.io && helm install tetragon cilium/tetragon -n kube-system

tools.name: rbac-lookup
tools.desc: Fairwinds CLI that reverses RBAC: give it a user, service account, or group and it prints every Role/ClusterRole bound to that identity, resolving the bindings for you.
tools.when: Audit 'what can this identity actually do?' across namespaces — the fastest path from a SA name to a least-privilege review.

tools.name: kubectl auth can-i
tools.desc: Built-in kubectl authorization self-check; 'kubectl auth can-i --list -A' dumps the full permission matrix for the current context in one shot.
tools.when: Zero-install RBAC sanity checks in an incident or review loop — verify a spyed SA cannot escalate before trusting it.

tools.name: Trivy Action
tools.desc: aquasecurity/trivy-action wraps Trivy in GitHub Actions for image, filesystem, config, and SBOM scans with severity gates and SARIF upload to code scanning.
tools.when: Per-PR image/filesystem scanning that fails the build above a severity threshold and feeds findings into GitHub Security tab.

tools.name: Anchore Scan Action
tools.desc: anchore/scan-action runs Grype with fine-grained gating (only-fixed, severity cutoff, OpenVEX) and emits SARIF, JSON, or CycloneDX outputs from images, paths, or existing SBOMs.
tools.when: Grype-grounded, license-clean security scanning where you want VEX and fix-availability filters ahead of generic fail-on-high scans.

tools.name: SBOM Action
tools.desc: anchore/sbom-action generates Syft SBOMs in CI, publishing them as release artifacts or GitHub SBOM attestations so downstream scanners (Clair, Grype, Docker Scout) consume them.
tools.when: Attach a CycloneDX/SPDX BOM to every released image git-tag artifact, proving what shipped for audit and supply-chain consumers.

tools.name: Kyverno Policies
tools.desc: Kyverno's community policy library: 130+ tested YAML policies covering Pod Security Standards, image signatures, network policy checks, and compliance presets.
tools.when: Start from a maintained, battle-tested policy set and adapt, rather than authoring every admission rule from scratch.

tools.name: KubeHound
tools.desc: DataDog's attack-graph engine: a collector ingests cluster RBAC, workload, and network data, then a graph query layer returns BloodHound-style attack paths between assets.
tools.when: Continuously model 'can this workload or identity reach the kubelet/cluster?' — ideal for validating least privilege and red-team path enumeration on your own cluster.

tools.name: KubiScan
tools.desc: CyberArk's RBAC attack-path scanner: lists risky roles, subjects, and clusterrolebindings, and highlights the write-access paths (secrets, exec) an attacker can abuse for cluster takeover.
tools.when: Systematically map RBAC escape routes on clusters you own and gather remediation evidence (which SA grants secret read, exec into pods, etc.).
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/CyberArk/KubiScan.git && cd KubiScan && sudo python3 setup.py install

tools.name: deepce
tools.desc: DEEPCE (Docker Enumeration, Escalation of Privileges and Container Escapes) is a single bash script that enumerates capabilities, mounts, sockets, env, and metadata, then suggests and attempts escapes.
tools.when: Fast assessment of a container you own in a lab/engagement: one script goes from recon to working escape candidates before you write custom exploit code.

tools.name: CDK
tools.desc: Zero-dependency Go container/Kubernetes penetration toolkit: capability evaluation, no-curl/wget binary delivery, and exploits for runC, docker.sock, containerd, etcd tokens, plus tunneling and reverse shells.
tools.when: Post-exploitation payload to drop into minimal/scratch containers where curl and wget are absent but you still need networking, probes, and K8s API calls.
tools.install: Download the release binary from github.com/cdk-team/CDK/releases

domains.name: Digital Forensics & Incident Response
domains.tagline: Analyze memory, disk, carved files, artifacts, and timelines from your own systems, lab evidence, and incident-response cases you legally possess.

tools.name: dd
tools.desc: GNU coreutils bit-copy utility that creates a byte-for-byte image of any block device — the universal imaging baseline every forensics distro ships.
tools.when: Quick raw image of your own drive, USB stick, or SD card when you just need a faithful copy and will hash it yourself.

tools.name: ddrescue
tools.desc: GNU data-recovery imager that resists read errors, logs bad blocks, and retries them after the rest of the media is copied — built to salvage failing or damaged storage.
tools.when: The drive clicks or returns I/O errors: let ddrescue build a mostly-complete image first, then analyze the rescued copy instead of the failing disk.

tools.name: dc3dd
tools.desc: Forensic fork of GNU dd that adds on-the-fly hashing, split output, pattern wiping, and a detailed acquisition log — evidence-grade imaging in one pass.
tools.when: Capture a definitive, hash-verified image of a source drive before analysis so you examine the copy, not the live evidence.

tools.name: FTK Imager
tools.desc: Exterro's free, widely-used acquisition and preview tool: images drives/memory to raw, E01, and AFF formats, computes hashes, and mounts images for instant browsing.
tools.when: Click-driven imaging with E01 support (or compressed raw) straight to a case folder; it also does live RAM acquisition when needed.
tools.install: Download the free installer from exterro.com and run FTK Imager

tools.name: Guymager
tools.desc: Linux GUI forensic imager producing flat (dd), EWF (E01), and AFF images with multi-threaded pipelined reads and verification progress per device.
tools.when: Window-based imaging with progress bars and check-verification on a Linux analysis box when you prefer a GUI over dc3dd's command line.

tools.name: KAPE
tools.desc: Kroll Artifact Parser and Extractor: selects forensically useful artifacts (registry hives, EVTX, Prefetch, MFT, browser files) from a live device or mounted image, then parses them with bundled tools in minutes.
tools.when: Speed triage in your own incident response or lab: point it at a live Windows box or mounted image and get parsed artifacts quickly; extend with community KapeFiles targets.
tools.install: Download KAPE from Kroll's site (or GitHub releases) and run kape.exe

tools.name: Magnet RAM Capture
tools.desc: Free Windows memory acquisition tool that dumps physical RAM to raw .DMP files with a small footprint and optional command-line mode — ideal for preserving volatile evidence before it disappears.
tools.when: Grab the memory of a live lab or incident host before anything else — the .DMP output feeds straight into Volatility.
tools.install: Fill the download form at magnetforensics.com and run the standalone capture utility

tools.name: The Sleuth Kit
tools.desc: Command-line suite for raw/EWF images: mmls for partition layout, fls/icat to list and extract inodes, istat for metadata, and tsk_recover for recovery — the engine underneath Autopsy.
tools.when: Scripted or headless analysis, or when you need precise inode-level answers Autopsy hides behind its GUI.

tools.name: Autopsy
tools.desc: GUI platform built on The Sleuth Kit: opens images and live drives, recovers deleted files, and runs ingest modules for web history, keyword search, and carving inside a case workflow.
tools.when: First-pass interactive examination of a drive or memory-card image from your own casework or lab — ingest everything, then drill into findings.
tools.install: Download the installer from sleuthkit.org/autopsy and run it

tools.name: foremost
tools.desc: AFOSI-origin header/footer and data-structure carver that extracts JPEG, ZIP, PDF, and other signatures from raw images or drives via a configurable file-type table.
tools.when: Unallocated-space fishing: run it on an image or free-space carve to recover deleted files the live filesystem no longer lists.

tools.name: scalpel
tools.desc: Filesystem-independent carver using a header/footer definition database — a rewrite of foremost's engine with per-type carve-size tuning; the original repo is stale, machn1k/scalpel-2.0 carries it on.
tools.when: Stubborn image carries where you need tuned per-type size limits or a second carving engine beyond foremost defaults.

tools.name: TestDisk / PhotoRec
tools.desc: Signature-based recovery of 440+ file formats plus TestDisk for partition-table repair and undelete; no filename reconstruction, but deep salvage on corrupted or reformatted media.
tools.when: Last-ditch recovery from a reformatted or damaged partition or thumb drive in your own hardware lab.

tools.name: bulk_extractor
tools.desc: Scans any input byte-by-byte and extracts emails, URLs, credit-card numbers, JPEGs, and JSON to feature files — recursively decoding compressed or encoded blocks without parsing the filesystem.
tools.when: Rapid 'what is in this blob' extraction over images or wiped drives before deep filesystem analysis.

tools.name: Volatility 3
tools.desc: The de-facto memory forensics framework: plugin-based analysis of RAM dumps (raw, EWF, crash/hibernation) across Windows, Linux, macOS, and Android — processes, network artifacts, injected code, and more.
tools.when: Start here with any memory dump from a lab box or captured incident host; run pslist/pscan, netscan, and malfind to build the runtime picture.

tools.name: Volatility 2
tools.desc: The classic Python 2 framework (archived but stable) with the deepest plugin ecosystem and profile-based analysis for older Windows, Linux, and macOS dumps.
tools.when: Reach for it when a legacy or niche image lacks a Volatility 3 symbol table, or a plugin you need only exists in the classic tree.

tools.name: Rekall
tools.desc: Google-origin memory forensics framework born from Volatility during the 2.x era — effectively dormant since ~2020 with legacy artifacts in gray matter for older Windows/Linux images.
tools.when: Reading old IR research or cross-checking a niche plugin result on a vintage dump; expect to maintain it yourself.

tools.name: MemProcFS
tools.desc: Mounts a memory dump or live target (PCILeech FPGA/LeechAgent) as a virtual filesystem of processes, registry, and artifacts, with a batch forensic mode and YARA scanning.
tools.when: Fast interactive triage of a Windows dump without plugin CLI gymnastics, or live acquisition during your own incident response.

tools.name: Redline
tools.desc: Mandiant's free endpoint and memory investigation GUI: collects a volatile data set (processes, network, services, registry) from a live host or a memory dump and flags suspicious items with ATT&CK mapping — slower-moving now but still used in FTK/IR workflows.
tools.when: Point-and-click triage of a live Windows endpoint or captured memory when the CLI frameworks feel heavy for your own casework.
tools.install: Download Redline from Mandiant's free-tools page and let the wizard collect or open a memory image

tools.name: strings
tools.desc: GNU binutils classic that extracts printable ASCII/Unicode sequences from a raw memory dump — still the fastest way to spot C2 URLs, commands, and keys before the framework work.
tools.when: Instant grep-ish pass over a dump for notable indicators, or targeted hunting using the output piped into a socket/crypto-constant search.
tools.install: sudo apt install binutils && strings <dump> | grep -E '[0-9]+\.'

tools.name: Eric Zimmerman's Tools
tools.desc: Suite of focused parsers — RECmd/Registry Explorer, PECmd (Prefetch), LECmd (LNK), JLECmd (JumpLists), ShellBags, Amcache, MFTECmd — answering execution-timeline questions from individual artifacts.
tools.when: Deep-dive a targeted artifact set: ask 'what executed, when, by whom' via Prefetch, LNK/JumpList, Amcache, and registry traces.

tools.name: EvtxECmd
tools.desc: Eric Zimmerman's direct EVTX event-log parser turning .evtx databases into CSV/JSON with formatted timestamps and named fields, ready for Timeline Explorer.
tools.when: Convert raw Windows event logs from a mounted image or collection set into a queryable CSV before building your timeline.
tools.install: Download from EricZimmerman GitHub releases (part of Get-ZimmermanTools)

tools.name: Hayabusa
tools.desc: Yamato Security's Rust-based Windows event-log fast forensics tool that applies a huge Mitre-Attack-mapped sigma-rule library to EVTX dumps and outputs alert timelines in seconds.
tools.when: Hunt lateral movement, logon anomalies, and persistence across a full C:\Windows\System32\winevt\Logs collection or exported .evtx set.
tools.install: Download the release binary for your OS and run hayabusa csv-timeline -d <evtx_dir>

tools.name: APT-Hunter
tools.desc: Python-based EVTX analysis tool feeding exported Windows event logs through threat-hunting queries to detect hacking activity and TTPs via suspicious event correlations.
tools.when: Point it at your exported .evtx logs for a quick attacker-TTP posture check before going deep with sigma/hunting frameworks.

tools.name: plaso / log2timeline
tools.desc: log2timeline extracts timestamped events (filesystem, registry, EVTX, browser, application logs) from an image or mount point into a Plaso storage file; psort turns it into a filtered super-timeline.
tools.when: Build the master super-timeline of an image: collect once with log2timeline, then slice and filter per question with psort.

tools.name: Timeline Explorer
tools.desc: Eric Zimmerman's high-performance CSV timeline viewer with filters, bookmarks, and quick histogramning — the companion screen for Plaso/EvtxECmd CSV output.
tools.when: Load a super-timeline or artifact CSV and filter/hide columns interactively to answer 'what happened when' without SQL.
tools.install: Download from ericzimmerman.github.io (Chocolatey: choco install timelineexplorer)

tools.name: Hindsight
tools.desc: Obsidian Forensics' Chromium/Chrome/Edge history parser: decrypts login data, decodes History/SQLite, typed URLs, cookies, and downloads into a readable report with timestamp decoding.
tools.when: Extract reconstructable browser activity from the Chrome/Edge profile directory of a mounted image or live host in your own case.

tools.name: DB Browser for SQLite
tools.desc: Full-featured GUI for reading and querying SQLite databases — the manual backstop when you need to poke raw browser History/places.sqlite rows yourself.
tools.when: Directly inspect a browser database (history, cookies, bookmarks, cache index) when a parser misses a field or you want ad-hoc SQL.

tools.name: BrowserHistoryViewer
tools.desc: Foxton Forensics' free viewer for Chrome, Edge, Firefox, IE, and Safari history with keyword/date filtering, timezone-aware timestamps, and easy CSV export.
tools.when: Quick, clean table of browsing history with proper timestamp conversion for a report or super-timeline merge.
tools.install: Download the free installer from foxtonforensics.com

tools.name: BrowsingHistoryView
tools.desc: NirSoft utility that reads history from all major browsers (Firefox, Chrome, IE/Edge, Opera) into one table across all user profiles, local or from an external drive.
tools.when: One-pass aggregation of every browser profile's history on a live system or mounted image into a single viewable export.
tools.install: Download BrowsingHistoryView.zip from nirsoft.net and run the executable

tools.name: ChromeHistoryView
tools.desc: NirSoft tool focused purely on Chrome/Chromium-based history: reads the local History database and dumps entries to CSV/HTML with optional read from the live profile.
tools.when: Chrome-only deep dive when you want granular control and export options Eclipse the general aggregators.

tools.name: ChromeCacheView
tools.desc: NirSoft Chrome cache reader that lists files stored in the Cache/Cache_Data folders with URLs, sizes, and download times, plus option to copy recoverable cached files to a folder.
tools.when: Recover cached images/videos being staged by a live chrome user, or enumerate what content was browsed even after history deletion.

domains.name: System Hardening, Compliance & Secure Configuration
domains.tagline: Audit, harden, and prove it: system security scans, compliance benchmarks, config automation, and network-service lockdown for defenders securing their own systems.

tools.name: Lynis
tools.desc: Agentless security-auditing tool for Linux, BSD, and macOS that runs 200+ checks across the whole OS, scores everything, and ends with a hardening index, disclosure status, and actionable remediation hints.
tools.when: First pass on any UNIX-like host you own — run a baseline audit, apply the suggestions, then re-run to watch the hardening index climb.

tools.name: OpenSCAP
tools.desc: NIST-certified SCAP 1.2 toolkit: loads security content (XCCDF/OVAL data streams) and evaluates or remediates a system against specific profiles from the command line.
tools.when: Repeatable, scriptable compliance evaluations against scap-security-guide content — the profile kills long manual audit checklists.

tools.name: auditd (Linux Audit)
tools.desc: Linux Audit framework userspace (auditd, auditctl, ausearch) recording privileged actions, file access, and security-relevant events to an immutable log across reboots.
tools.when: Build the audit trail that CIS/STIG rules require before the auditor arrives; verify live rules with auditctl -l and query with ausearch.

tools.name: CIS Ubuntu Linux Benchmark
tools.desc: Free CIS configuration guide for Ubuntu with scored and unscored hardening entries that scanners and auditors measure against.
tools.when: Hand-harden an Ubuntu/Debian-family host to a known-good baseline when no CIS-CAT scan is available.

tools.name: audit2allow
tools.desc: Core utility from policycoreutils that converts SELinux AVC denials from the audit log into targeted allow or dontaudit policy modules.
tools.when: See denials in journal/AVC logs and turn the desired ones into a proper local policy module instead of disabling SELinux.

tools.name: SETools
tools.desc: SELinux Project's policy analysis suite: seinfo, sesearch, sediff, sedta, seinfoflow, and the apol GUI for querying rules and information-flow in the installed policy.
tools.when: Reverse-engineer or audit what your SELinux policy actually allows between domains before writing new modules.

tools.name: SELinux Reference Policy
tools.desc: The community-maintained reference policy source tree that generated distributions extend; the base for understanding and building custom SELinux policy.
tools.when: Contribute to or build custom policy from source, or learn the module structure behind your distro's policy.

tools.name: ufw
tools.desc: Ubuntu's uncomplicated frontend over iptables: allow/deny rules for ports and services in a few commands, with sane IPv6 defaults and a status view.
tools.when: Simple proven host firewall on Debian/Ubuntu; default-deny inbound, allow only what a service genuinely needs.

tools.name: firewalld
tools.desc: Dynamic firewall daemon with zone-based policy, a D-Bus service API, and runtime-vs-permanent config separation; the default firewall manager on RHEL/CentOS/Fedora/SUSE.
tools.when: Host firewalling on RHEL-family systems: open only the services a zone needs and test in runtime before committing permanently.

tools.name: nftables
tools.desc: Netfilter's modern packet-filtering framework with a single, scriptable ruleset language that replaces iptables chains; the base engine ufw/firewalld sit on.
tools.when: Write a compact, atomic, version-controllable firewall ruleset for servers that need more control than ufw offers.

tools.name: ssh-audit
tools.desc: Audits SSH server and client configuration end-to-end: grades every KEX, cipher, MAC, and host-key algorithm, flags weak or vulnerable combos, and ships per-distro hardening guides.
tools.when: Audit sshd before changing anything, apply the printed hardening guide, then re-scan until all-secure.

tools.name: Mozilla OpenSSH Configuration
tools.desc: Reference hardening guide for sshd_config with Modern/Intermediate/MFA profiles and concrete HostKey, KEX, cipher, and MAC lists for each OpenSSH generation.
tools.when: Write a known-good SSH baseline, then confirm the result with ssh-audit.

tools.name: HardeningKitty
tools.desc: PowerShell tool that retrieves the current Windows configuration, assesses it against CIS Benchmarks, Microsoft baselines, STIG, and BSI guides, and can apply settings itself (HailMary mode).
tools.when: Automated CIS/Microsoft-baseline audit of Windows endpoints with minimal setup and a CSV scorecard.

tools.name: LGPO.exe
tools.desc: Microsoft's local group-policy utility (shipped in the Security Compliance Toolkit) that imports/repairs registry.pol files and audits local policy settings.
tools.when: Apply a downloaded security baseline GPO backup to standalone or non-domain machines and verify local policy compliance.
tools.install: Download from Microsoft Security Compliance Toolkit (55319)

tools.name: CIS Microsoft Windows Benchmark
tools.desc: Free CIS configuration benchmark for Windows Server and client editions with scored and unscored hardening entries.
tools.when: Know exactly which GPO/registry settings an auditor will check, and harden by hand when scanner licensing is unavailable.

tools.name: Microsoft Security Baselines
tools.desc: Microsoft's recommended security configuration settings curated from the Windows Security Configuration Framework, shipped as GPO backups ready for LGPO import.
tools.when: Start from Microsoft's own baseline rather than writing group policy from scratch; the SCT download includes the LGPO import tooling.

tools.name: CIS Cisco IOS/XE Benchmark
tools.desc: CIS configuration benchmark covering Cisco IOS and IOS-XE: AAA, management-plane protection, SNMP, NTP, and platform-specific hardening entries.
tools.when: Hardening Cisco routers/switches to a defensible baseline before a compliance scan or external assessment.

tools.name: MikroTik RouterOS Security Guide
tools.desc: RouterOS documentation covering access hardening, service lockdown, firewall filter rules, brute-force protection, and secure defaults for MikroTik devices.
tools.when: Locking down MikroTik routers/switches you manage: follow the guide, restrict winbox/API, and add the recommended filter rules.

tools.name: Batfish
tools.desc: Network configuration analyzer that parses real device configs and answers questions about reachability, ACLs, and announced routes without touching the network.
tools.when: Validate that hardening changes (ACLs, filters, BGP policies) don't break intended reachability before pushing them.

tools.name: testssl.sh
tools.desc: Command-line TLS checker that tests every cipher, protocol, certificate, and vulnerability (Heartbleed, ROBOT, BEAST, and friends) against a live endpoint and grades the config.
tools.when: Audit the TLS posture of every service you expose before and after removing weak ciphers and protocols.

tools.name: sslscan
tools.desc: Lightweight TLS/SSL scanner that enumerates supported ciphers, protocols, and certificate details using OpenSSL, ideal for scripting into pipeline checks.
tools.when: Quick scriptable cipher/protocol inventory across many hosts when you only need raw output, not a full report.

tools.name: Trivy
tools.desc: Aqua's all-in-one scanner for OS packages, SBOMs, IaC misconfigs, and Kubernetes manifests/contexts; as a k8s subcommand it scans your cluster's deployed workload posture.
tools.when: Scan container images in CI and scan the live cluster (trivy k8s) for image and config findings in one tool.

tools.name: kube-linter
tools.desc: StackRox's Kubernetes YAML checker with 50+ built-in lint checks for security anti-patterns such as privileged containers, runAsRoot, and host-network exposure.
tools.when: Catch obvious YAML security anti-patterns in Git before charts reach the cluster.

tools.name: checkov
tools.desc: Bridgecrew/Prisma's policy-as-code scanner for Terraform, CloudFormation, Kubernetes, Helm, Dockerfile, and more, with 1000+ built-in checks including CIS Kubernetes.
tools.when: Unified IaC-and-manifest scanning across your whole infrastructure-as-code estate in CI.

tools.name: kubesec
tools.desc: Risk analysis tool that scores Kubernetes resources on 10+ security criteria (privileges, capabilities, runAsNonRoot) and returns a risk score with pointers.
tools.when: Ten-second risk score for a single manifest before deploy or during review.

tools.name: kube-bench
tools.desc: Aqua's CIS Kubernetes Benchmark checker: audits control plane, etcd, worker nodes, and RBAC against the official benchmark, runnable as a DaemonSet or binary.
tools.when: Prove your cluster meets the CIS Kubernetes benchmark and track remediation over time.

tools.name: kubescape
tools.desc: ARMO's Kubernetes posture scanner covering NSA/CISA hardening guidance, MITRE ATT&CK, and 50+ frameworks, plus admission-controller enforcement of failed controls.
tools.when: Full-framework posture scanning of a live cluster that goes beyond the CIS benchmark into runtime control enforcement.

tools.name: Istio
tools.desc: Service mesh providing mTLS between workloads, authorization policies (peer/request authentication), and encrypted east-west traffic for zero-trust workload identity.
tools.when: Enforce workload-to-workload mTLS and least-privilege authorization policies in a cluster that already runs a mesh.

tools.name: Cilium
tools.desc: eBPF-based CNI that enforces identity-aware L3-L7 NetworkPolicies without sidecars, including encrypted traffic and observability at scale.
tools.when: Enforce zero-trust network policy at the CNI layer when you don't want to adopt a full sidecar-based mesh.

tools.name: CIS Cloud Benchmarks
tools.desc: Free CIS benchmark sets for AWS, Azure, and GCP covering IAM, storage, networking, logging, and monitoring controls in each provider's console-accessible language.
tools.when: Know which cloud console/service settings an auditor checks, provider by provider.

tools.name: Prowler
tools.desc: Runs 1,000+ read-only checks across AWS, Azure, and GCP against CIS Benchmarks and 70+ compliance frameworks, with remediation guidance per finding.
tools.when: Default CIS/NIST posture review of any account you own; the coverage map and remediation pointers make fixing straightforward.

tools.name: Scout Suite
tools.desc: NCC Group's multi-cloud auditor pulls configuration from provider APIs and renders a browsable point-in-time HTML report of risk areas for AWS, Azure, and GCP.
tools.when: A clean visual HTML report of config risk in one account as a second opinion alongside Prowler.

tools.name: scap-security-guide
tools.desc: OpenSCAP's official security content: prebuilt SCAP data streams with profiles for CIS, DISA STIG, PCI-DSS, and HIPAA, plus bundled bash and Ansible remediation scripts that apply the fixes.
tools.when: Every compliance scan starts here — grab the data stream for your distro, feed it to openscap, review failures, then remediate with the generated scripts.

tools.name: CIS Benchmarks
tools.desc: Free, consensus-built configuration guides (PDF) for hundreds of OS, server, cloud, and application targets — the de-facto hardening standard auditors and scanners measure against.
tools.when: Hand-hardening to a known-good baseline with no scanner available; open the benchmark PDF for your platform and apply the entries manually.
tools.install: preinstalled (web) — free PDF download after registering a CIS account

tools.name: STIG Viewer
tools.desc: Browser database of the entire DISA Security Technical Implementation Guide set — rule-by-rule requirements with severity, CCI/NIST 800-53 mappings, and concrete fix text.
tools.when: Federal or DISA-style compliance: look up the exact configuration a STIG rule demands before touching config files.

tools.name: InSpec
tools.desc: Chef's open-source compliance language that turns CIS/STIG baselines into executable profile code (many public profiles exist) and runs them over local and remote systems.
tools.when: Version-controllable, reusable compliance profiles that you run in CI or on-demand without a commercial scanner.

tools.name: CIS-CAT Pro Assessor
tools.desc: Commercial CIS scanner (SecureSuite membership) that turns CIS Benchmarks into automated scans and compliance score/report output; a free CIS-CAT Lite covers a small set of select benchmarks.
tools.when: Audits that must document conformance to a specific CIS Benchmark version with vendor-supported mapping and reporting.

tools.name: ansible-hardening
tools.desc: dev-sec's battle-tested Ansible collection (devsec.hardening) that hardens OS, SSH, nginx, and MySQL/MariaDB at scale, aligned with the InSpec baselines the same team maintains.
tools.when: Apply the same hardening repeatedly to many hosts you manage — idempotent automation beats hand-editing configs on every box.

tools.name: systemd-analyze security
tools.desc: Built-in systemd command that scores each service unit 0-10 on exposure (PrivateTmp, NoNewPrivileges, ProtectSystem, and more) and lists the exact directives dragging the score down.
tools.when: Zero-install per-service hardening review on any systemd host — tighten the worst offenders on long-running units.

domains.name: Honeypots & Deception Technology
domains.tagline: Deception for defenders: fake services, canaries, honeynets, and tripwires placed inside your own estate to catch attackers early and learn their methods.

tools.name: T-Pot
tools.desc: Bundles 20+ honeypots (Cowrie, Dionaea, Conpot, Snare, Log4Pot, qeeqbox) behind one Docker Compose deploy, with the Elastic stack, Kibana dashboards, Suricata, and a live attack map from the German PSNC/Telekom Security team.
tools.when: Stand up a whole instrumented honeynet with dashboards in a weekend instead of wiring sensors together — the standard starting point for a lab or personal deception farm.

tools.name: HFish
tools.desc: Golang-based enterprise honeypot platform (HackLC) shipping SSH, Telnet, FTP, Redis, MySQL, VNC, HTTP(S), and deep-module decoys with a web dashboard, alerting, and distributed-cluster support.
tools.when: When you want a corporate-feel deception console with many built-in service decoys and low operational overhead beyond T-Pot's all-Docker weight.

tools.name: Modern Honey Network
tools.desc: Centralized server and web UI that deploys sensors (Cowrie, Dionaea, Conpot, Glastopf) over SSH and aggregates events via HPFeeds into Elasticsearch for viewing and searching.
tools.when: Fleet-manage many sensors from one Python-2-era control plane on an older distro — expect friction, as the project is effectively unmaintained and community forks carry the torch.

tools.name: HPFeeds
tools.desc: Honeynet Project's authenticated publish-subscribe protocol that ships JSON and binary honeypot events (dionaea.capture, cowrie.sessions, conpot.events) from sensors to collectors, MISP, ELK, and SIEMs.
tools.when: The glue beneath MHN, T-Pot, and community honeynets once you run several sensors: consume structured channels instead of scraping individual logs.

tools.name: honeynet-filebeat
tools.desc: Honeynet Project's custom Filebeat image for shipping T-Pot and honeypot JSON logs from sensors to a central Elasticsearch cluster without inventing your own transport.
tools.when: Batch-forward tpot/honeypot logs to your existing ELK or SIEM pipeline when you are not using an HPFeeds-based collector.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/honeynet/honeynet-filebeat && cd honeynet-filebeat && docker build -t honeynet-filebeat .

tools.name: Cowrie
tools.desc: Medium-to-high interaction SSH and Telnet honeypot that emulates a fake UNIX filesystem, logs every keystroke and transferred file, records replayable sessions, and can proxy to real boxes.
tools.when: The default SSH honeypot — let credential stuffers 'win' and replay exactly what a post-breach attacker does, from recon commands to malware staging.

tools.name: kippo
tools.desc: The original medium-interaction SSH honeypot whose fake 'ubuntu' root shell recorded replayable TTY sessions; Cowrie is its direct fork and successor.
tools.when: Never for fresh deployments — read its Python-2 source and session-replay utilities to understand how Cowrie's fake-shell design evolved.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/desaster/kippo && cd kippo && pip install -r requirements.txt

tools.name: Beelzebub
tools.desc: Low-code Go deception runtime (a T-Pot 24.04 component) that serves YAML-defined decoy SSH, HTTP, TCP, Telnet, and MCP services, with LLM backends generating convincing real-time replies.
tools.when: When static command emulation is too thin and you want adaptive high-interaction engagement plus prompt-injection traps, with an OpenAI or local Ollama key in hand.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/mariocandela/beelzebub && cd beelzebub && docker compose up -d

tools.name: sshesame
tools.desc: Go-based fake SSH server that lets any login through, never executes anything, and logs channels, requests, commands, and port-forward activity as JSON.
tools.when: A one-binary lab or public decoy when you want configurable, JSON-logged session telemetry without emulating a whole filesystem.

tools.name: ssh-honeypot
tools.desc: C-based fake sshd (droberson) that accepts connections and logs IP, username, and password plus HASSH-fingerprints the SSH client — without granting a shell.
tools.when: When you care only about brute-force credential and client-fingerprint telemetry with a tiny footprint, not full shell-level interaction.
tools.install: apt install libssh-dev libjson-c-dev libpcap-dev libssl-dev && make

tools.name: Dionaea
tools.desc: Nepenthes-successor low-interaction honeypot emulating SMB, FTP, HTTP, MSSQL, MySQL, SIP, UPnP, and more; embeds Python, uses libemu to detect captured shellcode, and stashes malware binaries.
tools.when: Attract self-spreading worms and malware ripping over SMB/FTP/MS-RPC and capture their payloads, complementing a credential-focused SSH honeypot.

tools.name: HoneyPy
tools.desc: Python low-to-medium interaction honeypot (fooSpider/Twisted) with plugins for SMTP, FTP, POP3, IMAP, SSH, Telnet, Elasticsearch, and more, plus Twitter and HoneyDB loggers (archived 2024).
tools.when: When you want one lightweight daemon with pluggable protocol emulation and HoneyDB/Redis-backed logging — treat it as legacy but stable.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/foospidy/HoneyPy && cd HoneyPy && pip install -r requirements.txt && python Honey.py -c etc/honeypy.cfg

tools.name: Snare + TANNER
tools.desc: Glastopf's successor: SNARE clones real web pages into sensor traps and forwards every request to TANNER, a central classification service that evaluates the attack and decides the reply.
tools.when: Realistic web deception with a central 'brain': point several SNARE clones at one TANNER to store, classify, and steer web-application attack responses.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/mushorg/snare && cd snare && pip3 install -r requirements.txt && python3 setup.py install

tools.name: Glastopf
tools.desc: Honeynet Project's original web-application honeypot emulating vulnerability types (LFI/RFI/SQLi) with a built-in PHP sandbox and Google dork luring; archived, with maintainers pointing to SNARE/TANNER.
tools.when: Historical study only: inspect the PHP-sandbox emulation and dork-collection design to learn how modern web honeypots behave — do not deploy fresh.

tools.name: glutton
tools.desc: Honeynet Project's generic low-interaction honeypot written in Go that proxies connections through PIPELINE-like protocol emulation and can chain to real services for high-interaction depth.
tools.when: When you want a protocol-agnostic sensor that buffers, parses, and replays many TCP service interactions and can fail over into a real honeypot backend.

tools.name: qeeqbox honeypots
tools.desc: 30 low-to-high interaction honeypots in one PyPI package: dhcp, dns, elastic, ftp, http(s), imap, ldap, mssql, mysql, ntp, pop3, postgres, rdp, redis, sip, smb, smtp, snmp, socks5, ssh, telnet, vnc.
tools.when: Spin up many protocol decoys in seconds with one pip install and simple --setup flags, or embed sensors inside T-Pot where it ships as a component.

tools.name: honeyd
tools.desc: Classic low-interaction daemon (Niels Provos) that fabricates thousands of virtual hosts with spoofed OS personalities and configurable fake TCP/UDP services on unused IP space.
tools.when: Instrument a whole dark/empty subnet rather than a single box — legacy research tooling (last original release 2007) built from the hobbyist-maintained fork.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/cowrie/honeyd && cd honeyd && mkdir build && cd build && cmake .. && sudo make install

tools.name: Conpot
tools.desc: Honeynet Project's ICS/SCADA honeypot emulating Modbus, S7, BACnet, EtherNet/IP, IEC-104, SNMP, and HTTP HMI stacks with tunable response delays to look like a real industrial process.
tools.when: Detect and profile OT/SCADA targeting — plant a fake PLC/HMI on your network before adversaries reach real controllers.

tools.name: RIoTPot
tools.desc: Honeynet Project's IoT/OT hybrid proxy honeypot that fronts emulated SSH, Telnet, HTTP, Modbus, MQTT, and CoAP services and can route interactions to any backend honeypot via a web UI.
tools.when: When your focus is IoT/OT protocol coverage (MQTT, CoAP, Modbus) and you want a Honeynet-endorsed plugin-architected emulator — expect a young, source-built project.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/honeynet/riotpot && cd riotpot && make

tools.name: DICOMHawk
tools.desc: Honeynet Project's DICOM (medical imaging) honeypot that detects and logs unauthorized access attempts against radiology PACS/DICOM endpoints that attackers increasingly probe.
tools.when: Deploy where healthcare DICOM devices must not be reached directly — catch unauthorized modality/PACS scans in medical environments.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/honeynet/DICOMHawk && cd DICOMHawk && pip install -r requirements.txt

tools.name: sweetcam
tools.desc: Honeynet Project's IP-camera honeypot: lures attackers with a fake webcam admin stream and logs their interactions, mirroring the flood of IoT camera scanning.
tools.when: When you want decoys that mimic the most-scanned IoT device category on your network to catch and log automated camera/IP-cam exploitation.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/honeynet/sweetcam && cd sweetcam && python -m http.server 8080

tools.name: Mailoney
tools.desc: Modern low-interaction SMTP honeypot (2.x rewrite) that simulates a vulnerable mail server, captures auth attempts and credentials, and stores sessions in PostgreSQL; ships AS open-relay and Postfix-cred modules.
tools.when: Detect spam, credential-harvesting, and open-relay abuse on port 25 while keeping structured DB logs you can feed your SIEM.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/phin3has/mailoney && cd mailoney && docker compose up -d

tools.name: mailhon
tools.desc: Minimalistic Python3 SMTP honeypot built on aiosmtpd that emulates an open relay and writes every interaction as JSON to a log file.
tools.when: When you want a tiny, dependency-light open-relay decoy that logs JSON for quick parsing without a database layer.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/CMSecurity/mailhon && cd mailhon && pip3 install -r requirements.txt && python3 main.py

tools.name: hermes
tools.desc: Avast's SMTP honeypot built on the Salmon mail server with SMTP AUTH support, exim4 integration, MQTT telemetry, and configurable relay policy to sieve real spam flows.
tools.when: When you need a fuller-featured SMTP sink with AUTH and relay controls, saving attachments and eml files for analysis, over the simplest cred-capturing daemons.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/avast/hermes && cd hermes && docker build -t hermes . && docker run -p 25:25 hermes

tools.name: dns-honeypot
tools.desc: Simple low-interaction DNS honeypot in Python/Twisted that answers queries on 53/5353 and logs every lookup, surfacing scan and exfil-style DNS traffic.
tools.when: A cheap tripwire for DNS probing and suspicious query patterns on a segment where only your resolver should be queried.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/0xNslabs/dns-honeypot && cd dns-honeypot && pip install twisted && python3 dns.py --host 0.0.0.0 --port 53

tools.name: FakeDns
tools.desc: Regular-expression based Python DNS server that resolves against a config or proxies unmatched queries upstream; the classic for DNS-tunneling and rebinding deception during engagements.
tools.when: When you want regex-ruled DNS answers (rebinding, round-robin) that log every query, ideal for malware C2/DNS-exfil detection labs.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/Crypt0s/FakeDns && cd FakeDns && ./fakedns.py -c dns.conf.example -i 10.0.0.1

tools.name: Canarytokens
tools.desc: Thinkst's free hosted (or self-hosted Docker) tripwire factory generating DNS, URL, document (PDF/Word), AWS-key, QR-code, and Slack tokens that alert by email/webhook the instant someone touches them.
tools.when: A full honeypot is overkill: sprinkle fake DNS names, URLs, or documents across AD, share drives, and public infra for cheap, near-instant detection of unauthorized access.
tools.install: preinstalled (canarytokens.org) - self-host: git clone https://github.com/thinkst/canarytokens-docker && docker compose up

tools.name: OpenCanary
tools.desc: Thinkst's open-source multi-protocol honeypot daemon (SSH, telnet, HTTP, FTP, SNMP, SMB, RDP, MySQL, ...) that fires syslog, email, Slack, and webhook alerts on any probe.
tools.when: Drop a near-zero-footprint daemon onto a jump host, file server, or DMZ and get alerting on unexpected interaction across ~10 protocols at once.

tools.name: ochi
tools.desc: Honeynet Project's Go-based network visualization showing co-occuring attack ports, source ASNs, and services across your honeypot logs in an interactive graph.
tools.when: Understand, present, and spot patterns in attacker traffic after the honeypots have run — the visualization Honeynet themselves use.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/honeynet/ochi && cd ochi && go build && ./ochi

tools.name: GreedyBear
tools.desc: Threat-intel platform for T-Pot deployments that ingests honeypot events via Elasticsearch, flags malicious IPs, maintains feeds, and publishes T-Pot-derived IOCs to ThreatFox.
tools.when: Turn your T-Pot farm's captures into a continuous IOC feed for your SIEM or ThreatFox instead of leaving payloads and IPs stuck in logs.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/GreedyBear-Project/GreedyBear && cd GreedyBear && docker compose up

tools.name: Log4Pot
tools.desc: Low-interaction honeypot for the Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) family: detects exploitation in request lines and headers, deobfuscates JNDI payloads, and recursively downloads exploit payloads.
tools.when: Catch and study Log4j/Log4Shell exploitation attempts on ports where vulnerable Java apps might sit, and collect the payloads attackers drop.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/thomaspatzke/Log4Pot && cd Log4Pot && pip install -r requirements.txt && python log4pot.py @log4pot.conf

tools.name: minecraft-log4j-honeypot
tools.desc: Go honeypot that runs a fake Minecraft server waiting to be hit by Log4Shell exploit variants targeting the game, saving captured payload classes to disk.
tools.when: Monitor for Log4j scanning aimed at game servers and other odd ports where naive exploit attempts still land.

tools.name: honeyscanner
tools.desc: Honeynet Project's vulnerability analyzer that automatically attacks a given honeypot to determine whether it is vulnerable to specific attack families (DDoS, sploit, fuzz, ssh).
tools.when: QA your own honeypots before exposing them: prove a decoy is safe to face the internet and characterize what it can and cannot absorb.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/honeynet/honeyscanner && cd honeyscanner && pipenv install && pipenv shell

tools.name: checkpot
tools.desc: Honeynet Project's Honeypot Checker (GSoC 2018): validates honeypot containers and checks whether deployed honeypots detect, replay, and act correctly on attacks.
tools.when: Regression-test a fleet of honeypot containers after upgrading or building new sensors — the scouting companion to honeyscanner's vuln assessment.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/honeynet/checkpot && cd checkpot && docker build -t checkpot . && docker run checkpot --help

domains.name: Malware Analysis & Reverse Engineering
domains.tagline: Static and dynamic analysis of samples you recovered — honeypot catches, quarantined files, lab targets, and public samples — to extract IOCs and understand behavior. Analyze, don't distribute.

tools.name: CAPE (CAPEv2)
tools.desc: The actively maintained Cuckoo successor: detonates a sample in an isolated Windows VM, instruments behavior, auto-unpacks, and extracts ransomware/botnet config via YARA-driven debugger hooks.
tools.when: Default detonation engine for any sample you regained — drop it in the lab and read the process/network/file report plus the unpacked payload it hands you.
tools.install: sudo bash cape2.sh all (from the CAPEv2 installer on Ubuntu 24.04 + Windows 10/11 guest)

tools.name: Cuckoo Sandbox
tools.desc: The original open-source automated-analysis sandbox and architectural ancestor of CAPE — repository archived April 2021 and unmaintained since, with a stalled community rewrite.
tools.when: Reading old published research or learning the plugin/API/signature model CAPE inherits — treat it as a museum reference, not a new deployment.

tools.name: DRAKVUF
tools.desc: Agentless malware analysis via Xen hypervisor introspection: watches a sample's execution from outside the guest using hardware virtualization, so no in-guest hooks can be detected or bypassed.
tools.when: Samples that fight in-VM agents or sandboxes — detonate in a Xen guest and let DRAKVUF capture syscalls, memory events, and File/Registry activity it cannot see.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/CERT-Polska/drakvuf && make (host with Xen 4.13+ installed)

tools.name: MalwareBazaar
tools.desc: abuse.ch's free, community-fed malware sample repository: search public samples by hash, family, tag, or YARA rule, download with full metadata, and get instant triage from its detection report.
tools.when: Verify a hash and pull context or a clean copy of a public sample to study — never upload anything sensitive, the feed is public by design.

tools.name: Hybrid Analysis
tools.desc: CrowdStrike Falcon Sandbox's free-tier cloud detonation service returning behavioral reports with process activity, dropped files, and network indicators for any submitted file.
tools.when: A zero-infrastructure second opinion on a public sample — remember submission exposes the file, so never upload anything you cannot share.
tools.install: preinstalled (web, free account; API keys after vetting)

tools.name: Joe Sandbox
tools.desc: Commercial multi-OS detonation platform (Windows, macOS, Android, documents) with deep behavior analysis, config extraction for common malware families, and easy exportable reports.
tools.when: A polished, repeatable cloud detonation workflow when you want evasive-analysis depth and clean reporting on a public sample or one you own.
tools.install: preinstalled (web, free analysis tier after registration)

tools.name: Any.Run
tools.desc: Interactive cloud sandbox with a live, controllable in-browser desktop view of the detonated environment — free tier covers public interactive analysis sessions.
tools.when: Watch the sample run in real time and click around the fake desktop (screenshots, process trees, network) — the free tier is ideal for quick public triage.

tools.name: YARA
tools.desc: Pattern-matching language for describing and classifying malware (byte strings, regexes, hex wildcards, PE conditionals) — the signature format AV engines and sandboxes consume. The C engine is in maintenance; the YARA-X Rust rewrite is the evolving successor.
tools.when: Fingerprint a sample and hunt the same family across your recovered-file collection; community rules (yara-forge, Malpedia) give instant triage hits.

tools.name: Loki
tools.desc: Neo23x0's free IOC scanner: YARA rule matches, hash blacklists, filename/path regexes, and registry indicators checked across a running system to flag known malware from a rules directory.
tools.when: Post-incident sweep of your own analysis box, honeypot host, or a mounted recovered drive for known-bad indicators before deep analysis begins.

tools.name: yaraScanner
tools.desc: Single-file Python YARA-based pattern scanner that can auto-fetch rules (e.g. Neo23x0's set), scan individual files or directories, and emit HTML or email reports.
tools.when: A lightweight scheduled or one-shot scan of a sample folder with auto-updated public rules, without standing up a full AV stack.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/iomoath/yara-scanner && pip3 install yara-python

tools.name: Detect-It-Easy (DIE)
tools.desc: Cross-platform signature + heuristic detector (GUI 'die', console 'diec') that identifies compilers, packers, protectors, and format anomalies across PE, ELF, Mach-O and more.
tools.when: Seconds-long first pass on any sample: the packer/protector verdict tells you whether unpacking is needed before pulling in a reversing suite.
tools.install: Download the die/diec release from GitHub (or 'choco install die' on Windows)

tools.name: PEiD
tools.desc: The classic Windows packer/compiler detector (last updated 2011, effectively dead) whose 600-entry signature database still catches legacy packers most modern tools no longer bother flagging.
tools.when: Historical or retro samples, or a second opinion on an old packer — expect it to miss anything post-2011 and keep DIE as the modern pass.
tools.install: Download the 0.95 release ZIP and run PEiD.exe against the sample

tools.name: FLOSS
tools.desc: Mandiant's FLARE Obfuscated String Solver: statically extracts plaintext strings AND decodes/deobfuscates stack strings and decrypted-in-memory strings so you see what the sample meant to hide.
tools.when: Grab URLs, domains, embedded payloads, and configuration from an unpacked sample without running it — run it right after unpacking.

tools.name: strings
tools.desc: GNU binutils classic that extracts printable ASCII/Unicode sequences from any file — the zero-setup raw look at what the binary references.
tools.when: Rapid eyeball pass for suspicious URLs, registry paths, and commands before bringing in smarter extraction tools.

tools.name: Ghidra
tools.desc: NSA's free reverse-engineering suite: interactive disassembler plus a decompiler emitting C-like pseudocode, with a Python API for automating config extraction and batch jobs.
tools.when: Primary static tool for a fully-understood unpacked payload — its decompiler reads close to source, and capa/floss integrate directly with its analysis.
tools.install: Download the current release zip from GitHub, unzip, and run ./ghidraRun

tools.name: radare2
tools.desc: Command-line reverse-engineering framework with analyzers, disassemblers, ESIL emulation, and r2pipe scripting for headless one-terminal analysis of ELF/PE/Mach-O and shellcode.
tools.when: Scripted or headless reversing: batch-analyze sample sets, grep crypto constants, or automate unpacking without opening a GUI.

tools.name: Cutter
tools.desc: Qt GUI front-end over the rizin engine (radare2's fork) offering point-and-click disassembly, patching, graph views, and annotation plus a Ghidra decompiler integration plugin.
tools.when: Mouse-driven visual exploration and annotation of a sample's functions and strings when the terminal workflow is not your preference.

tools.name: Process Hacker / System Informer
tools.desc: Powerful Windows process viewer (continued as System Informer after Process Hacker's repo went read-only) showing full process trees, handles, threads, memory maps, and network connections.
tools.when: Watch a detonating sample create/destroy processes, inject into others, and open network handles — the daily driver triage view in your analysis VM.
tools.install: Download the System Informer release installer from winsiderss/systeminformer

tools.name: Process Monitor
tools.desc: Microsoft Sysinternals tool that records real-time file system, registry, process/thread, and DLL activity for the whole system with non-destructive filtering, process trees, and boot logging.
tools.when: Capture exactly what a detonating sample touches — files written, keys created, processes spawned — and save the trace as evidence.

tools.name: API Monitor
tools.desc: rohitab's free tool that intercepts and logs Win32/.NET API calls of a target process, optionally before it starts, showing return values and parameters for each invocation.
tools.when: Deep-dive into the exact API call sequence and parameters a decoding/decrypting routine issues while it runs in your lab VM.
tools.install: Download from the rohitab.com site and run api_monitor_x64+x86 as administrator

tools.name: x64dbg
tools.desc: Open-source user-mode Windows debugger (x32dbg + x64dbg in one package) with an IDA-like interface, API breakpoints, memory/register views, and a scriptable plugin engine — the standard for Windows malware.
tools.when: Step through an unpacked Windows sample inside FLARE VM: break on suspicious API calls, dump decrypted buffers, and unwind anti-analysis logic.
tools.install: Download the latest snapshot release and run x96dbg.exe

tools.name: dnSpy / dnSpyEx
tools.desc: .NET assembly debugger and editor that decompiles C# on open and lets you set breakpoints and edit IL in place — the original is archived, the dnSpyEx fork is the maintained successor.
tools.when: Reversing .NET loaders, droppers, and stealer families where the managed code is the entire payload — read the decompiled source as you debug.
tools.install: Download the latest dnSpyEx release ZIP from GitHub

tools.name: Dependency Walker
tools.desc: The classic Windows DLL dependency scanner (last release 2018, effectively legacy) that graphs which modules a PE imports and what each function resolves to.
tools.when: OLD but classic for spotting import tampering, missing DLLs, or exotic ordinals in a sample before analysis — keep 64-bit quirks in mind.
tools.install: Download the release ZIP from dependencywalker.com and run depends.exe

tools.name: INetSim
tools.desc: Fake TCP/UDP service suite emulating HTTP(S), SMTP, DNS, IRC, and dozens of protocols so a sample thinks C2 is live — all traffic lands in an inetsim report instead of reaching the Internet.
tools.when: Dangerous-sounding C2 domains between you and the real world: point the analysis VM's DNS at INetSim and let the malware talk to ghosts you control.
tools.install: sudo apt install inetsim && sudo inetsim

tools.name: FakeNet-NG
tools.desc: Mandiant FLARE's lightweight cross-platform network simulation tool capturing and responding to HTTP, DNS, TLS, and other protocols with a simple config and easy logging.
tools.when: Quick per-host fake networking in a Windows analysis VM without standing up a full INetSim deployment.

tools.name: UPX
tools.desc: The ubiquitous executable packer whose own -d switch cleanly decompresses UPX-packed samples in seconds — and whose unpacking stub reveals the pattern most custom packers imitate.
